title: Fraunhofer stabilises aluminium anodes for lithium-ion batteries - electrive.com
content:
The Fraunhofer IPA and the University of Stuttgart have developed a new cell and electrode technology for aluminum anodes. It is intended to make the previously problematic volume changes during charging and discharging manageable, thereby enabling the use of aluminum as an anode material for practical battery applications.
The aluminum foil is active material and current collector.
Image: Fraunhofer IPA/Rainer Bez
Aluminium has long been considered a potential replacement for graphite or silicon in lithium-ion batteries. The material is relatively inexpensive, widely available, and offers high capacities. However, in practice, this approach has so far failed due to mechanical stress on the electrode: during charging and discharging, aluminium undergoes volume changes that can lead to cracks, pores, and ultimately pulverisation of the electrode material. The result is capacity loss and a limited lifespan.
The Fraunhofer Institute for Manufacturing Engineering and Automation IPA, together with the Institute for Photovoltaics at the University of Stuttgart, has now developed and patented a cell and electrode technology that addresses these ageing processes. According to the researchers, the approach stabilises the materials during operation and maintains electrical contact within the electrode over many charge and discharge cycles.
“We are making a battery technology that has been known for a long time but has been difficult to control practically usable,” said Kai Peter Birke, Scientific Director for Battery and Hydrogen Systems and Storage at Fraunhofer IPA, in a German-language press release.
The approach completely eliminates graphite and silicon from the anode. This could not only reduce the demand for graphite, which is considered a critical raw material for the European battery industry; it would also eliminate the problems associated with significant volume changes in highly silicon-based anodes. Another difference lies in the structure of the electrode. The starting material is a commercially available alloyed aluminium foil, which serves as both the active material and the current collector. This eliminates the need for the copper foil typically used in conventional anodes.
Aluminium foil serves as active material and current collector
A separate coating process, used to apply the active material to the current collector, is also eliminated. This is expected to reduce both process costs and energy consumption during electrode manufacturing. The researchers cite lithium manganese oxide (LMO) as a possible cathode. In combination with the aluminium anode, a competitive energy density could be achieved. At the same time, the cell chemistry would be phosphate-free and could thus represent a cost-effective alternative to lithium iron phosphate cells.
The aluminium anode could also be combined with electrolyte solvents with a high flash point. Together with a fluorine-free LMO cathode, Fraunhofer states that a completely fluorine- and thus PFAS-free cell structure would even be possible. This would also avoid the risk of hydrogen fluoride formation in the event of a battery fire.
Fraunhofer sees initial applications primarily in areas where safety, robustness, and compact installation space are particularly important. These include, among others, air freight applications, tracking systems for transport containers, and specialised medical devices.
For later industrial use, it is relevant that the cell chemistry could be produced on existing production facilities. According to the institute, a complete rebuild of the manufacturing infrastructure would therefore not be necessary. Several prototypes have already been built and are currently being tested at the Fraunhofer IPA’s Centre for Digitalised Battery Cell Production. The institute has not yet provided details on specific cycle numbers, gravimetric or volumetric energy density in its current announcement.
In parallel, Fraunhofer is working on further approaches to improve battery cells at the material and architecture levels. In September, the
Fraunhofer ISE
presented a cell architecture with significantly thicker electrodes. By reducing the proportion of current collectors, the energy density could be increased by ten to 15 per cent, depending on the battery type and design. This approach is still at the research stage and must first prove its industrial scalability.

title: ProLogium and Rimac target 2028 for solid-state battery vehicle tests - electrive.com
content:
ProLogium and Rimac Technology are continuing to move forward with their next-gen battery collaboration. At the Paris Motor Show, the partners are initially showcasing a pack mockup; functional hardware and a complete battery pack are expected to follow in 2027, with the first vehicle tests planned for 2028.
The battery pack is still a mockup; the hardware is expected to follow in 2027.
Image: ProLogium
In Paris, the two companies have unveiled a concept mock-up of the planned battery pack for the first time. The next step of development is a functional battery segment, which will be used to test thermal management, cell integration and pack architecture, among other aspects.
The focus is on a cell-to-pack architecture for pouch cells. Rimac Technology describes it as a scalable integration solution for solid-state pouch cells. ProLogium contributes its cell technology, while Rimac handles system development and integration.
However, this is explicitly not yet about a near-series battery pack. The companies are pursuing a multi-stage development path: following the current mock-up, a functional battery segment will be developed first, then a fully functional battery pack, and finally integration into a vehicle.
The technical core of the collaboration lies at the system level. High energy densities at the cell level cannot automatically translate into a lighter or more compact vehicle battery system. Only the pack design, cooling, mechanical integration and safety concept determine which advantages actually benefit the vehicle.
Thermal management and cell integration in focus
Rimac is therefore investigating several integration variants in parallel. These include different approaches to thermal management, handling cell swelling, mechanical cell integration and system design. Some concepts aim primarily at maximum energy density and reduced installation space or weight, while others focus more on high performance. According to Rimac, the goal is to develop the battery from the vehicle perspective: components and functions should be consolidated, complexity and weight reduced, while simultaneously maintaining high levels of charging power and performance output.
If the approach proves successful at the vehicle level, manufacturers could utilise the weight advantages in various ways. Possible options include more energy – and thus greater range – with the same battery weight, a smaller and lighter battery pack with the same range, or hybrid solutions combining both approaches.
ProLogium CEO Vincent Yang emphasises that the step from the cell lab to the vehicle goes far beyond good cell performance. Only integration into a battery pack tailored to thermal, architectural and mechanical requirements makes the technology usable for electric vehicles.
Functional segment in 2027, road tests in 2028
There is already a timeline for the further development steps. According to Rimac Technology, the functional battery segment currently under development will be showcased at CES 2027. A fully functional battery pack is then planned for the second half of 2027.
In the second half of 2028, vehicle tests on public roads are finally set to begin. This would gradually expand the validation of individual integration concepts up to full-scale vehicle deployment. ProLogium itself refers to its latest cell generation as the “Superfluidized Inorganic Next-Generation Lithium Ceramic Battery”. The technology is said to combine properties of solid-state and liquid electrolyte concepts while remaining industrially scalable.
The fact that ProLogium’s cell technology is already generating interest from major manufacturers is also evident from its collaboration with Mercedes-Benz. Since September 2026, Mercedes has been testing ProLogium’s Gen4 cells in its own and external testing facilities for electrical, thermal and safety-relevant properties. A decision on series production has not yet been made.
For the European supply chain, ProLogium’s expansion in France is also relevant. A gigafactory is currently under construction in the French city of
, with the first phase designed for an annual production capacity of 4 GWh. This capacity is to be gradually increased by 2030. In the long term, the site is planned to reach up to 44 GWh per year.
As early as 2024, ProLogium also opened a
research and development centre in Paris-Saclay
. This is intended to more closely link development and future production in France.
Rimac Technology is also expanding its role as a battery system supplier. For BMW, the Croatian company is developing and producing a new
high-voltage storage system for the revised i7
. There, Rimac combines cylindrical Gen6 cells in the 4695 format with a Gen5 module design; the finished battery systems are produced in Croatia and delivered to BMW’s Dingolfing plant.

title: Robot Dogs, Mobile Chargers Shown at Detroit Test Site
content:
Battery Applications
Charging
Design & Manufacturing
At the Detroit Smart Parking Lab, Boston Dynamics, Ion Dynamics Energy, and Tareen AI showed how battery innovation is reshaping mobility, cleaning, and robotics.
October 13, 2026
3 Min Read
Spot, Boston Dynamics four-legged "agile mobile robot," at Detroit's Smart Parking Lab on October 12, 2026
M. Anderson / Battery Technology
At a Glance
Ion Dynamics Energy's FlashBot delivers mobile DC fast and Level 2 EV charging without fixed infrastructure costs.
Tareen AI supplies and services autonomous cleaning robots with full U.S.-based installation and support.
Boston Dynamics' Spot is being tested citywide in Detroit for inspections, security patrols, and litter pickup.
Detroit's push to become a testing ground for next-generation mobility technology was on full view October 12 at the
Detroit Smart Parking Lab
(DSPL), held in conjunction with
The Battery Show North America
. Operating out of the ground floor of the Assembly Garage parking structure, DSPL gives technology developers a real-world setting to test parking-related mobility, logistics, and EV charging solutions. The initiative, backed by Bedrock Detroit, the Michigan Economic Development Corporation, and Ford Motor Company, showcased three battery-powered devices that illustrate how far mobile power and robotics have progressed.
Ion Dynamics Energy: Mobile charging without the infrastructure
As a grant recipient in DSPL's autonomous movement initiative,
Ion Dynamics Energy
brought its FlashBot to the Assembly Garage to demonstrate a battery-integrated, self-driving charging solution capable of both DC fast charging and AC Level 2 service. The pilot highlighted a key advantage: deploying DC fast-charging capability without the cost and delay of fixed charging infrastructure.
Related:
Public-Private Collaboration Advances Nuclear Power for Space Exploration
Iondynamics Energy's Flashbot at the Smart Parking Lab event. Credit: M. Anderson / Battery Technology
Each FlashBot runs on a 104 kWh battery and, when paired with the company's FlashHub intelligent power-conversion gateway, can also supply clean, lower-cost power for events of any scale. Ion Dynamics says a facility can have charging live in as little as two hours, bypassing the design, permitting, and construction timelines typical of permanent installations. Output specs include60 kW DC fast charging, or Level 2 service at 7 kW across as many as 12 vehicles per FlashBot-and-FlashHub pairing. The DSPL pilot has already led to additional partnerships, including support for a public transit autonomous shuttle program in Detroit, where FlashBot handles intraday DC fast-charging needs.
Tareen AI: Autonomous cleaning, backed by local service
Tareen AI
brought a different angle to autonomous robotics, showcasing commercial and industrial cleaning robots designed to help facilities shift from manual cleaning routines to autonomous workflows. The company differentiates itself through its service model: rather than relying on overseas manufacturing support, Tareen AI supplies, installs, and services its robots directly, offering U.S.-based installation, training, maintenance, and repair.
Boston Dynamics: Spot shows its senses
Boston Dynamics
rounded out the display with Spot, its four-legged "agile mobile robot." Senior consultant Joe Tenbusch demonstrated Spot's 365-degree vision and thermal-imaging capabilities on a tablet, along with the robot's docking station for recharging. Tenbusch noted that most users opt for battery swapping to keep Spot running efficiently, since the battery sits in an easily accessible compartment on the robot's underside — a design that has defined Spot since its commercial debut, when it was first offered through an early-adopter leasing program .dongascience.com
Related:
Which Battery Company Will Supply Which Carmaker in 2026?
The DSPL appearance comes as Spot's footprint in Detroit expands well beyond the lab. Bedrock Detroit and Boston Dynamics have been quietly testing Spot units downtown for the past six to eight months, with public visibility starting as early as the following week. Last week at a press conference covered by FOX 2 News, Kevin Mull, Bedrock's senior director for the Office of Urban Strategy,
described the robots as an "autonomous mobile sensing platform"
suited to tasks that are tedious, dangerous, or dirty — from building inspections and parking-garage security patrols to package handling and litter pickup, including trash as small as a cigarette butt. Mull emphasized that moving robots from wide-open warehouse settings into human-occupied spaces demands far greater navigational sophistication — climbing stairs, opening doors, and operating safely around people.
Related:
Battery Swapping Products Drive Innovation in Construction
Taken together, the three technologies on display at DSPL — mobile charging, autonomous cleaning, and sensing robotics — reflect a common thread: battery systems are no longer just powering devices, they're enabling entirely new categories of mobile, on-demand service in spaces built for people.

title: DHL Connects New Global Healthcare Supply Chains
content:
DHL Connects New Global Healthcare Supply Chains
Prioritise Us
on Google
DHL is expanding its healthcare logistics capabilities with new trade corridors. Credit: DHL
DHL is expanding its cold chain network, driving greater control and reliability, explains Henk Venema, Global Head of Air Freight at DHL Global Forwarding
In a market where reliability and access are key to operations, DHL Global Forwarding is
expanding its cold chain network
The introduction of six new corridors will result in greater connectivity between Europe, North America and Asia.
According to DHL, this will lead to a strengthened connectivity between supply chains, resulting in more reliability, consistency and risk mitigation.
Supply chain expansion
Pharmaceutical supply chains
are a complex system, needing timely distribution and tightly controlled logistics at all times. Transported around the world, often to save lives, the products within these networks are critical.
To make distribution easier, DHL Global Forwarding has announced the expansion of its DHL Health Logistics Cold Chain Network. The air and ocean freight specialist has revealed that six new Life Sciences & Healthcare (LSH) air corridors will come into operation.
The air corridors will connect Europe and North America with Asia, giving greater access to key healthcare and pharmaceutical hubs. By doing this, it is ensuring critical products can travel directly across continents, reaching patients at the other end with fewer handoffs and less risk.
The new corridors are:
Liège-Shanghai
Brussels-Shanghai
Brussels-Singapore
Cincinnati-Singapore
Cincinnati-Tokyo Narita
Cincinnati-Seoul Incheon
“These new corridors further expand our Cold Chain Network into strategically important healthcare markets across Asia,” explains Henk Venema, Global Head of Air Freight, DHL Global Forwarding.
“They respond to customer demand for reliable connectivity between major healthcare markets while giving us greater control over critical quality parameters throughout the transportation process. This enables our customers to move critical healthcare products with greater confidence and reliability.”
In recent years, DHL has invested heavily in its healthcare network, having committed to an investment of €500m (US$559m) in Asia Pacific by 2030. It has also announced it will be investing more than €400m (US$447.8m) across
Central and Eastern Europe
The new corridors are evidence of its investments, as they are strengthening connectivity across its growing temperature-controlled healthcare logistics network. This includes major pharmaceutical manufacturing, research and distribution hubs.
DHL is anticipating improved routing flexibility, more access to temperature-controlled capacity and greater consistency in performance across key markets. This maintains product integrity and
reduces supply chain risk
Henk Venema, Global Head of Air Freight, DHL Global Forwarding
These new corridors further expand our Cold Chain Network into strategically important healthcare markets across Asia.
Henk Venema, Global Head of Air Freight, DHL Global Forwarding
Specialist network
The corridors are being supported through DHL’s dedicated aircraft network, meaning that shipments stay within the DHL network. Due to this, there are less handovers where issues could arise and DHL has more control over its cargo. As a result, it is demonstrating
consistency and reliability
while handling temperature-sensitive products.
DHL is expanding its Cold Chain Network, having also launched its Brussels-Cincinnati air corridor in early 2026. Within the network, there are a range of dedicated healthcare corridors, specialised operational processes and validated handling procedures.
Temperature-controlled shipments are supported within this network, relying on thermal-blanket solutions and limited exposure to outside temperatures.
Exposure risk is high during handling and transfer, which is why handovers are limited and processes are in place to ensure it operates smoothly.
DHL fact sheet
Six new dedicated Life Sciences & Healthcare (LSH) air corridors are being introduced
DHL deploys Boeing 777 freighter aircraft on its routes
The network includes dedicated 2-8° Celsius and 15-25° Celsius storage and handling areas
DHL Global Forwarding has moved more than 2.1 million air freight tons
More than 167,000 customers are supported by DHL Global Forwarding every day
Increasing competition
The aim of this expanded network is to ensure the safe transportation and distribution of pharmaceuticals, biologics, vaccines, clinical trial materials and other healthcare products. By developing an integrated Cold Chain Network, DHL will be able to securely move critical products across trade lanes, with controlled and cost-competitive solutions.
Singapore is growing in importance across DHL’s Healthcare supply chain, following the introduction of DHL Global Forwarding’s Singapore Coldchain Hub. Once the hub is complete, the region will have a total pharmaceutical logistics footprint of 16,000 sqm, with room to accommodate approximately 12,000 pallet positions.
The new corridors will make use of this expansion, as DHL has found the region to be a critical part of its global network. By
connecting the US to Europe
and Asia, DHL is developing strategic pathways working to meet growing markets and increased demand, alongside ongoing innovation within its healthcare logistics.
Customers can be reassured that their vaccines and other products are being transported with consistency and security. Now, with the corridors, it will be easier to drive collaboration and innovation within the pharmaceutical supply chain space.
DHL has added six new corridors to its healthcare network. Credit: DHL
Key partners
DHL Global Forwarding
DHL Global Forwarding is the air and ocean freight specialist division of Deutsche Post DHL Group, supporting over 167,000 customers daily. The company operates a dedicated Cold Chain Network for temperature-sensitive healthcare products, moving 2.1 million air freight tons annually. With €900 million investments by 2030, it connects pharmaceutical manufacturers globally through specialized corridors and validated handling procedures.
DHL, part of Deutsche Post DHL Group, is the world's leading logistics company providing international express delivery, freight transportation, and comprehensive supply chain management solutions. Operating in over 220 countries and territories, DHL employs approximately 600,000 people worldwide. The company specializes in advanced temperature-controlled logistics. DHL's network includes healthcare corridors, Boeing 777 freighters, and cold chain infrastructure supporting pharmaceutical manufacturers globally.
DHL deploys Boeing 777 freighter aircraft across its Cold Chain Network, leveraging the aerospace manufacturer's advanced cargo capabilities. The partnership ensures temperature-sensitive healthcare products maintain integrity during long-haul flights. Boeing's freighter technology provides the reliability and capacity needed for DHL's expanding pharmaceutical logistics operations across European, North American and Asian corridors.

title: Exploring Amazon's Supply Chain Decarbonisation Journey
content:
Exploring Amazon's Supply Chain Decarbonisation Journey
Prioritise Us
on Google
Michelle Jolly, Director of Sustainability Solutions and Services at Amazon, speaking at Sustainability LIVE @ CWNYC, September 2026
Michelle Jolly, Director of Sustainability Solutions and Services at Amazon, explores how The Carbon Pledge is empowering suppliers to decarbonise
Multinational companies face pressure
to report and cut Scope 3 greenhouse gas emissions
as new regulations like the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive approach.
Michelle Jolly, Director of Sustainability Solutions and Services at Amazon, spoke to business leaders at Sustainability LIVE @ CWNYC in September and explained that data analytics, capacity building and cross-sector collaboration are methods companies can use to
reduce emissions in complex supply chains
According to Michelle, 76% of Amazon's carbon footprint sits within its supply chain. In 2019, Amazon committed to net zero carbon by 2040 and created the Climate Pledge, which focuses on tackling emissions within its supply chain by working with suppliers.
We're all interconnected and so the more that we can drive interest and things that we know work, the better we'll all be.
Michelle Jolly, Director of Sustainability Solutions and Services at Amazon
Engaging thousands of suppliers
Amazon works with tens of thousands of companies across different sectors. These suppliers help power film sets, data centres and the retail business.
"It takes all shapes and forms, and we work with all of them to enable them on this journey and at this scale, we take a three step approach," Michelle said. "And this is something we're welcoming others who are newer on their potential supplier journey as well."
Decarbonising large supply chains
presents challenges for corporate climate teams. Standardising reporting across thousands of global vendors requires coordinated effort.
Michelle tells delegates that companies need to combine scale with supplier support to achieve emission cuts in retail, logistics and data centre supply chains. "We know that we need to meet them at the right education and resource point and to provide them with solutions," she said.
Prioritising high impact partners
Amazon begins by engaging its top suppliers, who represent more than 70% of its supply chain emissions. As of 2025, 62% of those top suppliers have decarbonisation plans in place.
The company spends more with partners who show progress on climate goals. However, changes are not always simple.
"One of the most common things we hear about is the challenge of accessing energy solutions across our supplier network, especially in the environment where costs are increasing and availability is scarce," Michelle said. Amazon covers facilitation fees for these services and has negotiated preferred deferred rates with suppliers of energy.
The company makes these options available to its supply chain on the exchange so that access becomes easier and more affordable. Suppliers receive direction towards trusted, high quality providers.
Amazon uses several methods to help suppliers decarbonise at pace:
Setting clear targets while meeting suppliers at their individual resource levels
Directing corporate procurement spend toward vendors making measurable progress in reducing emissions
Providing open access to vetted decarbonisation playbooks via the Sustainability Exchange platform
Covering facilitation fees and negotiating preferred deferred rates for access to carbon-free energy
Supplying low-minimum-order-quantity biodiesel fuel inset credits derived from waste-based feedstocks.
Michelle Jolly, Director of Sustainability Solutions and Services at Amazon
Beyond direct emission cuts, global supply chain decarbonisation uses trusted carbon credits and inset mechanisms to tackle transport and manufacturing emissions. Michelle points out that choosing the right credits remains a challenge for smaller companies.
Carbon credit portfolio access
Michelle spent time in the Climate Pledge signatory
community and amongst suppliers
learning which pieces of their commitment to net zero were easy and which ones remained unmanaged or felt intimidating. "Carbon credits was near the top of the list," she said.
"So we decided to open our portfolio of carbon neutralisation or offset credits and inset credits to our value chain."
The Climate Pledge now includes more than 700 companies aiming for net zero carbon across all three scopes by 2040. According to Michelle, the portfolio focuses on projects with proven impact, such as stopping deforestation, destroying harmful refrigerants and using new rice farming methods in India to cut methane and reduce water use by up to 30%.
Giving supply chain partners
better access to market-based tools could help them take organised climate action across complex transport networks. Michelle says lower-carbon transport fuels need clear market signals and easy ways to buy them.
Transportation fuel challenges
Many organisations operate in multimodal form across road, maritime or aviation fuels. This means they have emissions across each transportation option.
"If you move people or products, you likely have these type of
transportation emissions in your footprint
," Michelle said. "And one of the best ways to decarbonise that transportation is by sending demand and market signals to these lower carbon fuels through environmental attribute certificates and fuel credits."
To keep demand strong, companies must set a net-zero target by 2050 to use the credit service. Climate Pledge signatories get discounts on credits and Amazon covers some costs to encourage companies to meet net-zero goals on time.
Michelle says collaboration forms part of this approach. "My scope one is your scope three. We're all interconnected and so the more that we can drive interest and things that we know work, the better we'll all be."

title: Rethinking Sourcing in Canada: Jaggaer's Executive Event
content:
Rethinking Sourcing in Canada: Jaggaer's Executive Event
Prioritise Us
on Google
Toronto generates roughly 10% of Canada's total gross domestic product according to the Toronto School of Management. Credit: Aditya Chinchure
Senior procurement leaders from Canadian manufacturing and transportation firms are invited to a Jaggaer executive dinner in Toronto on November 26
Canadian manufacturers have now spent more than a year adjusting to US tariffs, and many are making decisions that will shape their supply chains for years.
A KPMG Canada survey of 275 Canadian manufacturers, carried out in May 2026, found 42% have already moved production to the US or are considering doing so.
The same survey found 57% have paused, reduced or cancelled capital investment projects.
On November 26 2026, procurement software company Jaggaer will host an executive dinner in Toronto, Canada, in association with
, the publisher of
Manufacturing Digital
The invitation-only evening will bring together C-suite and senior procurement leaders from Canadian organisations to discuss the future of procurement and supply chain amid AI adoption and economic volatility.
Contact our team to register your interest
Tariffs and the cost of uncertainty
The pressure is showing up in sourcing and investment plans as much as in trade figures.
Export Development Canada says the US share of Canada's goods exports fell from 76% in 2024 to 72% in 2025, citing Statistics Canada data, in an analysis of the first year of tariffs published in June 2026.
A Canadian Manufacturers & Exporters (CME) survey published the same month found 74% of manufacturers hit by April's US metal tariff changes reported a significant or moderate negative impact.
CME also found 73% of manufacturers say unresolved or recurring reviews of the Canada-United States-Mexico Agreement (CUSMA) would negatively affect their business.
This uncertainty can make long-term sourcing decisions harder to commit to.
What the dinner will cover
Jaggaer has designed the evening around open, strategic discussion between peers.
The discussion will focus on four themes:
strategic sourcing and resilience, and how to diversify supply chains while protecting cost efficiency
Canada-first sourcing, and what is realistic for domestic substitution in manufacturing and transportation
peer intelligence exchange between senior procurement leaders.
Each theme reflects a problem procurement teams in Canada are dealing with now: tariff disruption, sourcing vulnerability, gaps in domestic supply and decision-making under uncertainty.
Who the evening is for
The dinner is aimed at procurement and supply chain leaders at Director level and above.
Toronto is the second-largest financial centre in North America. Credit: Marcin Skalij
Guests will come from large manufacturing, transportation and commercial organisations in Canada.
Attendance is by invitation only and guests will come from non-competing companies.
What attendees will take away
Jaggaer says guests will leave with:
a peer network of Vice President and Director-level procurement leaders from non-competing Canadian companies
a practical framework for tariff response and sourcing strategy
expert perspective on trade policy
a post-dinner brief with key insights and curated resources.
The dinner takes place in Toronto on Thursday November 26 2026.
Senior procurement and supply chain leaders who would like to attend can
contact our team to register their interest

title: Cencora: Visibility and Risk in Pharmaceutical Supply Chains
content:
Cencora: Visibility and Risk in Pharmaceutical Supply Chains
Prioritise Us
on Google
Brent Wilhelm, SVP of Supply Chain Planning & Optimisation at Cencora
Brent Wilhelm, SVP of Supply Chain Planning & Optimisation at Cencora, explores preparedness and risk management in pharmaceutical supply chains
Supply chains are continuously facing disruption and risk in today's world. Internal pressures and external pressures are at high, driven by an ageing workforce, a growing skills gap and worsening climate pressures.
In pharmaceutical supply chains, demand is warring with resilience. These supply chains must run with extreme precision, operating
under strict temperature-controlled conditions
, being delivered without delay and reducing waste.
Brent Wilhelm,  Senior Vice President of Supply Chain Planning & Optimisation at Cencora, oversees supply chain design and strategy at the organisation. With this, he is working towards continuous improvement, integrated business planning and thorough transportation capabilities.
He has a background in transportation, purchasing, distribution, project management and he serves on the Health Distribution Alliance’s US Pharmaceutical Cold Chain Advisory Committee.
Supply Chain Digital spoke to Brent in order to hear the
challenges Cencora is facing, and how it is ensuring
reliable operations amid a time of great disruption.
How is the increasing number of weather events impacting operations at Cencora?
Extreme weather increases the number of variables we have to plan around, from road closures and power outages to carrier limitations and changing access to affected communities. That is especially important in pharmaceutical distribution because a delay can affect access to essential medications, and the risk is even greater for products with strict temperature requirements.
Our focus is on preparing the network so we have options when an event occurs. That includes working with customers in advance, understanding where additional inventory may be needed, coordinating with carrier partners on alternate routes and maintaining relationships with organisations such as FEMA, local officials and Healthcare Ready when access to disaster-affected areas becomes difficult.
What does effective preparedness look like across the pharmaceutical supply chain?
Preparedness starts well before a storm is on the radar. It requires visibility into the network, clear contingency plans and close
coordination among distributors, manufacturers
, carriers, providers and public-sector partners.
For distributors, flexibility within the distribution network is critical. A centralised point-of-entry model, for example, can simplify how products with different temperature requirements move into the network and give distributors greater ability to sort, package and route them based on changing conditions. Effective preparedness also means understanding carrier capabilities and limitations ahead of time and knowing which alternate routes or partners can be activated when normal operations are disrupted.
Flexibility across the distribution network is vital for Cencora's operations. Credit: Cencora
How can advance planning, alternate routing and real-time monitoring help prevent delays and temperature excursions?
Those capabilities work best together. Advance planning gives teams a primary route and a set of alternatives before a shipment moves. Alternate routing creates options if weather, capacity constraints or another disruption closes the original path. Real-time monitoring then provides the visibility needed to determine whether the shipment remains within acceptable conditions and whether intervention is required.
For temperature-sensitive products, that visibility is especially important. Monitoring technology can track product conditions throughout transit and alert teams to a temperature change before it becomes a larger issue. For more complex therapies,
effective visibility increasingly
means combining location and temperature data with route information, remaining product life and the patient’s treatment window so teams can make informed decisions quickly.
Why is growing demand for temperature-sensitive therapies raising the stakes for emergency preparedness?
The margin for disruption is getting smaller. Many specialty and advanced therapies have narrow temperature ranges, limited stability windows or patient-specific requirements. In some cases, a delay can mean more than a late delivery. It can disrupt a scheduled procedure, compromise the product or force a patient to wait for treatment.
As these therapies become more common, logistics networks have to support more specialised packaging, continuous monitoring and tighter coordination across each handoff. That makes emergency preparedness part of the treatment pathway itself. Teams need to know not only how to protect the product, but how to recover the shipment if the planned route becomes unavailable.
Our focus is on preparing the network so we have options when an event occurs.
Brent Wilhelm, Senior Vice President of Supply Chain Planning & Optimisation at Cencora
Technology across the supply chain is helping increase efficiency. Credit: Cencora
How can organisations stay resilient in the face of volatility?
Resilience comes from combining strong fundamentals with better information. Technology can help organisations identify risk earlier, model different scenarios and make faster decisions. AI-driven analytics, for example, can flag emerging supply constraints and help teams respond through actions such as rerouting shipments or adjusting inventory before a shortage or disruption becomes more severe.
But technology is only as useful as the processes and infrastructure around it. Standardised systems, reliable data, clear ownership and collaboration across
manufacturers, logistics providers, regulators
and healthcare organisations remain essential.
What is your key piece of advice to someone starting out in the logistics industry today?
My single biggest piece of advice is to learn the operation from the ground up — and never lose that perspective. The most effective leaders in logistics are the ones who truly understand the work being done at every level of the organisation, from the distribution center floor to the carrier relationship to the customer's front door.
Stay curious. Logistics is an
industry that never stops evolving
— technology, regulation, customer expectations, and global dynamics are constantly shifting the landscape. The people who thrive are the ones who embrace that complexity and never stop learning.
Build relationships early and invest in them often. Logistics is a people business at its core — and the network you build, the trust you earn and the reputation you establish will open more doors than any title or credential ever will.
And finally — always keep the customer and the patient at the center of every decision you make. In healthcare logistics especially, what we do every day has a direct impact on people's lives. Never lose sight of that. It is what makes this work meaningful.

title: Walmart Opens Automated West Coast Fulfilment Hub
content:
Walmart Opens Automated West Coast Fulfilment Hub
Prioritise Us
on Google
The automated systems deployed at Walmart’s next-generation fulfilment centres have condensed the twelve-step fulfilment workflow into five. Credit: Unsplash / David Montero
Walmart’s Stockton fulfilment centre is “people-led and tech-powered”, says Karisa Sprague, SVP of Fulfilment Operations, as the hub halves workflows
has unveiled its fifth
next-generation fulfilment centre
designed to combine machine learning with a skilled workforce in Stockton, California.
The company estimates it will now be able to provide next-day or two-day delivery services to 95% of the US.
“This facility is about more than advanced automation,” writes
Karisa Sprague
, Senior Vice President of Fulfilment Operations at Walmart US, on LinkedIn.
Karisa Sprague, Senior Vice President of Fulfilment Operations at Walmart US. Credit: Karisa Sprague via LinkedIn
“It’s about combining the best of people and technology to better serve customers, support the continued growth of our marketplace sellers and create new opportunities for associates,” she continues.
The Stockton facility serves as an operational anchor for Walmart’s broader West Coast infrastructure, promising to compress transit times across major West Coast urban centres, including Los Angeles and San Francisco.
Key facts – Walmart’s Stockton fulfilment centre:
The centre is the fifth to join Walmart’s next-generation fulfilment network.
Walmart reports a workforce of more than 102,900 associates in California.
The centre spans 900,000 square feet, with two million containers of capacity.
In 2025, Walmart spent US$36.5bn with California suppliers.
The retailer expects the new centre to create more than 1,000 jobs.
Automating Walmart’s fulfilment process
Traditional manual order processing across large-scale retail distribution centres typically involves a 12-step workflow.
automated systems
deployed at Walmart’s next-generation fulfilment centres have condensed this process into just five steps: receiving, decanting, automated picking, packing and shipping.
Walmart says this cuts its fulfilment timeline by more than half.
The company’s fulfilment model utilises an automated storage and retrieval system instead of relying on the physical movement of inventory.
The retailer has partnered with Austrian technology provider KNAPP to produce an automated shuttle system to transport deliveries across its hubs. The system has a capacity of almost two million containers and was designed to optimise space.
The system is supported by KNAPP’s KiSoft software suite, which centralises inventory coordination and handles order processes. The suite provides analytical tools that can enhance the fulfilment process with operational data.
However, Walmart says that human associates remain central to the process.
The automated infrastructure reduces unnecessary manual labour and repetitive work, but quality checks and the physical packing of orders are still carried out by workers.
Expanding Walmart’s automated network
Walmart is already
operating automated systems
like this across its network.
The company says that around 50% of its US e-commerce fulfilment centres incorporate automated processes.
Across the US, 60% of its store locations have begun receiving freight from its automated distribution centres.
The Stockton facility  is Walmart’s fifth across the US, with further outposts in Illinois, Indiana, Texas and Pennsylvania.
Its strategic location in California’s Central Valley will bring inventory closer to major West Coast urban centres, which could help to cut transit times across customer hubs including Los Angeles and San Francisco.
Walmart says that the new centre will allow it to offer next-day or two-day shipping to 95% of its US customer base. Credit: Walmart
“This facility is an important investment in the Central Valley and a critical part of how we’re building the next generation of Walmart’s fulfillment network across the West Coast,” explains Karisa.
The centre’s opening follows Walmart’s May 2026 announcement of an enhanced supply chain strategy.
The programme is targeting significant cost reduction and greater efficiency throughout the retailer’s US network, aiming to build a more connected, automated and data-driven supply chain, supporting its omnichannel retail model.

title: DSV and CMA CGM target 12,000t ACT+ CO2 cut
content:
DSV and CMA CGM target 12,000t ACT+ CO2 cut
Prioritise Us
on Google
CMA CGM operates a number of LNG-fuelled low carbon container feeder vessels in Northern Europe.
DSV’s Michael Hollstein explains how CMA CGM’s ACT+ and UCOME biofuels will target 12,000 tonnes of CO2 cuts over two years
In October, liner operator CMA CGM announced that it had signed a deal with DSV to reduce DSV’s CO2 emissions by 12,000 tonnes using a second generation UCOME biofuel.
DSV currently offers low carbon fuel options to its aviation and shipping customers, as well as a book-and-claim based offset model for its road logistics customers to make low-emission logistics easier and more accessible.
While the volume of UCOME based biodiesel required for the deal has not been disclosed, Supply Chain Digital notes that a similar deal between CMA CGM and DHL in December 2025 indicated that an estimated 25,000t of CO₂e well-to-wake emission reductions would require 8,990t of UCOME second-generation biofuel.
"At DSV, reducing emissions across global supply chains requires strong collaboration and scalable solutions,” says Michael Hollstein, DSV, SVP Global Ocean Product.
“Through our partnership with CMA CGM and the use of the ACT+ solution, we are expanding access to lower-carbon shipping options for our customers. This agreement reflects our shared commitment to advancing lower-carbon transport and helping customers achieve their sustainability goals."
"Our partnership demonstrates how strong collaboration drives more resilient and sustainable logistics, while delivering high-performance solutions for our customers,” says Amandine Paulet, Vice President and Deputy Chief Commercial Officer, CMA CGM.
Amandine Paulet, Vice President and Deputy Chief Commercial Officer, CMA CGM
There has been a growth in demand for offset-based mechanisms using low carbon fuels in the maritime transportation sector. This has been driven by greater interest in low emission shipping solutions, amid concern about the extension of the Emissions Trading System (ETS) to cover shipping within the EU, as well as wider concerns about the potential introduction of decarbonisation targets at the International Maritime Organisation (IMO).
CMA CGM will use second-generation UCOME-based biodiesel. As UCOME is produced from used cooking oil, it does not rely directly on food-grade vegetable oils as its feedstock.
On 1 October, the acquisition of Fedex Supply Chain by CEVA Logistics in North America was finalised. Credit: CMA CGM
What is UCOME?
UCOME stands for Used Cooking Oil Methyl Ester.
It is produced from used cooking oil, a waste-based feedstock.
It is classified as a second-generation biodiesel.
It can be used as a drop-in fuel in compatible diesel engines.
It can help reduce lifecycle emissions compared with fossil diesel, depending on the feedstock, production pathway and accounting methodology.
Its sustainability benefits depend on traceability, certification and the treatment of upstream emissions.
UCOME production for a trial at Singapore's Changi airport

Founded in 1976 by nine independent hauliers, DSV A/S has grown into a global logistics giant. Through strategic acquisitions, the Danish company now operates in more than 80 countries. Its services span road, air, sea and rail transport. In 2025, the company acquired DB Schenker, strengthening its position as the world’s largest freight forwarder.

CMA CGM is one of the world’s largest container liner operators. The company has diversified into logistics and offers global rail, air and logistics solutions in addition to maritime freight. The company maintains operations in 184 countries. The company’s fleet of over 700 vessels includes more than 350 operated by CMA Ships. The company supports two port operators: Terminal Link and CMA Terminals. The company’s logistics focused subsidiary CEVA Logistics operates over 1,000 warehouses. title: BYD launches luxury Han EV with more than 1,000 km of range, starting at $35,000
content:
Peter Johnson
| Oct 13 2026 - 8:59 am PT
latest flagship EV, the Great Han, is now on sale in China, starting at about $35,000 with a CLTC range of over 1,000 km (621 miles).
BYD Great Han EV prices and range
The Great Han, or “Da Han” as it’s sold in China, is BYD’s first fully electric D-segment flagship sedan under its Dynasty series.
BYD launched the luxury sedan in China on Tuesday with three variants, priced from 235,900 yuan, or about $35,000.
It’s available in single- and dual-motor powertrains. The base rear-wheel-drive (RWD) Premium model offers a CLTC range of up to 1,008 km (626 miles), while the top-spec all-wheel-drive (AWD) Flagship variant provides 880 km (546 miles).
All variants use a 102.326 kWh BYD Blade 2.0 battery pack. The RWD models have a single 370 kW (496 hp) motor, while the AWD variant adds a 200 kW front motor for a combined 570 kW (764 hp).
All Great Han models also include a roof-mounted LiDAR and BYD’s God’s Eye B intelligent driver assistance system.
The setup offers safety and convenience features including Navigate on Autopilot on highways and in cities, plus remote autonomous parking.
With BYD’s second-gen Blade Batteries and Flash Charging technology, the flagship EV can charge from 10% to 70% in just 5 minutes. A full recharge (10% to 97%) takes just 9 minutes.
The Great Han is 5,256 mm long, 1,999 mm wide, and 1,510 mm high, with a 3,130 mm wheelbase, or slightly bigger than the Tesla Model S and Lucid Air. It’s about the size of the long-wheelbase Mercedes -Benz S-Class.
Like many of BYD’s new luxury vehicles, the Great Han is loaded with premium extras, such as its DiSus-A dual-chamber air suspension system, rear-wheel steering, and zero-gravity front seats.
The Great Han joins the Great Tang SUV as the flagship sedan under BYD’s Dynasty lineup. After launching the Great Tang in mid-June,
BYD sold over 10,000
units each month in its first three months on the market.
Will BYD’s luxury Great Han EV sedan draw the same demand? Share your thoughts in the comments.

title: Tesla's China business is flipping: sales down 12%, exports double
content:
Tesla sold 381,088 cars to Chinese buyers through the first nine months of 2026, down 11.9% from last year, according to CPCA data. Over the same period, Giga Shanghai’s exports more than doubled to 361,972 vehicles.
Nearly half of what Tesla builds in China now leaves China. And Beijing just announced it will cut the tax rebate on EV exports next year.
“Affordable cars must be made on same continent as customers”
When Tesla broke ground on Giga Shanghai in January 2019, Elon Musk was clear about who the factory was for.
“Shanghai Giga will produce affordable versions of 3/Y for greater China,” Musk wrote at the time. He added that the Model S, Model X and “higher cost versions” of the Model 3 and Model Y would “still be built in US for WW market, incl China.” In another post that same week, he summed up the philosophy: “Affordable cars must be made on same continent as customers.”
That lasted about a year and a half. By late 2020, Shanghai was building right-hand-drive Model 3s for Australia and New Zealand and shipping Model 3s to Europe. Today it supplies Europe, Asia-Pacific and, since this year, Canada again under Ottawa’s new China EV import quota.
None of those customers are on the same continent as Shanghai.
Tesla’s China sales keep sliding
Here’s how Tesla’s China business looks through September, based on CPCA data:
| Tesla China | Jan–Sep 2025 | Jan–Sep 2026 | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Retail (domestic) | 432,704 | 381,088 | -11.9% |
| Exports | 173,660 | 361,972 | +108% |
| Wholesale (total) | 606,364 | 743,060 | +22.5% |
| Exports as share of wholesale | 29% | 49% | +20 pts |
The domestic number is the lowest first nine months Tesla has posted in China in at least four years. It’s down 17% from the 460,203 cars Tesla sold there over the same period in 2024.
Q3 was worse. Tesla’s Chinese retail sales fell 16% to 142,133 units, and July alone was down 33%. September (64,837 units, down 9.4%) was the best month of the quarter, but it was still a decline.
The whole Chinese EV market is shrinking this year, so some of this isn’t Tesla-specific. NEV retail sales in China are down 12.8% through September, according to the CPCA, after Beijing cut the purchase tax exemption in half on January 1. So Tesla is roughly tracking the market year-to-date. But in Q3, the market was down about 10% and Tesla was down 16%.
The wholesale numbers hide it
You wouldn’t know any of this from Tesla China’s headline numbers. Wholesale, which counts both domestic sales and exports, is up 22.5% this year, and July’s 93,579 units was the factory’s best July ever.
That’s all exports. Tesla has already shipped more cars out of China this year (361,972) than it did in all of 2023 (344,078), 2024 (259,548) or 2025 (226,034).
As we pointed out in our H1 analysis, Shanghai has become Tesla’s pressure valve. It can keep running near capacity even as Chinese buyers walk away, because the cars go somewhere else.
And it’s carrying the whole company. Shanghai’s wholesale volume in Q3 was 275,111 vehicles, equal to 57% of the 486,532 cars Tesla delivered worldwide. Chinese buyers accounted for just 29%.
Beijing is cutting the export rebate
On Monday, China’s Ministry of Finance and State Taxation Administration announced that the VAT export rebate on new energy vehicles will drop from 13% to 9% on April 1, 2027. It covers battery-electric and plug-in hybrid cars, and the rate is based on the export date on the customs declaration.
It’s part of a pattern. Beijing already eliminated the export rebate on solar panels in April, and the battery rebate was cut from 9% to 6% and goes to zero on January 1, 2027.
The mechanics are simple. Chinese exporters get the VAT they paid refunded when a product leaves the country. Whatever isn’t refunded becomes a cost. So starting in April, automakers eat an extra 4% of the export value on every EV they ship out of China.
For Tesla, that’s real money. Assuming an average export value of around ¥220,000 per Model 3 or Model Y, the cut costs about ¥8,800 ($1,235) per car. At this year’s export pace of roughly 480,000 vehicles a year, that’s around $600 million annually that Tesla either absorbs or passes on to buyers in Europe, Canada and Asia. That’s our estimate, not a Tesla figure.
Tesla isn’t alone. China exported more than 4 million NEVs in the first nine months of the year, more than double last year, according to the China Association of Automobile Manufacturers. Every Chinese automaker that’s been using exports to offset weak demand at home gets the same bill.
But few are as exposed as Tesla, with half its Chinese production going abroad and its domestic sales falling.
There’s one more effect to watch. Since the rate depends on the customs declaration date, expect automakers, Tesla included, to cram as many exports as possible into Q4 and Q1 before the deadline. That should make Tesla China’s wholesale numbers look great for two more quarters, before the cost shows up in Q2 2027.
Electrek’s Take
Musk said Giga Shanghai would build affordable cars for China. It did, for about a year. Then it became Tesla’s export hub, and now it’s more than that: it’s the thing propping up Tesla’s China numbers and a big chunk of its global deliveries.
That shift was a reaction to falling demand. Tesla’s lineup in China is still the Model 3 and Model Y, while BYD, Xiaomi, Xpeng and a dozen others launch new models every few months at lower prices. Chinese buyers have options, and fewer of them are picking Tesla. Exports let Tesla keep the factory busy without cutting production, and the “record” wholesale did the rest.
Top comment by Beario
Tesla has the 3 and the Y as their primary sellers. It will most likely stay that way. As long as Musk wants to have the flexibility to dabble in venture into things like cybercabs and robots, Tesla will only be limited to a few car models. I only say venture because the cybercab and Optimus are not large scale yet and there are other issues to work out before that happens. Also, as long as gas prices are high, the 3 and Y will sell well and it is actually not a bad thing that gas prices are helping EV adoption.
Beijing’s rebate cut makes that model more expensive. Tesla has three options, and none of them are good. It can raise prices abroad, in markets like Europe where its sales are already weak. It can eat a margin hit of roughly $600 million a year at a time when its automotive margins are already thin. Or it can build fewer cars in Shanghai.
Berlin could take on more Model Y volume for Europe, but that doesn’t help the Model 3, Canada or Asia-Pacific.
So the question for 2027 is this: what happens to Giga Shanghai when both its home market and its export valve shrink at the same time?

title: Volkswagen's new ID. Buzz will be more affordable, and it's bringing 'lots of secret sauce'
content:
Volkswagen
ID. Buzz
Peter Johnson
| Oct 13 2026 - 7:22 am PT
The electric minibus is getting an overhaul. Volkswagen said a new
ID. Buzz
is in the works, bringing much more than just a lower price tag.
When is VW launching the new ID. Buzz?
When Volkswagen first brought the ID. Buzz to the US in 2024, its electric spin on the iconic hippie van had plenty of people talking.
While many were thrilled to see VW finally bring the electric minibus to the US, much of that excitement turned out to be nostalgia.
Starting at around $60,000, the ID. Buzz wasn’t exactly cheap. Plus, it only offered a range of up to 234 miles.
Volkswagen looks to change that with the next-generation ID. Buzz. During an interview with
Auto Express
at the 2026 Paris Auto Show this week, VW brand CEO Thomas Schäfer confirmed “they’re working on it,” when asked about the future of the electric minibus.
Schäfer admitted that the ID. Buzz “is in the wrong cost base,” confirming the new model will be more affordable.
2025 Volkswagen ID. Buzz (Source: Volkswagen)
It will also be based on the Group’s new Scalable Systems Platform (SSP), which VW promises will reduce costs and pave the way for software-defined vehicles.
While Volkswagen is revamping its lineup, using some of its most popular nameplates like the Polo and Tiguan, Schäfer said that the company will not reuse all of its iconic names. However, “the iconic stuff, you need to use, because the other new brands don’t have that. They have no history,” he added.
2025 Volkswagen ID. Buzz (Source: Volkswagen)
What will the new ID. Buzz look like? According to Volkswagen’s design boss, Andreas Mindt, it will require “lots of secret sauce,” a cornerstone of its new design language.
Although Mindt admitted that “people get tired” of retro-looking vehicles, as was the case with the new Beetle, the next-gen ID. Buzz will likely stay true to its timeless design with a modern twist.
“When you have a van, it doesn’t have too much character; one white van looks like the other white van. So what do you do to make it interesting?” Mindt asked.
2025 Volkswagen ID. Buzz (Source: Volkswagen)
The ID. Buzz is “one of the interesting ones,” he said, adding, “This I can promise you in the future: it will be interesting.”
Like the new ID. Polo and ID. Tiguan, the new electric minibus will feature Volkswagen’s updated interior design and infotainment system, including the return of physical buttons.
Based on VW’s new SSP platform, the next-generation ID. Buzz will offer improved driving range, faster charging, and more advanced software. The platform is designed to reduce costs, while Schäfer hinted it could also use lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries to enable lower prices.
Volkswagen ID. Tiguan interior (Source: Volkswagen)
Schäfer didn’t reveal any other details, including when the next-gen ID. Buzz will launch. The first SSP-based EV was initially set to arrive in 2026, but VW is now saying it will arrive “by the end of the decade.” The new ID. Buzz will likely launch shortly after.
In the meantime, Volkswagen recently
delayed the return of the ID. Buzz
in the US until the 2028 model year.
Volkswagen Group of America VP and chief communications officer, Jeannine Ginivan, told
Electrek
in December that the ID. Buzz
would not receive a 2026 model year
for the US. The company planned to move straight to the 2027 model.
Ginivan also confirmed with
Electrek
that “Volkswagen is not canceling the ID. Buzz for the US market.”
third quarter
, Volkswagen sold just 432 ID. Buzz models in the US, down 82.5% from nearly 2,500 in Q3 2025.

title: Tesla pauses Model 3 orders in Canada amid China EV quota
content:
Tesla Model 3
Fred Lambert
| Oct 13 2026 - 7:07 am PT
Tesla Model 3 (Source: Tesla)
Tesla has stopped taking orders for the Model 3 Premium in Canada, the Shanghai-built trim that brought the electric sedan down to $39,490 CAD. The automaker says it has used up its import quota for Chinese-made EVs and doesn’t expect to reopen orders until March 2027.
But the Canadian government’s own tracker tells a different story: 33,069 of the 49,000 permits for China-made EVs in the current quota year are still available.
“Tesla’s import quota”
The change shows up in Tesla’s Canadian configurator. Both Model 3 Premium versions, RWD and AWD, are gone from the order page. The only Model 3 you can order in Canada right now is the Performance AWD, listed at $936 per month in financing.
Tesla explains the pause with a short message on its site: “Model 3 Premium orders paused after high demand exhausted Tesla’s import quota. Ordering resumes if Govt of Canada issues more quota, expected March 2027.”
Canada’s quota runs on a March-to-February year, so March 1, 2027, is when a fresh 49,000 permits become available.
The Model 3 Premium RWD has been a hit since
Tesla launched it in Canada at a record-low $39,490 in May
. That’s roughly the price of a base Camry. Before it arrived, the cheapest Model 3 you could order in Canada was the $79,990 Long Range AWD, built in Fremont and hit by Canada’s 25% counter-tariff on US-made vehicles. Tesla
shipped its remaining US-built Model 3 inventory out of Canada
back in March to make room.
Ottawa’s numbers don’t show an exhausted quota
Canada cut its tariff on Chinese EVs from 100% to 6.1% in January
, it set a single national cap of 49,000 vehicles per year, split into two six-month periods. Global Affairs Canada’s notice for the current period says permits are issued “on a first-come, first-served (FCFS) basis” to automakers or their Canadian agents. There’s no per-manufacturer limit in it.
According to the Export and Import Controls tracker, updated October 9, only 15,931 permits have been used since March 1. That leaves 33,069, or 67% of the year’s quota, sitting unused. The current period alone started with 33,397 permits: the base 24,500 plus 8,897 left over from the first six months.
And the monthly breakdown shows when things stopped. Imports of electric cars valued at or under $35,000 (the customs bucket a $39,490 Model 3 RWD would fall into, since the threshold applies to import value, not sticker price) went from 465 in June to 4,743 in July and 2,597 in August. That ramp lines up with Model 3 Premium deliveries. Then September came in at just seven vehicles, and October was at zero as of the latest update.
So Tesla went from importing thousands of cheap Chinese-built cars a month to nearly none, while two-thirds of the quota stayed on the table.
The likely explanation
There’s one line in Global Affairs Canada’s notice that could explain it. The department says it will monitor permit applications “for the purpose of providing equitable access to the quota to eligible applicants,” which “could include setting aside a portion of the available quota for the use of OEMs, including new entrants.”
In plain terms, Ottawa gave itself room to stop one company from eating the whole thing. And Tesla is the obvious candidate. It had a head start because its Shanghai-built cars were already in Transport Canada’s certification database in March, while BYD and Geely are still setting up their Canadian dealer networks.
Tesla’s wording, “Tesla’s import quota,” points the same way. If permits were still open first-come, first-served, Tesla could simply keep applying. Global Affairs Canada hasn’t published any company-specific allocation, so the details of what Tesla was given, and when, aren’t public.
The other possibility is that Tesla’s order backlog is big enough that it already covers every permit it expects to get before February. Either way, Canadians who want a $39,490 Model 3 are now waiting until next spring at the earliest.
Electrek’s Take
The demand part of Tesla’s message is real. A Model 3 at $39,490 CAD is the best EV deal in Canada, full stop, and Canadians bought it in big numbers despite the anger at Elon Musk that’s still very visible here. That says a lot about how much price matters.
But “exhausted Tesla’s import quota” is doing a lot of work in that sentence. Canada’s official tracker shows two-thirds of the quota unused. If Ottawa quietly capped Tesla to keep room for BYD, Geely and others, we think that’s a defensible policy choice. The whole point of opening the door to Chinese EVs was more competition and lower prices, not a Tesla monopoly on the cheap import lane. If that’s what happened, though, the government should say so and publish the allocations. Automakers, dealers and buyers are all making decisions in the dark right now.
The bigger issue is the 49,000 cap itself. Canada sells roughly 1.9 million new vehicles a year. One affordable sedan from one automaker was enough to max out whatever share Tesla was allowed in about four months of deliveries. That’s a sign the quota is too small, not that demand is too big.
The quota is supposed to be reviewed, and the deal already calls for it to grow to 70,000 by 2030. After this, will Ottawa move faster than that?

title: Tesla still leads US fast-charger growth – but it's raised its prices
content:
DC fast charging
EV charging stations
electric vehicle charging
Michelle Lewis
| Oct 13 2026 - 5:00 am PT
Volvo EX60 at a Tesla Supercharger (Source: Volvo)
The US has passed 80,000 public EV fast-charging ports, and new charging stops are getting bigger and packing more power. That’s good news for drivers looking for an open stall. The price story is more mixed: Most networks are holding steady, but Tesla Supercharger costs have gone up.
EV charging data platform Paren’s Q3 2026
State of the US Fast EV Charging Industry report
finds that operators added 4,106 fast-charging ports at 664 stations from July through September. That brings the US total to 80,964 ports across 14,614 locations.
The rollout slowed compared to Q2, when 4,618 ports opened. Through September, operators added about 9% fewer ports and opened about 20% fewer stations than in the same period last year.
But the stations that are opening have more places to plug in. New non-Tesla sites averaged five ports, up from 4.1 a year earlier. Locations with just one or two ports made up less than a third of new non-Tesla stops, down from nearly half.
For drivers, a bigger site means more chances to grab a charger when they arrive.
IONNA and Walmart pick up speed
Tesla still added more ports than any other network: 1,287 during Q3, plus another 124 through its Supercharger for Business program.
IONNA took second place with 378 ports, more than double its Q2 additions. Walmart came in third with 344.
Much of IONNA’s jump came from converting former Circle K charging locations, including 44 stations during the quarter. There’s a counting detail to note here: Paren treats replacement chargers as new infrastructure when another operator takes over and replaces the equipment.
Tesla’s new stations averaged 13.1 ports. It opened 11 locations with at least 24 stalls, the largest of which was a 48-stall site in Fort Lauderdale, Florida.
And the new equipment is getting more powerful. Across all networks, 73% of new ports were rated at least 250 kilowatts (kW), up from 60% a year earlier. Outside Tesla’s network, ports rated at 400 kW or more accounted for 35% of additions, compared with just 10% a year ago.
More chargers, more charging
Drivers are putting the growing network to use. Paren tracked 50.4 million fast-charging sessions in Q3, up 26% year over year. July set a monthly record with 17.6 million sessions.
National utilization barely moved, reaching 15.9%, compared with 15.8% in Q2. That’s the share of monitored time a port spends charging a vehicle, including unsuccessful attempts.
That national average hides some big differences. Ports in the 30 largest charging markets averaged 21.1% utilization, compared with 11% elsewhere. Los Angeles led those metros at 31.8% – twice the national average.
Reliability held steady, too, with a national score of 93.9. Paren’s index accounts for successful sessions, retries, failed attempts, and downtime, so it isn’t simply a charger uptime percentage.
Fifty of the 52 states and territories assessed scored at least 90, up from 46 a year earlier. Only Oklahoma and Vermont remained below that mark.
Tesla charging gets pricier
Drivers who use Superchargers may have noticed a bigger dent in their wallets.
In Q3, the national average fast-charging price reached 54 cents per kilowatt-hour, up 2.7% year over year. Paren attributes that increase to Tesla.
Tesla’s average non-member Supercharger price rose 15% over the year to 56.9 cents per kWh. Its member price increased 9% to 39.6 cents.
Meanwhile, the average across non-Tesla networks stayed near 53.3 cents per kWh for the fifth consecutive quarter.
When you plug in can make a difference, too. At stations with time-of-use pricing, average peak rates reached 63.7 cents per kWh, while off-peak rates held at 43.8 cents. That’s nearly a 20-cent gap for the same amount of electricity.
Where the next chargers go also matters. Urban markets received 90% of Q3’s new stations, while rural markets got 68 of the 664 additions. Larger charging stops are welcome, but drivers beyond those urban areas still need more places to stop.

title: Lectric launches lighter, lower-cost version of its bestselling urban e-bike: Lectric XPress Lite
content:
Micah Toll
| Oct 13 2026 - 3:58 am PT
Lectric eBikes
has spent the last several years steadily expanding from its original folding fat-tire e-bikes into just about every corner of the affordable electric bicycle market. Now the company is returning its attention to the commuter category with the new Lectric XPress Lite, a lighter and more affordable version of its popular XPress2 urban e-bike.
Priced at
, the XPress Lite takes the general formula of the more powerful
and pares it down into a lighter, more nimble package aimed squarely at everyday city riders. Lectric describes the new model as prioritizing portability and agility rather than the heavier-duty performance of the XPress2.
For those who prioritize a solid ride over raw power, the intuitive and smooth torque sensor matched with modest but not over-the-top power will feel right at home.
And at 45.6 lb (20.7 kg) with the battery removed, it certainly lands on the lighter end of Lectric’s lineup – a key feature for those needing to lift the bike into a car or carry it up stairs. It’s not an ultralight e-bike by conventional bicycle standards, but for an affordable, full-size commuter e-bike with this level of equipment, that’s a fairly manageable figure.
Power comes from a 500W nominal rear hub motor that peaks at 864W and produces just over 61 Nm of torque. That motor gets paired with an eight-speed Shimano Altus drivetrain and, importantly, an in-house-designed torque sensor. Lectric also includes its XPerience Switch system, allowing riders to switch between torque-sensor and cadence-sensor operation.
That last feature is particularly interesting at this price. Torque sensors have become increasingly common on affordable e-bikes, but giving riders the ability to choose between the more natural bicycle-like response of a torque sensor and the easier, more relaxed operation of a cadence sensor offers the best of both worlds.
While I personally prefer the natural pedal feel of a good torque sensor, those who want to get more oomph out of their motor without having to lean too hard into the pedaling will appreciate the cadence sensor. That’s perfect for anyone with mobility issues who wants to remain active but might not have the same pedaling strength as higher-performance riders.
The bike can be configured for Class 1, 2, or 3 operation where local laws permit, and includes five pedal-assist levels plus an under-the-bar, paddle-style thumb throttle.
Hydraulic disc brakes handle stopping duties, while the 27.5 x 1.95-inch puncture-resistant street-oriented tires come pre-Slimed from the factory. That factory-installed tire Slime means that riders likely won’t even realize how many fat tires they didn’t get, since the Slime takes care of sealing tire punctures before they can become a problem.
There’s also a 3.5-inch color TFT display and an integrated rear light with brake-light and turn-signal functionality.
The biggest compromise appears to be battery capacity. The 7.8 Ah battery packs in 375 Wh of capacity and is rated for up to 45 miles (72 km) of range on pedal assist, though as usual, expect real-world range to depend heavily on assist level, terrain, rider weight, speed, and other conditions. Both the complete e-bike and its battery carry UL certifications, keeping up with ever-evolving requirements and adding more peace of mind for riders.
And while it might be a smaller battery than many premium e-bikes these days, the
budget-focused $1,099 price
means riders are making up for it with extra value. Lectric has plenty of models with twice as much battery capacity as this one, and thus the Lectric XPress Lite is likely positioned more for riders who favor the low-cost, low-weight, high-efficiency approach of smaller battery commuter e-bikes. And considering my daily driver e-bike has the same sized battery and still nets me around 43 miles (70 km) of range on pedal assist, the Xpress Lite’s 375 Wh battery will still likely be plenty for many riders.
The XPress Lite is now available in four colors – Toasted Marshmallow, Pine Green, Glacier White, and Stratus White – and Lectric offers the usual laundry list of accessories, including racks, fenders, panniers, a suspension seatpost, comfort saddle, mirrors, phone mount, and more. All color options use the same mid-step frame, striking a balance between rigidity and accessibility with a frame that is easier to mount by swinging a leg through the center.
The new model also helps fill another niche in what has become an
impressively broad Lectric lineup
. The Phoenix-based company first made its name with the wildly popular XP folding e-bike series, but has since expanded into cargo bikes, trikes, full-size commuters, lightweight folders, and other models designed around different types of riders. In fact, just about the only type of bike they
make is a unicycle, and at this point, I wouldn’t be too surprised to see one land in my inbox.
A diversity of offerings has been one of Lectric’s strengths: instead of simply making its original bike more expensive and more sophisticated every year, the company has continued branching outward at relatively approachable price points.
At the same time, Lectric has leveraged its industry connections and buying power as the largest e-bike maker in North America
to help launch the new premium e-bike brand, Monarc,
offering higher performance and higher-shelf components that stick to Lectric’s signature affordable pricing ethos.
The XPress Lite feels like another example of that diversification-for-value strategy. Not everyone needs a monster motor, huge battery, fat tires, or a 70-pound e-bike. For riders who primarily want an affordable commuter that’s easier to carry up a few stairs, maneuver through an apartment building, or simply pedal around town, shaving weight and price can be every bit as useful as adding more power.
At $1,099
, the XPress Lite looks like Lectric’s attempt to prove that sometimes less e-bike is actually more.

title: US power prices fall with utility-scale solar, rise with rooftop - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
MIT researchers say there is no link between renewable portfolio standards or utility-scale wind and solar and higher US residential power prices, but rooftop solar correlates with higher rates and distribution costs.
Brian Publicover
13 Oct 2026
Research & Development
Rooftop PV
Utility-scale
Researchers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) have found that renewable portfolio standards (RPS) and utility-scale renewables are not associated with higher residential electricity prices in the United States, while rooftop solar is associated with higher prices.
Fischer J. Espiritu Argosino and Christopher R. Knittel of the MIT Center for Energy and Environmental Policy Research (CEEPR) built a state-utility panel covering 1998 to 2023. It links residential prices, RPS stringency, generation mixes and utility spending, using data from the US Energy Information Administration (EIA), the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) and Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (LBNL).
“Using a two way fixed effects regression model that controls for unobserved differences across years and between states, we find that RPSs and utility scale renewables are not associated with higher residential electricity prices,” the researchers said in a summary of the paper. “Instead, RPSs have virtually zero impact on prices and utility scale renewables are modestly associated with lower prices; in particular, utility-scale solar is strongly linked with lower prices.”
Based on the paper’s regression coefficients, which measure generation shares relative to coal, a 10-percentage-point rise in utility-scale solar’s share of generation is associated with residential prices just over 8% lower. A 5-percentage-point rise in rooftop solar’s share is associated with prices roughly 16% higher. The authors cautioned that the results are correlations and said further work will apply “more rigorous econometric techniques to further strengthen the causal interpretation of these estimates.”
“One explanation is that large solar plants may reduce network congestion and place downward pressure on overall generation costs because they do not require fuel inputs,” the researchers said. A second model, which also controls for differences between utilities, found utility-scale solar strongly associated with lower transmission, distribution and total operation and maintenance (O&M) costs.
The researchers suggested tariff design may partly explain the rooftop solar result.
“One possible reason for this is that current rate structures in some states shift fixed costs associated with rooftop solar from the owners onto other ratepayers,” they said. “In effect, this means that those without rooftop solar often fund those who do through an additional volumetric rate.”
Distribution strain
Rooftop solar was also strongly correlated with higher distribution O&M costs.
“One reason for this is that the distribution network was not designed for bidirectional power flows,” the researchers said.
CEEPR does not peer-review working papers before posting them.
“Policymakers can secure an affordable energy future by improving the integration of low-cost renewables while implementing more equitable cost recovery strategies,” the researchers said.
A June 2025 LBNL study led by Ryan Wiser reached a similar conclusion on utility-scale renewables. It found that the roughly 75% of US utility-scale wind and solar built outside RPS programs had no broadly discernible upward effect on retail prices.
The rooftop solar finding feeds into a long-running dispute over cost-shifting in California. The California Public Utilities Commission’s Public Advocates Office has estimated an $8.5 billion cost shift from rooftop solar customers to other ratepayers. A 2025 report by M.Cubed Consulting and the California Solar and Storage Association found instead that
rooftop solar delivered a $1.5 billion net benefit
to all California ratepayers. Solar advocates have also argued that
rising transmission and distribution spending
is a larger driver of rate increases.
The researchers described their findings in “
Renewables and Electricity Affordability: Untangling Correlation from Causation
,” published as MIT CEEPR Working Paper 2025-22.
