title: Leapting launches autonomous forklift for solar module transport - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
The Chinese robotics manufacturer has introduced an autonomous tracked forklift capable of transporting solar module pallets weighing up to 3,000 kg. The battery-powered machine features a maximum lifting height of 3 m, a 30-degree climbing capability and a navigation system combining GNSS-RTK, laser SLAM and computer vision.
Lior Kahana
13 Oct 2026
Technology & Products
Commercial & industrial
Utility-scale
The Auto-Navigation Forklift Robot
Leapting
, a developer of robotic automation solutions for the PV industry, has unveiled a new autonomous forklift for utility-scale solar construction sites.
Dubbed Auto-Navigation Forklift Robot (AFR), the system can transport pallets of solar modules weighing up to 3,000 kg from laydown yards to installation rows without a human operator.
“The AFR combines GPS-RTK, laser-based simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM), and 3D computer vision to locate pallets, identify fork-hole coordinates in real time, and auto-plan insertion paths,” the company said in a statement. “It further features 360-degree multi-line LiDAR, intelligent obstacle avoidance, and a three-tier braking system.”
The navigation system combines high-precision GNSS-RTK positioning with SLAM for local perception and positioning corrections. According to the manufacturer, the system can identify pallet locations, orientation angles and the three-dimensional coordinates of fork openings in real time. It then automatically calculates insertion and extraction paths and adjusts the mast and forks for pallet handling.
The company said the system can also detect whether pallets contain materials and recognize common pallet standards, including European EUR/EPAL and Japanese JIS specifications.
The AFR measures 4.8 m × 1.8 m × 2.15 m and weighs 5,500 kg. It has a standard load center distance of 600 mm and a maximum lifting height of 3 m. Its two-stage, full-free-lift mast features laterally adjustable forks for precise pallet alignment, the company said.
The forklift uses a tracked chassis with two independently driven 4 kW motors. It reaches a maximum speed of 3 km/h when fully loaded and 4 km/h when unloaded, with adjustable driving speeds. Differential track steering allows the machine to rotate on the spot.
“High-strength engineering-grade steel tracks, with low ground contact pressure, are suitable for diverse complex road conditions and provide stable loads,” the company said.
According to the technical datasheet, the AFR can negotiate gradients of at least 30 degrees on hard surfaces and has a maximum wading depth of 0.3 m. It also supports a maximum forward inclination angle of 4 degrees and a maximum pitch angle of 11 degrees. The manufacturer said the machine is suitable for hard roads, desert terrain, gravel surfaces and lightly uneven or muddy ground.
The AFR is powered by a 48 V, 400 Ah lithium battery, providing a nominal energy capacity of 19.2 kWh and at least eight hours of operation under standard conditions. It supports automatic charging and manual fast charging, with AC 220 V and AC 380 V charging connections. In addition to fully autonomous operation, users can select semi-automatic or manual remote-control modes.
For safety, the forklift incorporates multi-line LiDAR sensors for 360-degree obstacle detection, along with audible and visual warnings. Its three-tier braking system combines electronic, mechanical and parking brakes. Emergency stop buttons are installed at several points on the vehicle exterior.
An integrated inertial measurement unit (IMU) continuously monitors the vehicle’s tilt angle and triggers an alarm and automatic stop if a preset threshold is exceeded.
The AFR offers an IP67 ingress protection rating, depending on the configuration. The company specifies an operating temperature range of -10 C to 50 C and a storage temperature range of -20 C to 60 C.

title: Exide launches modular 125 kW/261 kWh battery for C&I applications - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
The French manufacturer has introduced a new lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery featuring an integrated 125 kW power conversion system, 261 kWh of storage capacity and a nominal round-trip efficiency of 86%.
Emiliano Bellini
13 Oct 2026
Technology & Products
Commercial & industrial
Energy Storage
Highlights
The Solition Powerflex battery
France-based Exide Technologies has launched Solition Powerflex, a modular battery energy storage system (BESS) designed for commercial and industrial applications, renewable energy integration, e-mobility infrastructure and agricultural facilities.
The new system combines a 261 kWh LFP battery with a 125 kW bidirectional power conversion system (PCS) in an outdoor cabinet. Up to 15 cabinets can be connected in parallel for grid-connected applications, providing a maximum combined capacity of 3.915 MWh and power output of 1.875 MW. For off-grid installations, the system supports up to five cabinets.
Each cabinet contains five battery packs with a capacity of 52.25 kWh each, based on 314 Ah LFP cells. The system supports charging and discharging rates of up to 0.5C and operates at an AC voltage of 400 V, with a frequency of 50 Hz or 60 Hz.
According to the manufacturer’s technical datasheet, the system offers a nominal round-trip efficiency of 86%, including auxiliary power consumption.
The IP55-rated outdoor cabinet measures 1,000 mm × 1,420 mm × 2,250 mm and weighs approximately 2,720 kg. It occupies a footprint of around 1.42 m² and is designed to operate at ambient temperatures ranging from -20 C to 50 C, with power derating above 45 C. It is IP55 rated for outdoor use.
Thermal management is provided by a dual-loop liquid cooling and heating system, with separate circuits for the battery and power conversion system, rated at 5 kW and 3 kW, respectively.
The cabinet integrates a battery management system, energy management system, PCS, thermal management and fire protection equipment. Safety features include automatic aerosol fire suppression, emergency shutdown, audible and visual alarms, explosion relief devices and a dedicated external firefighting interface.
Exide said the system incorporates a European-developed Storage Control System (SCS) that enables integration with on-site generation assets, grid operators and energy markets. Supported applications include peak shaving, self-consumption optimization, spot-market trading and ancillary services.
The control platform also offers remote monitoring, over-the-air software updates and interfaces for third-party systems. According to Exide, its digital architecture includes encrypted remote connections, EU-based data hosting and multilayer access controls.
“Organizations are increasingly seeking to improve energy resilience, integrate renewable generation and optimize energy costs,” said Serge Arbes, senior business director global, energy solutions, at Exide Technologies. “Solition Powerflex has been designed to address these evolving requirements, combining a scalable architecture with advanced control capabilities in a solution that can adapt to changing business needs.”
Exide has not disclosed standard warranty terms. The technical datasheet indicates that battery capacity and system warranty conditions are available on request.

title: Three-molecule blend boosts inverted perovskite solar cell efficiency to 27.5% - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Chinese researchers have developed high-entropy molecular contacts that enabled inverted perovskite solar cells to achieve a certified steady-state efficiency of 27.31%. The approach also improves thermal stability by preventing molecular contact degradation.
Lior Kahana
13 Oct 2026
Research & Development
Cells & modules
The device
Improving power conversion efficiency and long-term operational stability remains a key challenge for perovskite solar cells, partly due to the thermal instability of conventional molecular contacts. Under thermal stress, single-component molecular contacts can lose their ordered molecular packing, compromising hole transport and accelerating device degradation. To address this issue, researchers in China have developed high-entropy molecular contacts (HE-MCs) designed to improve both device efficiency and operational stability.
“Developing high-entropy packing in hole-selective self-assembled molecule (HSM) systems to prevent molecular contact (MC) collapse remains unexplored,” the researchers said. “The key challenge is balancing ordered HSM self-assembly with high-entropy structural complexity while maintaining efficient hole transport.”
The researchers said their approach involves blending several specially designed HSMs with similar chemical structures but non-centrosymmetric units to promote complex molecular stacking. Mixing the molecules increases configurational disorder and enables the formation of HE-MCs at the hole-selective interface.
The group fabricated inverted perovskite solar cells using a molecular contact consisting of three related carbazole-based molecules: CbzNaph, CbzNaphBF and CbzNaphBT. The latter two incorporate oxygen- and sulfur-containing units, respectively, resulting in different intermolecular interactions and packing arrangements.
The researchers mixed the molecules at a 1:1:1 molar ratio, spin-coated the solution onto cleaned fluorine-doped tin oxide (FTO) glass substrates, and annealed it at 100 C for 10 minutes to form the hole-selective contact.
They then deposited a perovskite absorber with a bandgap of 1.55 eV using a two-step spin-coating process with chlorobenzene as an antisolvent, followed by annealing at 100 C for 30 minutes. After surface passivation, they deposited a 30 nm fullerene (C60) layer by thermal evaporation, a 40 nm tin oxide (SnO2) layer by atomic layer deposition, and a 100 nm copper rear electrode by thermal evaporation.
The researchers also applied a 120 nm magnesium fluoride coating to the back of the glass substrate to reduce reflection losses. The resulting cell featured an FTO/HE-MCs/perovskite/C60/SnO2/Cu architecture.
The team used molecular dynamics simulations, density functional theory calculations, and structural and spectroscopic measurements to investigate molecular packing and charge transport before and after thermal aging. It also evaluated the completed devices through efficiency measurements, prolonged exposure to 85 C, thermal cycling between room temperature and 85 C, and maximum power point tracking under continuous one-sun illumination at 85 C.
“The HE-MC-based devices showed improved average power conversion efficiency (PCE) from 26.37% to 27.29% compared with the CbzNaph-based device, accompanied by the enhanced open-circuit voltage (VOC) and fill factor (FF), which could be attributed to the enhanced hole-selectivity and interfacial passivation,” the researchers said.
The champion device achieved a power conversion efficiency of 27.50% under reverse-scan conditions, with an open-circuit voltage of 1.202 V, a short-circuit current density of 26.40 mA/cm2, and a fill factor of 86.67%. The researchers reported negligible hysteresis under forward-scan conditions.
The device also achieved an integrated short-circuit current density of 25.72 mA/cm2 based on external quantum efficiency measurements, in good agreement with the current density obtained from current-voltage measurements. The Tianjin Institute of Metrological Supervision and Testing independently certified a steady-state efficiency of 27.31% for one of the fabricated cells.
The certified result is slightly below the 27.41% efficiency reported in May 2026 for an inverted perovskite solar cell fabricated by researchers led by Shaanxi Normal University in China, in collaboration with Linköping University in Sweden and other institutions. The earlier result, published in
, was certified under reverse-scan conditions.
The researchers presented their findings in “
High-entropy molecular contacts enable high-efficiency and stable perovskite solar cells
,” published in
Nature Photonics
. The research team included scientists from China’s City University of Hong Kong, Jilin University, and Sun Yat-sen University.

title: Stationary, moving, flexible: Batteries are the low-cost backbone of the future energy system - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
While it is known that batteries are indispensable for the future energy system dominated by solar PV, they are still seen as a bottleneck technology mostly related to raw material supply. Sodium-ion batteries can resolve this issue. Batteries are more than a stationary storage technology, also with bright prospects for vehicle-to-grid (V2G) and smart charging of electric vehicles within a broad flexibility technology portfolio.
LUT University
13 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Batteries
Energy Storage
Batteries are already low cost but are still experiencing significant learning. Previous cost assumptions were too high.
The resolved issue of batteries as bottleneck
Battery technology is often associated with the material bottleneck issue: A stringent transition to highly renewable energy systems in combination with high electrification would require large capacities for battery storage, both stationary and mobile, for which there is not enough Lithium available. Lithium criticality is, indeed, an important topic, while
previous research
has found that well-established recycling, vehicle-to-grid (V2G), and transport with low Lithium intensity (non-battery electric) would be required.
recent study
took a closer look at one of the most promising alternatives to Lithium-ion batteries (LIB) on the horizon: Sodium-ion batteries (SIB). Contrary to LIBs, SIBs are based on abundant raw materials, also beyond the cathode material: Anodes can be made of hard carbon instead of natural graphite, and copper as a current collector at the anode can be substituted with the more available and cheaper aluminum.
Previous energy system simulations
resulted in close to 75 TWh
stationary battery demand by 2050, while an estimation for mobile batteries revealed a dominating role of moving batteries at up to almost 275 TWh
Latest findings
indicate a ratio of needed battery capacity to installed solar PV capacity of about 0.8 kWh
/kW in a cost-optimized and flexible global energy system that is run entirely on renewable energy. Adding the niche of electronics and other applications, the
total battery demand
may reach over 350 TWh
The bottom-up, cell-level to system-level cost assessment showed that SIBs are already close to cost parity with their Lithium counterpart. In 2025, system-level costs were estimated to be ca. €120 /kWh
. By applying different learning rates, costs may be reduced until 2050 to a range of €28.5-51.9 /kWh
. This allows for the conclusion that batteries are ruled out as a bottleneck because of raw material limitations, but also for cost reasons. Furthermore, SIBs as a drop-in technology can be easily produced on existing production lines set up originally for LIBs.
PV prosumers: More than stationary
Solar PV prosumers, an actors who are both producers and consumers of electricity, do not necessarily require batteries to have a secure electricity supply. Using the connection to the electricity grid, surplus electricity from the rooftop PV system can be fed into the grid and reimbursed, and at times of low or no solar PV yield, electricity can be drawn from the grid. Increasing grid electricity prices and decreasing battery costs, however, may make it economically beneficial to equip the prosumer system with a battery to optimize the overall supply cost of energy.
An initial study
on the cost-optimization of solar PV prosumers has already shown that PV-battery systems for prosumers are widely beneficial in terms of the total cost of energy supply. Key is the electrification of the heat supply via heating rods or heat pumps. Very low-cost solar PV is no limitation, even though residential
rooftop PV yields ca. 18% less electricity
than ground-mounted systems. The combination with stationary battery storage enables high demand and heat cover ratios globally. Battery capacity optimization depends on the inclusion of electric vehicles (EV). High benefits have been found for cars that can supply the system with electricity, so-called vehicle-to-home (V2H).
In a follow-up study
, it has been investigated whether a seasonal hydrogen storage is beneficial for residential PV prosumer systems. The long-term storage option has been found to play only a niche role for Nordic countries in an off-grid scenario, even with a
significant cost reduction potential
. With the updated optimization model, it has been shown that most of the regions will reach grid parity by 2035, with more than half of the regions having reached parity already in 2020. The improved optimization model confirmed that batteries play an important role. For the on-grid cases, a maximum battery-to-PV ratio of 1.6-1.8 kWh
/kW has been found. In off-grid cases, this ratio increases to 3-4 kWh
The case of smart charging and vehicle-to-grid (V2G)
The EV fleet is
growing fast around the world
, already accumulating battery capacity on the terawatt-hour scale and
driving solar PV capacity demand
. Using this battery capacity for power system balancing is a promising solution for energy systems with a growing share of variable renewable electricity generation. Smart charging alone provides valuable flexibility by increasing electricity consumption during renewable electricity generation peaks and reducing it during periods of generation deficit. V2G goes a step further, turning EVs into distributed battery storage on wheels that can supply electricity to the grid during deficit periods.
study analyzing the impact of smart charging and V2G
confirmed substantial benefits for the energy system. These technologies allow the system to reduce installed utility-scale battery storage capacity by about 50%, which indirectly reduces critical material use in batteries and also lowers the need for other energy storage technologies. Enabling these two technologies alone may reduce the total annual system costs by about 4%.
However, V2G cannot be free for the system: EV owners must be incentivized to participate and compensated for battery wear. The role and impact of V2G will depend strongly on the cost of this service to the system, but even at €50-100 /MWh, V2G still provides benefits for the system. The main challenge for V2G is the public infrastructure needed for EVs to charge or feed high-quality AC power into the grid whenever they are parked, especially during the midday PV generation peak, when additional storage capacity is most valuable.
A flexibility perspective
Flexibility is needed to mitigate the variability of renewable energy sources arising from their weather-dependent nature. Battery energy storage systems have gained widespread attention as a potential leading technology for this role. Their advantages include high energy density, rapid response, reliable power delivery, sustained discharge capability, and geographical independence.
The continued reduction in battery manufacturing costs has further strengthened the role of battery storage in facilitating renewable energy integration, particularly for solar PV. A
comprehensive review of flexibility options
in over 1000 research articles found that compared with other storage technologies, including
pumped hydro energy storage
, thermal energy storage, and e-hydrogen storage, battery technologies currently offer an attractive combination of rapid response, modularity, efficiency, and technological maturity. Nevertheless, one should not regard batteries and pumped hydro energy storage as substitutes but as complements to serve the same need, as also highlighted in
the case of India
A key factor underpinning the attractiveness of battery technology as a flexibility option is the sustained reduction in battery costs, despite fluctuations in raw material prices. Moreover, this cost reduction has been observed across both mobile and stationary applications, highlighting the versatility and improving cost competitiveness of battery technologies across a wide range of applications.
This technological advancement, driven by continued innovation, is expected to play a significant role in accelerating the deployment of solar PV across the global Sunbelt and other regions, such as
, and in particular also for
off-grid applications
. The rise of solar PV would not be thinkable without electricity storage and in particular battery storage, as shown in a recent analysis in
major milestones for solar PV
in energy transition scenarios which also led a projected primary
energy supply share of solar PV
of about 61% in energy transition studies on a global average by mid-century. Overall,
solar PV is expected to play a major role
also outside of the Sunbelt. In smaller and isolated grids, such as islands and off-grid systems, rising diesel fuel costs, combined with the rapid decline in the costs of renewable energy technologies, have increased the competitiveness of renewable energy sources and enhanced the relevance of battery-based energy storage solutions. This trend is driving the increasing adoption of off-grid and decentralized autonomous power systems, including PV-battery and wind-battery configurations.
Authors: Dominik Keiner, Siavash Khalili, Dmitrii Bogdanov, and Christian Breyer
This article is part of a monthly column by the LUT University.
Research at
LUT University
encompasses various analyses related to power, heat, transport, industry, desalination, and negative CO
emission options. Power-to-X research is a core topic at the university, integrated into the focus areas of Planetary Resources, Business and Society, Digital Revolution, and Energy Transition. Solar energy plays a key role in all research aspects.
The views and opinions expressed in this article are the author’s own, and do not necessarily reflect those held by

title: European PPA prices rise 5% in September - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
European PPA prices rose 5% in September, driven by higher forward electricity and gas prices, while Spain and Portugal recorded declines. Contracting activity rebounded, with 25 deals totaling 1.2 GW, alongside growing interest in hybrid PPAs and battery storage agreements.
Pilar Sánchez Molina
13 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Highlights
Utility-scale
Swiss consultancy Pexapark’s EURO Composite Index rose 5% in September, driven by higher forward electricity prices across most European markets. Rising gas prices pushed up power purchase agreement (PPA) fair values, although calibration adjustments also contributed to the increase.
Great Britain recorded the largest monthly increase, at 10.9%, followed by Italy and Poland (6.9% each), the Nordic countries (4.3%) and the Netherlands (4.1%). Germany and France posted increases of 3.6% and 3.1%, respectively. The Iberian Peninsula was the exception, with PPA prices falling 3.5% in Spain and 1.4% in Portugal.
Pexapark also recalibrated PPA fair values in Denmark after buyers increased the risk discounts applied to their pricing. The adjustment reduced 10-year baseload values for contracts starting in 2028 by approximately €5 ($5.6)/MWh, although an upward revision to capture curves partially offset the impact on pay-as-produced PPAs.
In Poland, an update to the hourly forward price curve increased the additional value available to solar PPAs paired with battery energy storage systems (BESS).
PPA contracting activity recovered after the summer slowdown. A total of 25 agreements representing approximately 1.2 GW of announced capacity were disclosed in September, compared with 14 contracts totaling 335 MW in August.
Corporate buyers accounted for 21 agreements and nearly 1.1 GW, representing 92% of the announced capacity. One of the largest deals was Google’s 22-year, 507 MW agreement supporting the extension of operations at Finland’s Loviisa nuclear power plant.
Onshore wind slightly exceeded solar PV in contracted capacity, with 281 MW and 276 MW, respectively. Solar projects paired with BESS accounted for an additional 167 MW.
Italy led in the number of agreements, with seven deals, including six small-scale, on-site self-consumption PPAs and Amazon’s virtual PPA covering 156 MW of capacity at the Big Fish agrivoltaic project in Sicily.
Flexible deals gain momentum
Flexible power agreements (FPAs) also gained momentum in September, with 16 deals announced across Europe, representing approximately 2.1 GW and 4.7 GWh of contracted capacity. This was more than double the 869 MW and 2.4 GWh recorded in August.
Four tolling agreements accounted for 925 MW, including a 10-year, 400 MW contract between Statkraft and Greenvolt, described as the first of its kind announced in Poland.
Agreements featuring revenue floors and profit-sharing mechanisms covered 548 MW, while merchant structures with revenue sharing accounted for just 80 MW, indicating a growing preference for revenue hedging.
Hybrid PPAs also gained traction, with three agreements announced in September, the highest monthly total to date. The third quarter also marked a record for these structures.
Zelestra signed a hybrid PPA with German steelmaker Salzgitter covering electricity from 147 MW of solar capacity and a 79 MW/237 MWh battery system charged exclusively by the solar plants. The agreement reflects growing interest among industrial electricity consumers in using storage to provide a more reliable renewable energy supply.
Other notable deals included Statkraft’s agreement with Wattmanufactur in Germany and Shell’s PPA for Abei Energy’s Arcos de la Frontera project in Spain. Both involve structures combining solar generation with storage optimization.

title: Enpal, Würth unveil safety platform for PV deployment on pitched roofs - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
The new RAST system combines roof access, fall protection and material transport in a standardized installation process. German trade associations BG ETEM and BG BAU supported its development.
Petra Hannen
13 Oct 2026
Technology & Products
Commercial & industrial
Residential
According to Enpal and Würth, a distinctive feature of the system is roof access via a newly designed mobile work platform.
German residential solar installer Enpal and fastening and assembly technology supplier Adolf Würth GmbH & Co. KG have developed the Roof Access Safety Transport System (RAST) for work on pitched roofs. According to the companies, the system is designed to improve occupational safety during the installations of rooftop PV arrays and can be adapted to different building configurations.
The system includes a mobile work platform for roof access, edge protection, personal fall protection equipment and fixed roof anchor points. It also features a material lift and emergency equipment.
According to the companies, a key component is a newly developed mobile work platform that provides access to the roof. They claim it is the first solution of its kind to be tested in accordance with DIN EN 13374, which is the German adoption of the European standard EN 13374 specifying safety and testing requirements for temporary edge protection systems.
Testing was carried out in cooperation with DGUV Test, the testing and certification system of the German Social Accident Insurance, with technical input from Germany’s statutory accident insurance institutions BG ETEM, which covers the energy, textile, electrical and media industries, and BG BAU, which covers the construction sector.
RAST is designed for pitched roofs with eaves heights of up to 8 meters. The work platform and a walkway along the roof edge provide installers with a working area comparable to scaffolding. The system also allows materials to be transported onto the roof without ladders.
“Working without ladders, in particular, will noticeably reduce the risk of accidents,” said Martin Umminger, product manager at Würth. The companies said secure roof access and material transport remain available throughout the installation process.
Enpal is preparing to roll out the system through training sessions at its Enpal Academy. RAST will then be gradually integrated into the company’s standard installation procedures.
The companies did not disclose investment or acquisition costs or indicate whether the system would be made available to other installation companies.

title: Qatar's renewable capacity share could more than double by 2035 - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Renewables could rise from 12% of Qatar’s power capacity in 2025 to 25.9% by 2035, says GlobalData, with solar leading while gas remains the backbone of its power and water system.
Brian Publicover
13 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Utility-scale
Qatar’s installed power capacity will grow at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 4.2% between 2025 and 2035, with solar expanding at a CAGR of 12.4% over the same period, according to a new report from GlobalData.
The analytics company said Qatar is accelerating utility-scale solar deployment to diversify its power mix, reduce domestic gas consumption for power generation and curb emissions intensity. It said it expects renewables to account for 25.9% of total power capacity by 2035, up from 12% in 2025.
“Qatar’s power sector is shifting from total reliance on natural gas toward a structured hybrid model,” said Attaurrahman Ojindaram Saibasan, power analyst at GlobalData. “Driven by the Qatar National Renewable Energy Strategy, the build-out of major solar facilities such as Al Kharsaah and the recently commissioned plants at Ras Laffan and Mesaieed, alongside the large-scale Dukhan development demonstrate substantial momentum in deploying low-cost clean generation across the peninsula.”
Solar pipeline
800 MW Al Kharsaah plant
began supplying the grid in June 2022. Project company Siraj-1 owns it. Siraj Energy, a joint venture of QatarEnergy and Qatar Electricity & Water Co. (QEWC), holds 60% of Siraj-1, while TotalEnergies and Marubeni hold the remaining 40%. The plant sells its output to state utility Kahramaa under a 25-year agreement.
QatarEnergy
inaugurated the 458 MW Ras Laffan and 417 MW Mesaieed plants
in April 2025, taking Qatar’s solar capacity to 1,675 MW. Samsung C&T built both plants. In September 2025, QatarEnergy
selected Samsung C&T as EPC contractor for the 2 GW Dukhan project
, which is due to connect its first 1 GW phase by the end of 2028 and reach full capacity by mid-2029.
QatarEnergy has said Dukhan and its existing plants will supply up to 30% of Qatar’s peak electricity demand and cut carbon dioxide emissions by about 4.7 million metric tons a year.
Kahramaa launched the Qatar National Renewable Energy Strategy in April 2024. It targets about 4 GW of utility-scale renewables and about 200 MW of distributed generation by 2030, raising the renewable share of the power mix from 5% to 18%. Under its updated nationally determined contribution, Qatar has pledged to cut greenhouse gas emissions by 25% by 2030 compared with a business-as-usual scenario.
Gas backbone
GlobalData said natural gas capacity will keep growing in absolute terms and account for about 74% of Qatar’s installed capacity in 2035. Combined-cycle gas turbines and cogeneration plants underpin the country’s independent water and power projects (IWPPs), which supply both electricity for summer cooling loads and thermal energy for seawater desalination.
“The cogeneration of potable water and power is a structural feature of Qatar’s utility system,” Saibasan said. “Gas-fired IWPP facilities provide critical firming capacity to absorb large influxes of solar energy during midday hours while securing baseload water desalination. Expanding flexible gas generation and modernizing grid management are essential prerequisites for accommodating the planned 4GW renewable target by 2030 without compromising system security.”
Qatar runs a single-buyer model, under which Kahramaa purchases electricity and desalinated water through long-term agreements. Kahramaa has also introduced net-billing rules for distributed generation.
Qatar has yet to commission a utility-scale battery. Kahramaa tendered consultancy services earlier this year for what it described as its first major utility-scale battery energy storage project, with bids due Feb. 15. It has not disclosed the project’s capacity.
“Qatar is leveraging its world-class solar irradiance and robust balance sheet to free up valuable natural gas volumes for liquefied natural gas (LNG) export markets while decarbonizing its domestic matrix,” Saibasan said. “Sustaining this pace will require continuing to align renewable integration with IWPP offtake commitments, meeting growing industrial demand, and maintaining high transmission reliability across the National Control Centre and regional GCC interconnection links.”
Kahramaa’s only grid-connected battery to date is a 1 MW/4 MWh pilot. It
installed the Tesla Powerpack system
at its Nuaijia substation in 2020.

title: Visionpark unveils new foundation-free solar carport for residential use - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
The Atlas range is scheduled to become available in January 2027, with three models offering PV capacities from 3 kW to 15 kW and heights of up to 4 meters.
François Puthod
13 Oct 2026
Technology & Products
Residential
French solar carport specialist
Visionpark
is expanding its portfolio with Atlas, a new range of single-arm precast concrete structures designed for residential, commercial and service-sector applications.
The Atlas carports feature a self-ballasting design that eliminates the need for foundations or ground anchors. The structures are placed directly on the ground, with their own weight providing the ballast required for each configuration.
According to the manufacturer, the design reduces civil engineering work and installation times. “Our goal is to offer a genuine energy station – designed and manufactured in France – that is delivered pre-equipped and can be installed in a single day by two technicians,” Armand Teolis, founder of Visionpark, told
pv magazine France
Three models
Visionpark said the structures and mounting systems have been designed to comply with Eurocodes, a set of European standards for structural design. The technical documentation includes a French technical assessment known as an ETN (
Étude de Technique Nouvelle
), which evaluates innovative construction systems not covered by established technical standards. The assessment covers both the carport structure and the PV mounting system.
Atlas uses an industrial prefabrication process, with the concrete structures manufactured off-site before delivery. The carports will feature PV modules from French manufacturer
Voltec Solar
, combined with an aluminum mounting system developed specifically for the range.
The Atlas range is scheduled to become available in January 2027, with three models offering PV capacities from 3 kW to 15 kW and heights of up to 4 meters.
Depending on the model and customer requirements, the carports can be pre-equipped with an electric vehicle charger, a PV inverter, integrated rooftop PV connections, an energy management system and battery storage with capacities ranging from 3 kWh to 20 kWh.
Visionpark previously

for larger applications in 2024, using prefabricated structures supplied by Italian manufacturer Paver. The self-ballasting structures, weighing around 10 metric tons each, were designed to cover up to eight parking spaces and accommodate different types of PV modules.
At the time, Visionpark said the system could be installed without conventional foundations, minimizing disruption to existing parking areas. The company also reported installation rates of 300 square meters to 500 square meters per day. The system used a French-made mounting structure supplied by Hydro.

title: Inside BESS manufacturing: Maxxen’s utility-scale storage factory in Europe - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
A detailed look at Maxxen’s advanced BESS factory from an on-the-ground tour.
Tristan Rayner
13 Oct 2026
Markets & Policy
Batteries
Energy Storage
Maxxen’s 5 MWh DC Box
“Made in Europe” isn’t an unusual tag in large-scale battery systems, but last week, at an open day held at Maxxen Energy’s facility in Aydın, Türkiye, an almost no-limits event was held for its factory that began operations in 2026 in a 20,000-square-meter containerized battery manufacturing facility.
Speaking on site during media tours and detailed interviews, Ruben Valiente, Maxxen’s Managing Director, staff, and leadership from parent company Kontek Energy, offered a rare, transparent look into the strategy, supply chain realities, and automated assembly powering their 20,000-square-meter containerized battery manufacturing plant.
Ruben Valiente, MD, Maxxen Energy, presenting the opening keynote.
Image: ESS News
Maxxen, which is headquartered in Switzerland, produces two main products: its 5 MWh DC Box container, and offers an optional MV Power Station dubbed MV Box, with a power output of 2.5 MW, 5.0 MW or 10 MW, and facility certifications include TÜV Accredited, ISO 27001, LEED Certified (100% self-sustained).
With a nameplate capacity of 5 GWh per year, and with current utilization at 1.5 GWh per year, the factory continues to ramp. The company announced that a total of 664 MWh has been sold across 21 global projects in the nine months from January 2026.
Maxxen emerged as a 100% owned subsidiary of Kontek Energy, a Turkish renewable energy specialist with more than 30 years of engineering expertise. It built the Maxxen factory, and  crucially, signed a layered agreement with Chinese battery cell and ESS manufacturer Hithium, which currently supplies 314 Ah cells for manufacture, each around approximately 1 kWh, with 5,000 packing into a single DC Box.
Maxxen’s products are essentially Hithium-spec, assembled in Europe, with significantly deep agreements between the two parties, though no ownership or equity stakes have been taken by either party. Hithium was chosen, among many criteria, for its strict focus on ESS.
The facility,
ESS News
was told, represented a $35 million investment designed to supply European, Middle Eastern, and regional utility-scale projects. Maxxen reps further indicated that the site will transition to using 587 Ah cells by end-2027.
Utility-scale
BESS assembly
Pleasingly, media tours of the ESS assembly factory were allowed to capture photos and videos of the product line, which included detailed explanations, questions, and flow chart visuals to aid understanding.
The following guide walk through the plant’s four main assembly stages. Automation is used throughout, but still involves on-site staff for key actions, including visual inspections. KUKA robotic arms are in use across the facility for picking and packing cells and modules.
Cell Pre-Charging & Testing stage
is completely automated, where Hithium-brandedPrismatic LFP cells, each rated at 314 Ah and 3.2 V nominal, undergo automated open-circuit voltage (OCV) testing and 100% barcode and QR-code scanning for digital traceability.
The facility treats each cell as an unknown, and each large prismatic and bright blue cell undergoes controlled pre-charging and testing to activate and stabilize chemistry. Energy used in this process is, for want of a better term, recycled and captured within the site’s own energy storage, fulfilling LEED self-sustained energy criteria. Charging and discharging losses through heat are compensated by solar generation in the day.
This section of the factory is sealed off as a clean room, under positive ventilation, producing a distinct white-noise din. In the case of a fire caused by a cell, strict safety routines are followed, and the room can be evacuated completely of oxygen within 100 seconds.
The second stage is
Robotic Stacking & Laser Welding.
KUKA robotic arms place cells into module structures, stacking cells into 2P52S module configurations (104 cells per module). End plates are installed, and the cell stack undergoes mechanical steel belt compression and PET auto-strapping. Pole surfaces on the cell are laser-cleaned to remove oxidation, and a flex-printed Cell Contact System (CCS) and circuit is installed. Laser welding joins the connection points. Automated 3D CCD cameras check the welds, followed by a final electrical safety test. Each module then weighs approximately 667 kg.
The third stage relates to the liquid-cooling setup, which keeps temperatures in check. Cells are bonded onto the thermal cooling plate using a glue described as a ‘structural thermal adhesive’. In this stage, the
Coolant & Water Verification,
each rack of cells and module cooling manifolds undergo pressurized liquid chiller leak testing and water verification checks prior to container loading.
In the final stage,
Container Integration & Load Testing
, which was the most manual and labor-intensive, finished battery modules are transferred via overhead cranes onto AGV (Automated Guided Vehicle) platforms, which position and slide each 667 kg rack into a standard 20ft container enclosure. Separately, power electronics, liquid cooling units and pumps, HVAC compartments, and automated fire protection systems are integrated, away from the battery cell line, before full functional load testing.
Eckhart Gouras
Logistics
and supply chains
Operational takeaway from the Aydin includes how Maxxen’s supply-chain strategy works. To hedge against maritime shipping delays from Asia (such as Red Sea vessels needing to reroute around the horn of Africa), Maxxen maintains a 200 to 250 MWh warehouse buffer stock of battery cells and raw materials directly on site.
This inventory buffer allows Maxxen to offer deliveries within 1 to 2 weeks by truck across mainland Europe (including, for example, Germany, Romania, Spain), enabling developers to receive containerized batteries when needed, and not earlier.
Target markets at this stage include Southern Europe, the Middle East, the Balkans, and regional utility-scale grid projects across mainland Europe.
In terms of certifications, Maxxen holds 27 official safety certificates directly under its own name. In terms of the so-called large-scale fire test, it relies on Hithium’s UL 9540A burn test data for container-level fire validation.
Early success
In its first nine months of operation (January to September), the factory delivered 664 MWh across 21 global projects, capturing an estimated 5% market share in its European target segment.
Vendor financing, a key pitch of Maxxen’s and one that has attracted considerable commercial interest.
Ruben Valiente, Maxxen’s Managing Director, told
ESS News
, “We have received letters of intent for 4 GWh. We have signed 2 or 3 activation fees already to deploy this over the next 6 to 12 months, and once the contract is signed, we are bound to commit and obliged to deliver.”

title: How SubCom builds the undersea cables that carry internet data across oceans
content: More than 99 percent of international data flows through submarine telecommunications cables, according to the International Telecommunication Union (ITU). These fiber-optic lines carry everything from cloud traffic and financial transactions to video calls between continents. Much of that hidden infrastructure depends on a surprisingly specialized industry: manufacturers who build cables designed to operate for decades beneath the ocean.One of the companies building that infrastructure is SubCom, which operates a roughly 50-acre manufacturing campus in Newington, New Hampshire. The company designs, manufactures, and installs undersea fiber-optic networks, bringing together factory production, optical engineering, marine operations, and system testing.The facility is now expanding as demand for international bandwidth grows. But its work involves more than producing long lengths of cable: each system must be engineered to transmit data across thousands of kilometers while withstanding pressure, water exposure, and the physical stresses of installation on the seabed.How glass fibers carry data across oceansAt the heart of a submarine communications cable are optical fibers. These extremely thin glass strands transmit information as pulses of light. Unlike conventional electrical cables, which carry signals as electrical currents, fiber optics can carry enormous amounts of digital information over long distances with relatively little signal loss.However, the fibers cannot simply be dropped into the ocean unprotected. Submarine cables are engineered with layers that shield the delicate glass from water, mechanical stress, and other environmental hazards. Depending on the route, manufacturers can add protective layers and steel-wire armoring to help the cable withstand demanding conditions, particularly in shallower waters where anchors and fishing equipment pose greater risks.The cable’s construction also depends on its intended operating environment. A lightweight design may be suitable for deep ocean sections, while more heavily protected versions are used in areas where external damage is more likely. This means a single submarine network can use different cable designs along its route rather than relying on one uniform construction.Why a cable needs more than glassEven with high-quality optical fibers, signals weaken over long distances. Submarine networks therefore use optical repeaters installed along the cable route to amplify the signals, allowing information to continue across ocean basins.These repeaters must operate reliably in an environment that is difficult and expensive to access. Their housings need to withstand immense water pressure, prevent water ingress, and protect sensitive components. The cable itself also needs an electrical conductor to deliver power from shore-based equipment to repeaters along the route.At SubCom’s Newington campus, cable manufacturing is part of a larger integration process. The company says it builds the components of its subsea systems at the facility, bringing the cable, repeaters, and other equipment together before deployment. The completed system is tested before it is loaded onto a cable-laying vessel.That factory-to-ship workflow matters because installing a cable across an ocean is a major marine engineering operation. Teams survey the seabed, plan a route, account for water depth and potential hazards, and carefully control how the cable is laid. Near shore, cables are often buried for added protection, while sections in deeper water may rest directly on the seabed.A factory expanding for global data demandSubCom’s Newington facility has a history dating back to 1953, when it operated as Simplex Wire & Cable. Today, it is a central part of a company that says it has deployed more than one million kilometers (about 621,000 miles) of subsea cable systems worldwide, enough to circle the Earth roughly 25 times.The company is expanding the site to increase production. According to a January 2026 report in the Portsmouth Herald, based on information from SubCom, the Newington facility was producing approximately 58,000 kilometers (36,000 miles) of cable annually. The company aims to raise that figure to around 77,000 kilometers (47,800 miles) by the end of 2026, with a longer-term target of 100,000 kilometers (62,000 miles) per year. The expansion includes more than 100,000 square feet of manufacturing space, new extrusion and power-conductor lines, and plans to add 75 to 100 jobs at the site.That capacity is intended to serve a market shaped by growing data traffic, cloud computing, and technology companies connecting data centers across continents. SubCom has worked on systems including Grace Hopper, which connects the United States, United Kingdom, and Spain, and SEA-ME-WE 6, a 19,200-kilometer (11,900 miles) network linking Southeast Asia, the Middle East, and Western Europe.Submarine cables remain vulnerable to anchors, fishing activity, seabed disturbances, and natural hazards, making careful route planning, maintenance, and repair essential. The ITU has highlighted the need to strengthen the resilience of these networks as they underpin international communications and economic activity.The result is an often-overlooked part of the internet’s physical infrastructure. Data may appear to travel invisibly between screens, but much of it depends on glass fibers manufactured in specialized facilities, assembled into pressure-resistant cables, tested on land, and laid across the ocean floor. In Newington, that work is becoming an even larger industrial operation as the world’s demand for international connectivity continues to grow.

title: Chalcogenide perovskites could be used in solar cells, light sensors
content: Researchers have experimentally shown that chalcogenide perovskites can emit light more efficiently than previous measurements suggested, strengthening the case for investigating the materials for future solar cells, photodetectors, and other optoelectronic devices.The team, led by Mirjana Dimitrievska at Switzerland’s Empa research institute, worked with researchers from the Helmholtz-Zentrum Berlin für Materialien und Energie and other partners. Their study examined barium zirconium sulfide, a chalcogenide perovskite whose light-emission properties Empa said researchers had not previously demonstrated experimentally. The results also revealed a challenge. Although single crystals showed relatively strong light emission, defects introduced during synthesis and processing significantly suppressed the same property in thin films.Measuring light outputPerovskites are defined by their crystal structure rather than one particular chemical composition. While halide perovskites have received considerable attention for solar cells, chalcogenide perovskites are being investigated as alternatives because they combine potentially useful optical and electronic properties with greater material stability and constituent elements that are abundant in Earth’s crust.The challenge has been establishing whether their predicted properties translate into measurable performance. Until now, Empa reports that the light-emission efficiency of chalcogenide perovskites has not been experimentally demonstrated.To investigate the material, the researchers used advanced spectroscopic techniques to measure photoluminescence in a barium zirconium sulfide crystal produced at the Helmholtz-Zentrum Berlin. Photoluminescence occurs when a material absorbs energy and subsequently emits light. The findings were published in Advanced Optical Materials.The measurements showed relatively strong emission from the single crystal, consistent with theoretical predictions. Thin films, however, exhibited substantially weaker photoluminescence. This difference matters because promising materials must eventually be synthesized and processed into practical device structures. Defects introduced during those steps can disrupt the electronic processes needed for efficient light emission, potentially limiting a material’s performance even when its underlying crystal structure is favorable. The researchers’ findings therefore provide both a positive result and a development challenge: the material’s intrinsic potential appears promising, but manufacturing processes will need further refinement.Potential beyond solar powerResearchers are investigating chalcogenide perovskites for applications including solar cells and photodetectors. Their stability and constituent elements could make them attractive candidates for optoelectronic technologies, although the research remains at an early stage.The new measurements help researchers distinguish between limitations inherent to a material and those caused by synthesis or processing. Spectroscopic analysis can reveal whether poor performance stems from defects in the material itself or from other issues in a prototype device, helping guide subsequent improvements.Empa emphasized that considerable development remains before chalcogenide perovskites are ready for practical applications. The results show promising light emission in single crystals, not a commercially viable solar cell or a proven improvement in solar-conversion efficiency.Unexpected structures attract attentionThe researchers are also investigating a second development emerging from the synthesis process. When chalcogenide perovskites are produced from their constituent elements, tiny needle-like structures with hexagonal cross-sections can form alongside the desired crystalline material.Previously considered an undesirable byproduct, these structures have displayed unusual optical properties, including the ability to polarize, refract, and conduct light in distinctive ways. They may also have potential as superconductors and quantum materials.With support from the Swiss National Science Foundation through its international Weave program, Dimitrievska’s team is collaborating with Friedrich-Alexander University Erlangen-Nürnberg in Germany to investigate these structures, improve their synthesis, and better understand their properties.The researchers ultimately aim to integrate the needle-like materials into initial photonic and electronic components. Together, the two research directions show how a deeper understanding of material behavior can open new possibilities in optoelectronics. Chalcogenide perovskites still face substantial engineering challenges, but experimentally confirming their light-emission properties provides a stronger foundation for deciding where further development may be worthwhile.

title: SpaceX inspired rocket catch tech takes center stage in China’s Nebula-2 development
content: The race for cheap, lightning-fast access to orbit has a new, giant metallic contestant.On Monday, Chinese commercial startup Deep Blue Aerospace announced that the 5-meter-diameter (16ft) stainless steel propellant tank for its Nebula-2 rocket has rolled off the assembly line. It is a massive piece of technology. Above all, it shows that China’s private space sector is ready to clone one of the most audacious tricks in modern rocketry: catching a returning booster mid-air with giant mechanical “chopsticks.” Reusability and rapid turnaround times remain the core measures of success in modern commercial spaceflight. Deep Blue Aerospace is narrowing the technological gap with Western space leaders through its pad-captured, stainless-steel rocket design.The heavy lifterDesigned to haul up to 25 tons into low Earth orbit, Nebula-2 is built for high-tempo commercial work. The first stage packs 11 Thunder-RS engines generating an immense 12,446 kilonewtons of liftoff thrust, while a single vacuum-optimized engine carries the upper stage.Global Times reported that the Nebula-2 has been designed for over 20 reuses. It aims to become the workhorse for China’s expanding satellite internet network and commercial payload demands. The newly completed 5-meter propellant tank sets a record for large-diameter stainless steel tank manufacturing in China’s private space sector. Tanks form the structural backbone of any rocket. Completing this component paves the way for a second-stage propulsion system test slated for the end of the year.Designed for high payload capacity and cost efficiency, Nebula-2 can support a wide range of space missions. The rocket will deploy large-scale satellite internet constellations. It will also launch high-value payloads into medium Earth orbit, geosynchronous transfer orbit, and other destinations for clients worldwide.Taking a page from SpaceX’s playbookIf the design feels familiar, that is because SpaceX pioneered it. SpaceX demonstrated that massive rockets can forgo heavy landing legs when its “Mechazilla” tower arms caught the 233-foot Super Heavy booster during Starship Flight 5. Catching the booster directly out of the sky at the pad reduced the need for sea-barge recoveries.Now, Deep Blue Aerospace wants a piece of that efficiency. The firm aims to eliminate separate landing zones and slash launch costs through an in-situ chopstick-style capture system on the Nebula-2 pad. Equipping the rocket with this mechanism enables faster turnaround times right at the launch site. As a result, the streamlined recovery process offers a far more efficient alternative to conventional off-site landings.China is actively advancing its reusable spaceflight capabilities at sea and on land. State-backed Long March-10B reached a major milestone on July 10 when it recovered its first stage at sea using an offshore platform net system. Shortly after, on August 19, LandSpace’s Zhuque-3 Y2 rocket completed China’s first successful land-based booster recovery using deployable landing legs. Together, these achievements show the country’s rapid progress in mastering diverse booster recovery techniques.There’s also high competition among the companies to build out the nation’s low-Earth orbit satellite internet infrastructure. Enterprise contenders like LandSpace, Space Pioneer, i-Space, and Galactic Energy are working to win contracts for national megaconstellations such as Guowang and Qianfan. Deep Blue Aerospace joins these rivals in attempting to capture market share in a rapidly expanding sector.

title: PhoneBot: New robot uses old Android phones to walk, see, and balance
content: The smartphones lying idle in drawers could serve as brains for the bipedal bot. Researchers at the University of California, Los Angeles, have built a compact walking robot called ‘PhoneBot’ using old, unused Android phones.Built as an open-source platform, the robot stands tall at about 19 inches (1.5 ft) and weighs under four pounds.To assist in bipedal movement, the team placed the phone as a torso. Its basic components include a camera, motion sensors, processor, and wireless connection. All these features help the bot to see, maintain balance, and calculate movements, much like the functions performed by the human brain.Graphical representation of PhoneBot. Credit: ArXiv study paperMotors mimic joints, aid gaitThe PhoneBot is also equipped with 13 low-cost DYNAMIXEL servo motors, with each leg carrying six of them, maintaining the traditional bipedal leg architecture. The joints at the hip, knee, and ankle help the robot to walk, turn, and recover as any being with a two-foot locomotory system would. Researchers kept the extra thirteenth joint in the torso to let the upper body spin. These side-to-side movements allow the torso joint the swing the mounted phone camera, helping the bot track a person without moving its feet.Phone as command centerThe smartphone sends commands to a Wi-Fi-enabled computer system installed in the lower body of the robot. These wireless information packages are translated into different motor positions. Researchers said the wireless contact between the phone and body was designed to keep the construction and replacement easier. The design is also kept simple to permit easier phone swapping without the requirement of rewiring, given that smartphones are the only variable factor influencing the costs, researchers added.Other equipment expenses that comprise the body, motors, and supporting electronics are more and less fixed at around four hundred dollars.In the experiments conducted by the UCLA engineers, they tested four different Android devices, including versions priced between $50 and $80. Based on their findings, all four performed basic functions, including walking, movement detection, and viewing ability.‘Phonebot’ trained with Carrot and Stick model The virtual robots were trained in simulation mode using reinforcement learning, where rewards are given for each correct response.During training, the bot earned rewards for standing upright, walking on one foot, and maintaining appropriate speed. Conversely, it incurred penalties for restricted actions, such as putting all its weight on a single foot, shrieking the brakes, or applying excessive torque.One of the major outcomes during the early training experiments was the use of only one foot for the majority of the work. To overcome this hurdle, the researchers resorted to the use of mirrored samples that switched the left and right sides. These techniques made the steps more evenly distributed with fewer fluctuations between runs.The latest study indicates that all the decisions were taken in real time via an Android app. TensorFlow Lite, a Google software tool, executes movements, including walking and recovery, using data from the phone’s internal sensors a few times per second.

title: Hydrogen-based synthetic fuels could boost military energy security
content: Nel ASA and Rheinmetall AG have agreed to work together on decentralized production of renewable synthetic fuels for defense and critical infrastructure. Announced on October 13, 2026, the partnership will bring together Nel’s electrolyzer technology and Rheinmetall’s Giga PtX concept to assess modular fuel production systems that could boost energy security.The companies aim to produce low-carbon synthetic fuels closer to where they are needed. These fuels could take the place of conventional fuels in current uses, which would help reduce reliance on centralized production and long, easily disrupted supply chains.Modular systems target energy securityAs part of the collaboration, Nel will provide its electrolyzer technology to make renewable hydrogen, and Rheinmetall will add its Giga PtX concept and systems-integration expertise. The companies will examine how these technologies can support local fuel production for both civilian and defense uses.Rheinmetall has been working with regional companies to move its Giga PtX project forward in certain markets. The agreement with Nel extends this network into Norway, where both companies see opportunities to develop decentralized synthetic fuel systems.The approach could allow fuel production facilities to operate closer to military installations, industrial sites and other critical infrastructure. Shorter supply routes could help reduce exposure to transport interruptions and improve access to essential fuels during emergencies.Norway offers a starting pointNorway is a potential starting market because of its renewable electricity resources, industrial capabilities, and developing carbon capture and utilization sector. The country also encounters difficulties in transmitting and distributing electricity, despite substantial power-generation capacity.Converting renewable electricity into hydrogen and synthetic fuels near production sites could provide another way to use available energy resources. This approach may also ease pressure on existing electricity infrastructure by storing and transporting energy as fuel.Norway’s dependence on international refining networks bring another challenge. The country operates only one oil refinery and exports significant volumes of crude oil to Europe for processing before refined products return for domestic consumption. Disruptions to external infrastructure could therefore affect parts of its fuel supply chain.Companies outline their ambitionsNel believes renewable hydrogen could help countries strengthen fuel security while cutting emissions.“Countries that depend on long and vulnerable fuel supply chains face increasing uncertainty. We believe renewable hydrogen can play an important role in enabling more resilient fuel systems while reducing emissions,” said Kjell Christian Bjørnsen, CFO of Nel. “Through this collaboration with Rheinmetall, we are exploring how our technology can be integrated into new value chains for synthetic fuels.”Rheinmetall sees the partnership as an opportunity to develop fuel systems for both civilian and defense requirements.“The transformation of energy systems requires new partnerships across industries,” stated Shena Britzen, Head of Hydrogen Program of Rheinmetall AG. “By working with Nel, we are exploring decentralized synthetic fuel solutions that can support both civilian and defense-related needs. We see localized synthetic fuel production, enabled by electrolysis, as an important element in strengthening energy security and future fuel supply chains.”Feasibility studies will guide next stepsThe companies will review potential production sites, infrastructure needs, access to renewable electricity, and sustainable carbon sources. They will also identify priority applications and evaluate the technical and commercial feasibility of the proposed systems.Pilot projects could follow to test modular production concepts and demonstrate how decentralized synthetic fuel networks might operate.The MoU is non-binding, meaning neither company has committed to a particular project or investment. Any further development will depend on mutual agreement and the outcome of their assessments. Although Norway is the initial focus, the partnership’s scope is not geographically restricted.

title: US Navy fleet upgrades SPY-6 radars to spot smaller, distant targets
content: US defense firm Raytheon has secured a contract to develop software upgrades to improve naval radar performance.The work will focus on helping radars detect smaller targets farther away and identify them faster. The improvements are intended for the US Navy’s SPY-6 radar family and other future naval systems.The project will combine software development and testing to enhance radar capabilities, with the upgrades expected to support naval operations through improved target detection and classification.Improves target detectionRTX’s Raytheon will develop software upgrades designed to improve the detection range, sensitivity, and processing efficiency of naval radar systems under a contract awarded by the US Office of Naval Research (ONR).The program will focus on advanced signal- and data-processing algorithms that can help radars detect smaller objects at greater distances and classify targets more quickly. Rather than relying solely on hardware modifications, the approach uses software improvements to enhance the performance of existing radar systems.The upgrades are intended for Raytheon’s SPY-6 family of naval radars and other future systems. Work under the contract will continue through 2031, with development and testing taking place at company facilities in Portsmouth, Rhode Island, and Andover, Massachusetts.Raytheon’s Advanced Technology team will develop and evaluate algorithms that process radar signals and the resulting data. These algorithms will be integrated through targeted software changes intended to improve how radar systems detect, distinguish, and classify objects.Radar systems transmit electromagnetic waves and analyze the signals objects reflect to determine their presence and characteristics. Detecting smaller targets at greater distances can be challenging because their reflections may be weaker and harder to distinguish from background signals and other sources of interference.Improvements in signal processing can help radar systems extract useful information from received signals, while data-processing algorithms can support the interpretation and classification of detected objects. The planned upgrades aim to improve these capabilities without requiring a complete replacement of existing radar hardware.The software will undergo laboratory and field testing to evaluate its performance and establish its suitability for operational use. The testing process will help determine whether the upgrades deliver the intended improvements before they are prepared for deployment.“Modernizing fielded radar systems with software-first upgrades is one of the fastest and most cost-effective ways to deliver mission-ready capability,” said Colin Whelan, president of Advanced Technology at Raytheon, in a statement.Smarter naval radar softwareThe program will support Raytheon’s SPY-6 family, which uses modular radar technology across different naval platforms. The family includes configurations designed to meet the requirements of aircraft carriers, amphibious assault ships, and other surface vessels.The SPY-6(V)2 uses a rotating antenna array and is designed for amphibious assault ships and Nimitz-class aircraft carriers. The SPY-6(V)3 uses three fixed antenna arrays and is intended for Ford-class aircraft carriers and guided-missile frigates.The radar family is designed to provide target and threat information to support naval operations. Raytheon says its systems can supply targeting and threat data for naval weapons, including all Standard Missile variants.Shared components and modular construction are intended to improve reliability while reducing maintenance costs across different radar configurations. Software improvements could further enhance the capabilities of these systems without requiring extensive changes to their physical architecture.The contract also builds on Raytheon’s work in software-defined apertures, an approach that uses software to influence how radar systems process signals and perform their functions. The company will draw on technical developments from earlier ONR initiatives, including ASPIRE and STORM, which supported advances in radar hardware and software.

title: Paper industry waste could help make cleaner, cheaper EV batteries
content: Researchers may have found an unexpected battery material solution within the discarded wood industry byproduct.The University of Limerick (UL) in Ireland and the University of Valencia in Spain found a way to repurpose lignosulfonate, a waste byproduct from the pulp and paper industry. The process converts this material into high-performance carbon nanofibers for sodium-ion batteries.The search for cleaner and more affordable electric vehicle batteries is driving a race to replace costly lithium-ion technology, which depends on scarce and environmentally damaging materials like lithium and cobalt. Converting this industrial waste into battery materials may offer a promising path past current supply issues toward sustainable, large-scale energy storage.“This research shows how an underused byproduct from the forestry and paper industries can be converted into a valuable battery material using a simple water-based process,” said Professor Maurice N Collins, lead of sustainable and resilient materials at the Bernal Institute, who led the study. Sustainable alternativeSodium is one of the most abundant elements on the planet, making sodium-ion technology a prime candidate to power the green transition. However, existing battery manufacturing processes still depend on toxic organic solvents, synthetic binders, and energy-intensive processing.The Irish-Spanish research team worked to change this. Using a green chemistry approach, the toxic solvents were eliminated in favor of simple water. They also combined lignosulfonate with natural ingredients to spin ultra-fine fibers without synthetic binders or extra additives.“What is particularly exciting about this research is that sustainability is built into every stage of the material’s development. We start with an abundant industrial byproduct, process it using water rather than organic solvents, and engineer its internal structure to improve sodium storage. This shows that high-performance battery materials can be designed with both electrochemical performance and environmental responsibility in mind,” said Tadhg Kennedy, co-director of the AMPEiRE Battery Research Center at the University of Limerick and co-author of the work. Interestingly, the central achievement rests in how researchers designed the carbon material at the nanoscale level.Scientists created an optimized pathway for sodium ions by fine-tuning the material’s chemistry and internal structure during synthesis. This particular design boosted energy storage and release efficiency throughout each charge and discharge cycle.“By carefully engineering the nanostructure of the carbon material, we were able to improve how efficiently sodium ions are stored and released during charging and discharging,” noted Collins, the lead researcher. Extensive further studies requiredResearchers combined sustainable, water-soluble bio-ingredients, specifically lignosulfonate, gelatin, and alginate, to develop nanostructures. During heat treatment, the gelatin and alginate serve as sacrificial templates, ultimately producing high-surface-area hollow carbon nanostructures.This discovery could provide both environmental and economic benefits. Paper manufacturing produces millions of tons of lignosulfonate annually, which is currently burned on-site for low-value heat recovery or discarded. However, there are challenges. Because lignosulfonate comes directly from paper mill wastewater, its chemical makeup varies with wood species and pulping techniques. To achieve consistent quality across large industrial batches, strict purification standards would likely be needed to standardize this raw byproduct for battery manufacturing.This study also raises key questions regarding material durability and environmental impact. Structural integrity remains a concern, particularly how hollow nanofibers withstand the physical stress of repeated sodium-ion movement over thousands of cycles.If successful, it could eventually transform unwanted paper and forestry waste into high-value materials using a clean, water-based process. And of course, this approach could accelerate the shift to sodium-ion technology and reduce global dependence on vulnerable lithium supply chains.

title: New two-phase system for chip cooling could reduce short-circuit risks
content: Researchers at Peking University in China have developed an embedded cooling system that uses an electrically insulating liquid to remove heat from electronic chips. It reaches a critical heat flux of 1,570 watts per square centimeter in initial tests.The design places tiny coolant channels close to heated regions inside the chip substrate. As the fluid passes through these channels, it absorbs heat and partly turns into vapor, which exits through specially arranged outlets.Bringing coolant closer to chip hotspotsIntegrated circuits contain interconnected components that process information or control electrical signals. Their operation generates heat, making effective cooling important for both performance and reliable operation over time.Embedded cooling tackles this problem by carving microscopic channels directly into the material supporting the circuits. This brings coolant close to the locations where heat is concentrated, allowing the fluid to absorb and carry it away.Water offers useful thermal properties, but its potential electrical conductivity requires precautions to protect chip components.“Embedded cooling—where microfluidic structures are directly etched into the chip substrate to send liquid coolants close to the hot spots—can offer dissipation of heat fluxes up to 3,000 W cm−2 using water as the coolant,” wrote Wei Xiao, Zhihu Wu, and their colleagues.The team instead used HFE-7100, a dielectric coolant, and designed its system around the fluid’s transition from liquid to vapor.Separate pathways for liquid and vaporThe researchers fabricated their cooling structure using techniques widely used in electronics manufacturing. Alongside channels near the heated regions of test chips, they created a manifold to distribute incoming coolant and collect fluid leaving the channels.The arrangement combines horizontal inlets with vertical outlets. Fresh liquid enters horizontally to replenish coolant, while the vertical pathways help vapor escape.HFE-7100 absorbs heat as it boils inside the channels. The resulting heated liquid–gas mixture then leaves through the outlets, carrying energy away from the chip.“Central to the enhanced heat transfer is the engineering of the horizontal-up manifold, which features horizontal inlets to facilitate liquid replenishment and vertical outlets to accelerate vapor evacuation,” wrote the authors.Testing the limits of dielectric coolingInitial tests recorded a critical heat flux of 1,570 watts per square centimeter. This marks the threshold beyond which boiling no longer provides effective cooling.The figure describes heat transfer per unit area, rather than the total heat removed from an entire chip. The authors reported that earlier dielectric cooling techniques were often limited to below 1,000 watts per square centimeter, even with pre-cooling and pre-pressurization.“Because our approach uses microelectromechanical systems technology, it can be directly integrated with standard semiconductor processes and scaled for future electronics,” wrote the researchers.Further testing on commercially available devices and over longer periods is needed to establish performance and reliability. Those experiments could clarify how effectively the design handles heat in practical electronic systems.Dielectric fluids reduce short-circuit risks, although their cooling performance is typically lower.Published in Nature Electronics, the work addresses a trade-off in chip cooling. Water removes heat effectively, but dissolved impurities can make it electrically conductive.
