title: Hyundai tests reusable drill to dig nuclear waste disposal holes
content: South Korea’s Hyundai Engineering & Construction has excavated a full-scale hole for used nuclear fuel disposal in bedrock, testing equipment designed to be retrieved and reused across multiple excavations.The demonstration took place in an underground research tunnel at the company’s research site, as part of a government-funded project led by the Korea Radioactive Waste Agency (KORAD). Hyundai E&C used real-time AI analysis to guide excavation and LiDAR mapping to check the completed hole.The work supports the development of construction technologies for underground disposal facilities as South Korea’s existing nuclear plant storage sites approach capacity.A cutterhead built for repeated excavationThe equipment measures about 5.7 feet in diameter and 18.7 feet long. Hyundai E&C developed it to meet deposition hole specifications and construction conditions for the Korea Advanced Disposal System, known as KORADIS.That system is tailored to South Korea’s geological environment and technical requirements. Deposition holes form part of the infrastructure needed to place used nuclear fuel underground.A central feature of the equipment is its foldable cutterhead. After excavation, the cutting assembly folds inward, allowing the machine to be safely removed and used again. This addresses the need to excavate multiple deposition holes repeatedly within a disposal facility.“This achievement is particularly significant because Hyundai E&C has become the first Korean builder to develop dedicated deposition hole excavation equipment and verify its performance and constructability through actual rock excavation,” an official from the HMG Construction Technology Research Institute said.AI guides excavation, LiDAR checks qualityDuring the demonstration, AI analyzed excavation data in real time to assess ground conditions. The findings supported adjustments to excavation based on the rock assessment and equipment performance.Once excavation was complete, LiDAR-based digital mapping helped verify construction quality and assess whether the deposition hole was suitable.Hyundai E&C is the only construction company participating in the KORAD-led project. Its work runs through the HMG Construction Technology Research Institute, the integrated research and development organization of Hyundai E&C and Hyundai Engineering.The research extends beyond excavation machinery. The company is developing concrete and grout intended to preserve the long-term performance of engineered barriers and control groundwater inflow.It is also advancing a rock classification system suited to South Korea’s geology, alongside digital technologies for rock assessment and monitoring.Storage pressure drives disposal researchUsed nuclear fuel in South Korea remains stored at individual nuclear power plant sites while a centralized interim storage facility is pending. Many of those on-site facilities are nearing full capacity.According to the supplied report, legislation passed in February 2025 sets timelines for interim storage facilities by 2050 and permanent disposal facilities by 2060.Deep geological repositories use engineered underground vaults and tunnels in bedrock to isolate higher-activity radioactive waste from the surface environment.“By strengthening our core capabilities across the entire nuclear lifecycle, from nuclear power plant construction and decommissioning to spent nuclear fuel disposal, we will continue to solidify Hyundai E&C’s position as a game changer in the global nuclear industry,” an official said.The demonstration marks a step toward developing the construction technologies needed for South Korea’s permanent used nuclear fuel disposal facilities.

title: US Army to get 9 new wheeled howitzers prototypes from Hanwha
content: The US Army has ordered nine prototype XM1776 Mobile Tactical Cannon systems, with an option for nine more, as Hanwha Defense USA looks to expand American artillery production.Hanwha Defense USA (HDUSA) unveiled the XM1776 at the Association of the US Army’s 2026 Annual Meeting and Exposition in Washington, DC, on October 12. The naming ceremony introduced the American designation for Hanwha’s K9 Mobile Howitzer, a wheeled artillery system based on the South Korean defense manufacturer’s established K9 artillery technology.The company said the Army has ordered nine prototypes and retains the option to acquire an additional nine systems. The announcement follows an earlier prototyping agreement and establishes a larger group of vehicles for evaluation.The XM1776 is intended to support the Army’s modernization objectives by combining 155 mm artillery firepower with the mobility of a wheeled platform. Unlike towed artillery, which requires a separate vehicle to move the weapon, a self-propelled howitzer integrates its gun and mobility system into a single vehicle. This can give artillery units greater flexibility when moving between firing positions.A new approach to mobile artilleryThe XM1776 is based on Hanwha’s K9 Mobile Howitzer, adapting technology from the company’s K9 family of tracked self-propelled howitzers into a wheeled configuration. The US designation reflects the system’s adaptation for the American Army, though the prototype still needs to be evaluated against US military requirements.Wheeled artillery can offer advantages in road mobility and operational flexibility, particularly when units need to reposition quickly alongside maneuver forces. Self-propelled systems can also reduce dependence on separate towing vehicles, potentially simplifying movement between firing locations.A new name for America’s new artillery.In today's naming ceremony, CEO Michael Coulter, COO Mike Smith, and @USArmy leaders unveiled the new designation for our K9 Mobile Howitzer: XM1776.New name. Proven foundation. Welcome to the Unfair Fight.https://t.co/XZ4OsCUlJE pic.twitter.com/z9EsRuXfGs— Hanwha Defense USA (@HanwhaDefenseUS) October 12, 2026These capabilities matter in battlefields where drones, surveillance systems, and counter-battery weapons can help opposing forces locate artillery positions. The ability to move after firing can reduce the time a gun remains exposed to retaliation. However, the Army must test the XM1776 to establish its performance, reliability, and suitability for operational service.The system remains a prototype effort, rather than an operational weapon approved for full-scale production. The latest announcement does not establish a production timeline or confirm how many systems the Army might eventually acquire.Hanwha plans to build US artillery capacityAlongside the unveiling, Hanwha Defense USA outlined plans to expand the domestic industrial infrastructure supporting the program. The company is establishing a Phase I site in Opelika, Alabama, which will serve as a US integration and testing facility for the XM1776 and other systems in Hanwha’s K9 Mobile Howitzer family.HDUSA also plans to meet with more than 70 existing and prospective suppliers to develop an Artillery Industrial Base Coalition. The initiative is intended to accelerate supply-chain localization and expand American participation in artillery production.“The XM-1776 Mobile Tactical Cannon represents the launch of the U.S. Army’s new long-range precision fires modernization effort,” Mike Smith, HDUSA’s COO and president of Land Systems, said in the announcement.Hanwha is drawing on the international production experience of its K9 artillery family. The company says it has fielded more than 2,500 K9 howitzers worldwide. That existing industrial footprint could provide a foundation for expanding production and supporting cooperation with allied operators, although the extent of shared components and sustainment arrangements for the American variant remains to be established.The effort comes as the US seeks to strengthen its defense industrial base and improve the capacity to produce and sustain artillery systems. A domestic integration and testing facility, along with a broader supplier network, could support the program if the Army decides to move beyond prototyping.

title: Urenco's uranium enrichment site reaches 75% capacity expansion target
content: The National Enrichment Facility, the only commercial uranium enrichment center in the US, has reached a key milestone by completing 75 percent of its capacity expansion target. The facility is looking to increase its uranium production capacity to seven million separative work units (SWU) over the next decade as it looks to boost uranium enrichment in the US. The demand for carbon-free energy sources is leading us back to nuclear energy which can produce power on demand without any associated carbon emissions. While earlier nuclear power projects have been marked by cost overruns and construction delays, newer approaches of building reactors at scale have brought in new hope about nuclear energy. Even though the US leads in the development of these new-age technologies, it is also the largest consumer of uranium but not a major producer. Nuclear facilities in the US rely on international purchases to feed their reactors, while there is only one facility that can actually enrich uranium. What is uranium enrichment? Naturally, uranium is found as two isotopes. U-238 and U-235. While U-238 is the stable form of uranium, it is the U-235 that is used as fuel in nuclear reactors. U-238 makes up 99.3 percent of natural uranium. U-235 levels must be increased to 3.5-5 percent of total uranium before it can be used in fission reactors, which is achieved through enrichment. For enrichment, mined uranium is first processed into yellowcake containing largely triuranium octoxide (U3O8), which is then converted to uranium hexafluoride (UF6). Even at low temperatures, UF6 can easily convert to the gaseous state, which is then pumped into gas centrifuges, spinning at tens of thousands of rotations per minute. At these high speeds, the slight differences in mass of U-235 and U-238 are sufficient to separate them, with the heavier U-238 settling outside and the U-235 concentrating in the middle. Hundreds and thousands of centrifuges are arranged in a cascade to pass the gas repeatedly from one stage to the next and increasing the purity of the U-235. Urenco’s enrichment capacity in the USSince each centrifuge contributes a small part to separation of U-235, it becomes difficult to quantify its individual capacity, Instead, facilities sum up the total work done by the centrifuges, in terms of how many kilograms of separation work they have done, to determine the capacity of a facility and is referred to as separation work units (SWU). Urenco’s uranium enrichment facility in Eunice, New Mexico, currently offers 4.3 million SWU per year, which is about a third of the US demand. With the US planning to increase its dependence on nuclear energy in the future, Urenco is building capacity for enrichment and plans to roll out seven million SWU over the next decade. Between 2025 and 2027, Urenco is adding new capacity of 700,000 SWU by adding eight centrifuge cascades at its existing site. With the beginning of installation of the sixth cascade, the company has reached an important milestone as it completes 75 percent of the planned capacity upgrade. Installation of the seventh cascade is also expected to be completed by the end of the year, while the eight and final cascade will be installed in 2027. “We are consistently delivering new capacity to help fuel the US nuclear industry and allied nations, and our teams are doing it ahead of schedule and on budget,” said Jody Blackshear, Managing Director of Urenco USA in a press release. “This experience will support our larger capacity programs in the years ahead as we look to increase our enrichment production by more than 50% to meet the needs of our customers with traditional and advanced reactors.”

title: Raytheon's upgraded drone killer passes three tests in just 15 months
content: American military firm Raytheon has completed three development tests of its Coyote Block 2C+RM counter-drone interceptor, advancing the upgrade from concept to testing in just 15 months.Announced on October 12, the company-funded effort aims to equip the military with a faster response to evolving drone threats, including more advanced Group 3 drones.RTX is replacing the existing interceptor’s turbojet propulsion with a solid rocket motor and adding a new seeker and warhead. Raytheon said the changes enable faster launches, higher flight speeds, and faster successive shots. They will also significantly improve range, although specific performance figures remain undisclosed.Rocket propulsion speeds up engagementsDrone threats are evolving quickly—and counter-drone technology has to evolve with them. Raytheon advanced its new Coyote Block 2C+RM upgrade from concept to initial field testing in just 15 months.🔗https://t.co/fLaahlifjF #AUSA2026— RTX (@RTX_News) October 12, 2026Existing Coyote Block 2 interceptors use a small rocket booster for launch before a turbojet engine powers the rest of their flight. The Block 2C+RM moves to rocket propulsion, bringing the system closer to a conventional surface-to-air missile.Thomas Laliberty, president of Land & Air Defense Systems at Raytheon, described the range difference as significant but did not provide figures. Raytheon also says the upgrade enables faster successive shots, helping operators engage incoming drone waves.Seeker and warhead address advanced dronesRaytheon has not detailed the changes to the seeker and warhead. Existing Block 2 interceptors receive targeting cues from ground radars and other sensors before onboard radio-frequency seekers guide the terminal engagement. They carry blast-fragmentation warheads.“Unfortunately, I can’t get into the specific threats, but I can tell you the intention is to have this cover all types of Class 3 drones,” Laliberty said.The U.S. military’s Group 3 category covers drones weighing 56 to 1,320 pounds, flying at altitudes up to 18,000 feet and reaching speeds no greater than 250 knots.Jet-powered one-way attack drones pose additional challenges because their higher speeds can reduce the time available for interception. Some reportedly reach approximately 270 to 320 knots, exceeding the Group 3 speed ceiling. The upgraded Coyote’s faster response and higher velocity are intended to help address these evolving threats more effectively.Laliberty also noted an overlap between some drone and cruise-missile capabilities, although the announcement did not establish a demonstrated cruise-missile interception capability.Upgrade builds on combat experience“With a common backbone, Raytheon can rapidly scale the Coyote family across counter-drone missions — so we’re accelerating the pace of innovation,” Laliberty said.“Coyote Block 2C+RM is the latest example of how we’re investing to deliver critical upgrades to combat-proven technology that give service members a decisive advantage on the battlefield,” he added. The Army, the largest known operator, previously outlined plans to buy at least 6,000 Block 2-series interceptors between fiscal years 2025 and 2029. Those plans do not establish purchases of the new variant.The Pentagon and Army have engaged with Raytheon on Block 2C+RM development, but formal U.S. military purchase contracts for this version remain unclear. The initial test series included several first-of-their-kind events, confirming initial integration with the current counter-drone architecture. It also marked the first launches of a Coyote effector equipped with a tactical rocket motor designed to shorten threat engagement times and enable faster successive shots.

title: US Navy adds anti-drone system to 18,479-ton USS Ohio submarine
content: The US Navy has deployed a counter-drone electronic warfare system aboard USS Ohio, an Ohio-class guided-missile submarine. The system would add another layer of protection against small unmanned aircraft during surface operations.According to defense publication Janes, the system is known as Drone Restricted Access Using Known Electromagnetic Warfare (DRAKE). It is designed to detect, identify, and track small drones before disrupting their communications through electronic jamming. Developed by Northrop Grumman, DRAKE gives crews a way to counter certain aerial threats without relying on missiles or guns to destroy them.The deployment highlights a growing challenge for naval forces as inexpensive drones become tools for surveillance and reconnaissance. Although submarines rely on concealment underwater, they face different security risks when surfaced or operating near ports and coastal facilities.How DRAKE counters drone threatsDRAKE uses software-defined radio technology to detect and track small unmanned aircraft. It can also interfere with radio-frequency links between a drone and its operator, potentially disrupting remote control and preventing the aircraft from completing its intended mission.Unlike kinetic counter-drone systems, which use projectiles or interceptor weapons to destroy an aircraft, DRAKE relies on electronic warfare. This approach can provide an additional response option without requiring the crew to launch a physical interceptor.However, jamming is not guaranteed to defeat every drone. Its effectiveness depends on the aircraft’s communications architecture and operating mode. A drone that can navigate autonomously or continue its mission without a continuous remote-control link may be less susceptible to this type of interference.The system therefore adds a capability rather than providing a universal defense against unmanned aircraft. Its practical effectiveness will depend on the threat encountered and the circumstances in which it is used.System upgrades draw on operational feedbackJanes has also reported upgrades to DRAKE, including an Android-based operator interface intended to simplify how personnel interact with the system.The updates reflect efforts to refine the technology using feedback from operational deployments. Software-based changes can potentially allow electronic warfare systems to adapt to evolving threats without requiring a complete hardware replacement.Northrop Grumman has developed DRAKE as part of its broader counter-unmanned aircraft and electronic warfare portfolio. The company also produces the Joint Counter-small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Electronic Warfare (JCREW) family of systems, designed to counter threats from small drones.The precise configuration of the system aboard USS Ohio has not been publicly detailed. Available reporting also does not establish whether the submarine has already received the latest interface upgrades, or disclose the installation’s detection range and jamming coverage.Protecting submarines during surface operationsUSS Ohio is one of four Ohio-class submarines converted from their original ballistic-missile role into guided-missile submarines, designated SSGNs. The vessels can carry up to 154 Tomahawk cruise missiles and support special operations forces.While remaining submerged helps a submarine avoid aerial observation, surface operations create different security challenges. Small drones can observe vessels, collect visual intelligence, or monitor activity near naval facilities without the cost and visibility of larger surveillance aircraft.DRAKE gives crews another way to respond when conditions require it. Its deployment also reflects a broader shift in naval defense, as militaries adapt electronic warfare capabilities to counter drones that are increasingly inexpensive, accessible, and useful for reconnaissance.The system does not eliminate the vulnerability of a surfaced submarine, nor does it guarantee protection against every type of drone. Instead, it adds an electronic countermeasure to the Navy’s available defensive options.For the US Navy, the challenge is to counter emerging aerial threats without compromising the operational flexibility and concealment that make submarines valuable assets. DRAKE addresses that challenge, though it has not disclosed further details about its deployment and performance aboard USS Ohio.

title: Video: Humanoid robots take to busy streets to help manage traffic
content: DEEP Robotics has deployed its DR02 humanoid robots to help manage traffic at busy intersections and tourist attractions in Hangzhou, China.The robots were tested in Xihu district in early October, when rain and increased visitor numbers put added pressure on local traffic personnel.They were stationed along major roads and at Xixi National Wetland Park, assisting with traffic direction, maintaining order, and answering basic public inquiries. The deployment demonstrates how humanoid robots could support traffic management in crowded urban environments, particularly during periods of heavy pedestrian and vehicle movement.Humanoids patrol streetsDEEP has deployed its DR02 humanoid robots to assist traffic personnel at busy intersections and tourist attractions in Hangzhou, China, testing their ability to navigate crowded streets and interact with the public in rainy conditions.The trials took place in early October, when heavy visitor and vehicle traffic placed additional demands on local traffic crews. The robots operated along Zheda Road and West Wenyi Road in Lingyin Subdistrict, as well as at Xixi National Wetland Park. Their tasks included directing traffic, reminding road users about violations, maintaining order, and answering basic questions from residents and visitors.The deployment provided an opportunity to evaluate the DR02’s ability to combine environmental perception, movement control, and human interaction in a real-world setting.Standing approximately 175 centimeters tall and weighing 143 pounds (65 kilograms), the DR02 is designed to operate in outdoor environments. Its IP66 protection rating resists dust and powerful water jets, supporting operation in wet weather. The robot is also rated to function in temperatures ranging from minus 20 to 55 degrees Celsius, giving it a broad operating range for outdoor duties.Its mobility is another important part of the system. The DR02 can walk at speeds up to 1.5 meters per second and negotiate stairs with rises of about 25 centimeters, as well as slopes up to 20 degrees. These capabilities allow it to move through environments that may include uneven surfaces, changes in elevation, pedestrians, and other obstacles.The robot uses a combination of wide-angle cameras, depth cameras, and light detection and ranging (LiDAR) sensors to perceive its surroundings. These sensing systems provide information about nearby people, vehicles, and objects, helping the machine assess its environment and adjust its movements. Its onboard computing system delivers a reported 275 trillion operations per second, supporting the processing required for perception and movement.Monitor road violationsDuring the trials, the DR02 demonstrated several traffic-related functions. It could remind cyclists to remain behind stop lines, announce when traffic signals turned green, and identify issues such as riders traveling without helmets, overloaded bicycles, and pedestrians crossing stop lines. Rather than issuing fines, the robot used verbal reminders and gestures to encourage road users to follow traffic rules.The system was also tested on public-facing duties beyond traffic direction. At tourist locations, the robots helped manage visitor flow and answered basic inquiries in multiple languages, including questions from residents and visitors. These tasks require the robot to interpret its surroundings while communicating instructions in a way people can understand.The trials are intended to assess how effectively the DR02 can recognize situations, coordinate its movements, and interact with people before any wider deployment. By assigning robots repetitive advisory duties, traffic personnel could devote more time to responsibilities such as accident investigations and enforcement.The Hangzhou tests illustrate a practical application of humanoid robotics that combines mobile navigation, environmental sensing, and public interaction. However, the deployment remains a trial, and its results will help determine how the DR02 could be used in future traffic-management operations.

title: Humanoid robot handles household chores smoothly with new system
content: Shanghai-based Archon Robotics has released its first demonstration of Whole-Body Intelligence (WBI), which coordinates humanoid robots’ movements with their understanding of tasks.The system links high-level task planning with coordinated full-body motion, enabling robots to perform complex activities in real-world environments.The demonstration features popular humanoid models performing tasks such as picking up objects, navigating steps, clearing tables, operating dishwashers, and organizing refrigerators. The firm said its approach uses human data for pretraining and real-robot data for post-training, with the showcased full demonstrations running autonomously at normal speed.Smarter humanoid movementArchon’s whole-body intelligence framework is designed to help humanoid robots translate task instructions into coordinated physical movements. The Shanghai-based company aims to develop general-purpose AI models that combine task understanding, motion planning, balance, and precise execution across different humanoid platforms.The approach, called Whole-Body Intelligence (WBI), combines large-scale human whole-body data for pretraining with real-robot demonstrations for post-training. The debut demonstration shows humanoids picking up objects, navigating steps, clearing tables, operating dishwashers, and organizing refrigerators.Archon’s framework aims to coordinate a robot’s entire body rather than treat individual actions as isolated commands. Its demonstration highlights two components, S1 and S0, which handle different aspects of the process. S1 processes task-related information and supports behavioral decision-making, while S0 focuses on whole-body motion control, including coordination, stabilization, and precise execution. Archon describes S0 as functioning like a cerebellum, translating targets into executable movements while maintaining physical stability.The company’s July technical blog described a broader four-layer architecture that also includes task planning and motion generation. However, the debut video focuses on S1 and S0 without clarifying whether this represents a change to the previously described framework.Archon combines human demonstrations with data collected from physical robots to develop its models. Human whole-body data provides examples of movement, while real-robot data helps adapt learned capabilities to the mechanical and control requirements of actual hardware. The company revealed that its data platform collects human demonstrations across multiple cities in China. The material undergoes automated checks, human spot checks, and reviews of flagged samples before training.Humanoids learn autonomyThe process also incorporates DAgger corrective data, which helps models learn how to respond when an action needs adjustment. These demonstrations show robots correcting mistakes and resuming tasks, complementing examples of successful execution. The approach is intended to develop transferable physical skills rather than rely exclusively on demonstrations of completed tasks. However, Archon has not disclosed its dataset sizes or published quantitative results showing how effectively the models transfer learned skills to unfamiliar situations.The footage features an AGIBOT A3, Booster T2 humanoids, and modified Unitree G1 robots. One sequence shows several machines performing different activities simultaneously in a shared kitchen and dining environment. The tasks involve handling cleaning equipment, manipulating household objects, and interacting with kitchen appliances. These activities require coordinated bending, reaching, balance, and object manipulation.The different platforms illustrate Archon’s work across multiple hardware configurations. However, the footage does not show whether all robots use identical model weights or coordinate as a team. Archon noted that its full demonstrations run autonomously at normal speed.The explanatory segments covering S0 and the DAgger training process include teleoperation, distinguishing autonomous execution from demonstrations used to develop and refine the system.The debut video outlines the company’s approach to combining AI-based task understanding with coordinated humanoid movement. However, it does not report task-completion rates, how often humans intervene, or comparative results across robot platforms.Experts said such measurements would help establish the framework’s reliability beyond staged demonstrations and show how well its capabilities transfer to unfamiliar tasks and environments.

title: NASA's Perseverance sets new Mars driving record at 28.10 miles
content: NASA’s Perseverance rover has set a new record for the longest distance driven by any vehicle on another world, reaching 28.10 miles (45.22 kilometers) on Mars and surpassing a record held by Opportunity for years.The six-wheeled rover crossed the milestone on October 11, during the 2,006th Martian day of its mission. It overtook Opportunity’s 28.06-mile (45.16-kilometer) record, covering the distance in about five and a half years compared with Opportunity’s nearly 15 years.Much of Perseverance’s progress comes from its autonomous navigation system, AutoNav, which allows the rover to identify obstacles and plan routes while moving. NASA says the system has guided more than 90% of its total driving distance, compared with about 5% for Opportunity’s early autonomous navigation system.Perseverance can travel up to 1,351 feet (412 meters) in a single Martian day. Its navigation software processes about 600,000 measurement points with each look at the terrain, compared with just 20 used by Sojourner, NASA’s first Mars rover.Autonomous driving extends explorationAutoNav uses onboard cameras to capture images of the surrounding terrain, builds a three-dimensional map of potential hazards and selects a safe route between waypoints chosen by engineers on Earth.The system allows Perseverance to make driving decisions without waiting for detailed instructions from mission controllers. NASA describes the process as “thinking while driving.”The record-breaking drive covered 299.6 feet (91.31 meters), pushing the rover beyond Opportunity’s previous mark.“The original mission called for no more than 12.4 miles of driving. We’ve blown well past that, and with all mobility systems fully operational and favorable extended-ground-life test results, we expect Perseverance to keep adding to this record for many years to come,” said Steven Lee, project manager for the Curiosity and Perseverance rovers at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory.NASA recently approved Perseverance’s first mission extension, which began in October and will continue its exploration of Jezero Crater’s rim through approximately the end of 2028.The rover is currently traveling through an area called Lac de Charmes toward Idubi, where scientists hope to identify evidence of ancient hydrothermal systems.These systems involve heated water interacting with surrounding rock and could provide clues about environments that may once have supported microbial life.Ancient rocks guide missionsPerseverance has collected 29 rock and soil samples while exploring Jezero Crater, including its former lakebed, ancient river delta and crater rim.Some rocks in the region are approximately 4 billion years old. NASA says the terrain could preserve geological evidence largely lost on Earth through erosion and plate tectonics.The rover previously identified a potential biosignature in a rock called Cheyava Falls. That finding remains a possible indicator of ancient life, not proof that life existed on Mars.Perseverance has also surpassed the distances traveled by Apollo 17’s lunar rover and the Soviet Union’s Lunokhod 2.NASA’s earlier Mars rovers established successive milestones. Sojourner traveled about 330 feet (100 meters), Spirit covered 4.8 miles (7.7 kilometers), and Curiosity has driven more than 23.65 miles (38.07 kilometers).After Lac de Charmes, Perseverance is expected to continue south toward Rainbow Falls, a 328-foot-wide (100-meter-wide) block of ancient crust exposed by the impact that formed Jezero CraterNASA is also improving the rover’s navigation software to reduce unnecessary steering and help it determine its position using orbital maps while driving.The agency hopes future improvements will allow rovers to operate longer each day, expanding the amount of Martian terrain they can investigate.

title: New microwave weapon can stop drone swarms without firing missiles
content: BAE Systems has unveiled two air defense technologies designed to help the US Army counter mass drone attacks without relying entirely on conventional missiles. The systems combine a high-power microwave weapon with an artillery platform that fires precision-guided projectiles against aerial and ground targets.Unveiled at the Association of the United States Army (AUSA) 2026 exhibition, the technologies offer different ways to tackle growing threats from unmanned aircraft. One uses directed energy to engage drones without conventional ammunition, while the other relies on high-velocity projectiles for kinetic interception.Microwave weapon targets swarmsBAE Systems’ High Power Microwave (HPM) system targets groups of drones using electromagnetic energy. It can engage successive threats as long as its power supply remains available, avoiding the ammunition resupply demands associated with conventional weapons.That capability could prove valuable against coordinated drone attacks designed to overwhelm air defenses. Missile-based interceptors carry finite ammunition supplies, and replacing each shot can create substantial logistical demands during prolonged engagements.The HPM system uses an architecture built around more than 99 percent commercial off-the-shelf components. BAE says this approach supports manufacturing and sustainment while allowing engineers to adapt the system across different operating environments.Its modular design supports four deployment configurations. These include fixed installations, towed systems, combat vehicle integration, and maritime platforms. Each configuration can accommodate different power requirements and operational needs.BAE also reports that the system has reached Technology Readiness Level 6. Outdoor range testing has validated its operation, including tests involving billions of microwave pulses to document effects on targets.Artillery adds kinetic firepowerThe Multi-Domain Artillery Cannon System (MDACS) provides a complementary approach to air defense. The air-transportable platform fires different precision-guided munitions according to the mission and target.Against aerial threats, MDACS can launch the Hypervelocity Projectile (HVP). The guided round gives the system a kinetic option for engaging incoming threats, complementing the microwave weapon’s directed-energy approach.MDACS can also fire Scorpio-XR, a precision-guided munition intended for fixed and moving ground targets. BAE says Scorpio-XR doubles the range of existing precision-guided projectiles launched from 155 mm cannons.That extended reach could help US forces strike targets from greater distances in contested environments. The system’s combination of air defense and ground-attack capabilities also broadens its potential battlefield role.Layered defense counters drone attacksBAE is positioning the two systems as complementary parts of a layered defense. HPM offers sustained engagement capacity against drone formations, while MDACS adds a projectile-based option for aerial and ground threats.Jason Casciotti, vice president of BAE Systems’ Weapon Systems product line, said the company wants to move mature technology toward operational use faster. He pointed to validated designs and a resilient supply chain as important factors in that effort.The systems address a central challenge for modern air defense: stopping large numbers of relatively inexpensive threats without exhausting costly interceptors. Directed energy could reduce ammunition demands, while kinetic weapons provide another way to engage targets.However, BAE’s announcement does not establish that the US Army has adopted either system for operational service. Their eventual role will depend on further development, testing, and procurement decisions.

title: Oil-field desalination offers an alternative to data center cooling
content: Can waste water from the oil and energy industry quench the thirst of data centers? Researchers at The University of Texas in Austin are betting it can.They suggest that established desalination technologies could allow data centers to use salty or contaminated water to meet their cooling needs, reducing their reliance on freshwater.Although there are various ways to separate salt from water, researchers said reverse osmosis, which uses pressure to push water through a semipermeable membrane, is more energy-efficient. However, the technology has one drawback: it struggles to treat water saltier than seawater.Heating water into vapor and then condensing it back into freshwater is another viable solution, but this method requires more energy.Turning wastewater into coolantAccording to the Environmental and Energy Study Institute, large data centers can consume up to 5 million gallons of water per day. The waste water generated by certain oil fields in Texas is over thousand fold higher than this amount.Data centers can become more efficient in their water usage if they reduce stress on local water resources without drastically increasing costs or overall energy demand, according to a recently published study in Water Research.“We’re not waiting for a futuristic technology to come along and solve this problem for us,” said Vaibhav Bahadur, who is a professor at the University’s Cockrell School of Engineering’s Walker Department of Mechanical Engineering and is one of the leaders of the research.Bahudur noted that though the desalinations methods are available but they incur a cost. These costs, however, will be a small fraction of a data center’s total energy footprint when compared even with the most energy-intensive water treatment.Texas oilfields offer alternativesHe proposed turning attention to the Permian Basin. This geological region in West Texas generates approximately 8 billion gallons of produced water per day during oil and gas extraction.The researcher said this water could be put to better use instead of being transported elsewhere for disposal, where it could pose long-term risks.“The Permian (Basin) puts out 1,200 Olympic-sized swimming pools per day, and right now this water is transported over long distances and injected underground. This is problematic in many ways including the risk of seismic activity,” Bahadur said. “We’re also running out of space to bury that water, by as early as 2030. We need to find a way to use it, and cleaning it up for data centers is a great way to do that.”The research finding becomes significant given that only less than 4 percent of Earth’s water is freshwater, and only a fraction of it, just 0.5 percent, is accessible and safe for human consumption. Additionally, by 2028, water consumption by data centers is expected to reach approximately 33 billion gallons, filling nearly 50,000 Olympic-sized pools, according to Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory.The study appears in the journal Water Research.

title: US fusion project targets plasma predictions in under 20 minutes
content: A new US Department of Energy-backed project aims to predict the behavior of plasma inside a fusion reactor in less than 20 minutes, using a digital replica of Commonwealth Fusion Systems’ (CFS) SPARC device.The project, led by the American fusion energy company, brings together four DOE national laboratories, NVIDIA, Google DeepMind and university researchers. It will develop a digital twin that uses physics simulations, experimental data and advanced computing to predict how SPARC will operate.The initiative is part of the DOE’s Genesis Mission, which announced its Phase II awards on October 8. Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory (PPPL) will contribute simulation software, experimental data and computing resources to the project.Unlike conventional simulations, the planned digital twin will be connected to the physical SPARC device, which is currently under construction. As experimental data becomes available, researchers intend to update the virtual model to improve its predictions and guide future experiments.Predicting plasma between experimentsSPARC is a tokamak, a fusion device that uses powerful magnetic fields to confine extremely hot plasma. Researchers must understand how the plasma behaves under different operating conditions to improve reactor performance.The digital twin is intended to predict a complete plasma pulse, or one experimental operating cycle, in under 20 minutes. That would allow scientists to analyze results and prepare adjustments between successive experiments.PPPL will contribute three established physics simulation codes: M3D-C1, TRANSP and XGC. These tools model different aspects of plasma behavior and will be combined with other software to generate predictions.The project will also use faster computational models trained on large simulation datasets. Known as surrogate models, they approximate the results of more complex calculations while requiring less computing time.“PPPL will play a central role in this project, contributing foundational software engineering and SI models, core physics models, historical tokamak data and high-performance compute resources,” said Michael Churchill, head of PPPL’s AI for Science Group.The planned 20-minute turnaround is a development target, not a demonstrated performance result. Researchers must still verify that the predictions remain accurate under actual operating conditions.Testing models before deploymentBefore applying the technology to SPARC, researchers will test and validate digital twin workflows using PPPL’s National Spherical Torus Experiment-Upgrade (NSTX-U).The experimental platform will allow scientists to assess how well their models reproduce plasma behavior and whether they can reliably support decisions during fusion experiments.Data from NSTX-U and earlier PPPL experiments will also help train and evaluate the models. Some of these datasets will be made available to the wider fusion research community.Beyond PPPL, the collaboration includes Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory and SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory.Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Carnegie Mellon University, General Atomics, NVIDIA, Google DeepMind and Synopsys will also participate.The project builds on CFS’ existing digital twin development efforts, expanding the work through DOE-supported research and collaboration.Its longer-term objective is to support ARC, the commercial fusion power plant CFS plans to develop after SPARC. Researchers hope the digital twin will help them evaluate operating conditions, refine reactor designs, and reduce the time needed to develop future fusion systems.However, SPARC remains under construction, and the new platform has not yet demonstrated its proposed prediction speed or accuracy. Its eventual contribution to commercial fusion power will depend on successful testing and validation.

title: Valkyrie combat drone flies in Europe with range topping 3,100 miles
content: Airbus and Kratos Defense & Security Solutions have flown the U740 Valkyrie uncrewed combat aircraft in Europe for the first time. The milestone advances their effort to deliver a combat-ready Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA) for Germany and other European military customers by 2029.The aircraft completed a series of maneuvers during testing at an undisclosed facility in Northern Europe. Its performance included rocket-assisted takeoff without a conventional runway, flight at speeds reaching Mach 0.8, and adjustments to mission parameters in the air.The partners now plan more advanced trials involving Airbus’ MARS mission system. The software will help the Valkyrie execute missions autonomously while preserving European control over its critical systems.Valkyrie completes European debutThe U740 Valkyrie measures 9.1 meters (29.9 feet) long and spans 8.2 meters (26.9 feet). It has an internal weapons bay and additional payload stations beneath its wings.The aircraft has a maximum takeoff weight of approximately three metric tons. Its range exceeds 3,100 miles, and it can operate at altitudes reaching 45,000 feet.These specifications position the Valkyrie for missions that expose conventional aircraft and their crews to significant risks. It can operate independently or coordinate with crewed fighters, including the Eurofighter.Airbus expects the drone to expand the reach and firepower of existing combat aircraft. Its design also offers a way to increase the number of available combat platforms without relying exclusively on expensive crewed fighters.The aircraft supports conventional runway operations, but its rail-launch capability offers another deployment option. Rocket assistance allows it to take off without depending on a traditional runway.MARS brings autonomous controlAirbus’ Multi-platform Autonomous Reconfigurable and Secure (MARS) system will provide the Valkyrie with its European mission architecture. The system gives European operators control over mission applications, software, data, and hardware.MARS uses AI-assisted software to manage autonomous missions and coordinate groups of aircraft. Human operators will retain oversight of the system, particularly when decisions involve established rules of engagement.That arrangement gives European forces a way to adopt autonomous combat aircraft without surrendering control of their mission systems to an external supplier. Future flight tests will examine how MARS integrates with the Valkyrie’s existing capabilities.Affordable mass drives developmentAirbus Defence and Space CEO Mike Schoellhorn said modern air forces need affordable ways to increase combat capacity in increasingly contested environments.“By pairing Kratos’ proven airframe as a ‘program of record’ with Airbus’ sovereign European mission system, we are able to offer a robust, sovereign, affordable, and combat-ready CCA system by the end of the decade,” Schoellhorn said.Kratos CEO Eric DeMarco also praised the first flight, citing the aircraft’s maturity and the integration work between both teams. He said the partnership could expand opportunities in Germany and other international markets.The 2029 target gives the companies several years to mature the aircraft and its autonomous mission software. Subsequent tests will determine how effectively the Valkyrie can combine affordable production, flexible deployment, and coordinated operations alongside crewed fighters.

title: Staying Active Could Have Two Major Benefits for People With Parkinson’s, Scientists Find
content:
Parkinson’s disease is a progressive neurological disorder that affects movement, balance, and coordination. It develops as dopamine-producing nerve cells in the brain become damaged or die, leading to symptoms such as tremors, muscle stiffness, and slowed movement. Credit: Stock
Researchers have uncovered a potential connection between the duration and intensity of everyday physical activity and how Parkinson’s symptoms change over time.
People with Parkinson’s disease who stay more physically active may experience slower declines in memory, thinking, and movement abilities, according to a study that followed participants for up to seven years. Researchers found that greater activity was consistently associated with more favorable outcomes, although the findings do not establish that exercise directly slows disease progression.
The study, published in
Neurology
, the medical journal of the American Academy of Neurology, examined how different amounts and intensities of physical activity related to changes in Parkinson’s symptoms.
“Parkinson’s disease is a brain disorder that causes movement and cognitive problems that gradually worsen, leading to disability and a loss of independence,” said study author Dong-Woo Ryu, MD, PhD, of the University of Cincinnati in Ohio. “Previous research has shown associations between physical activity and movement symptoms. Our study found physical activity may have dual benefits, with associations with slower declines in movement and cognition.”
How Researchers Measured Physical Activity
The study included 294 adults with mild to moderate Parkinson’s disease, whose average age was 66. Participants reported how much time they spent being physically active each week, including activities at work, around the house, and during recreation. Moderate activities included brisk walking, light swimming, doubles tennis, vacuuming, and mowing the lawn. Vigorous activities included jogging, fast cycling, competitive sports, shoveling, and carrying heavy loads.
Researchers evaluated activity in three ways: total weekly time spent exercising at moderate or vigorous intensity, overall activity volume adjusted for intensity, and time spent performing vigorous activities. For total activity time, participants were classified into three groups: those active for up to four hours weekly, those active for four to eight hours, and those exceeding eight hours. Annual assessments tracked changes in cognitive performance and movement symptoms.
Greater Activity Linked to Slower Cognitive Decline
Differences between the activity groups emerged in tests of thinking and memory. On a 30-point cognitive assessment, where lower scores indicate poorer performance, the least active participants experienced an estimated average decline of 0.478 points per year. The middle group declined by 0.090 points annually, while the most active group showed almost no average decline, at just 0.007 points per year.
Movement assessments also showed different patterns. Researchers used a 132-point scale, with higher scores indicating more severe symptoms. Participants began with an average score of 23. Over time, the least active group showed an estimated annual increase of 0.143 points, suggesting modest worsening. In contrast, scores decreased by 0.225 points annually in the moderately active group and by 0.783 points in the most active group, indicating more favorable movement outcomes.
The associations remained after researchers accounted for participants’ age, sex, and duration of Parkinson’s disease. Higher values across all three measures of physical activity were associated with slower cognitive decline and less worsening of movement symptoms, suggesting that both activity duration and intensity may be relevant.
Why the Findings Require Caution
“The possible benefits of physical activity for people with Parkinson’s disease may depend on how long they stay active and whether they continue exercising over time,” said Ryu. “While our study found small differences between activity levels, these differences may become more meaningful over time. Since participants generally had good thinking and memory skills at the start of the study, our results should be interpreted with caution and further studies are needed.”
One limitation was that participants reported their own physical activity, potentially introducing inaccuracies in estimates of exercise duration and intensity. Because the study was observational, researchers also could not determine whether greater activity helped preserve neurological function or whether people with less severe symptoms were better able to remain active. Further research is needed to establish whether increasing physical activity can directly influence the progression of Parkinson’s disease.
Reference: “Physical Activity and Motor and Cognitive Progression in Parkinson Disease: A Longitudinal Cohort Study” by Dong-Woo Ryu, Kevin R. Duque, Luca Marsili, Jesus Abanto, Nathaly Chinchihualpa Paredes, Heba A. Deraz, Andrea Herrera Gorriti, Emily J. Hill, Abhimanyu Mahajan, Andrew Duker and Alberto J. Espay, 7 October 2026,
Neurology

title: Scientists Discover Aspirin May Slash Dementia Risk by 70% – but Only for Certain People
content:
Aspirin is a widely used medication known for relieving pain, reducing inflammation, and lowering fever. Credit: Stock
Aspirin was linked to a sharply lower dementia risk in some older adults, and their genes may hold the clue.
Monash University
analysis found that older adults with a particular genetic profile had about a 70 percent lower relative risk of dementia when taking low-dose aspirin. But serious bleeding was also more common in this group, leaving researchers with a promising lead that needs further testing.
The research, published in
Alzheimer’s & Dementia: The Journal of the Alzheimer’s Association
, examined genetic data from more than 13,500 participants in the ASPREE Trial (Aspirin in Reducing Events in the Elderly). Researchers compared genetic scores to investigate whether inherited differences could help explain who might benefit from aspirin.
A Genetic Signal Linked to Platelets
The strongest finding involved a genetic score associated with platelet count. Researchers ranked participants by that score, then compared dementia outcomes among those assigned aspirin or a placebo.
Among participants in the highest 20 percent, dementia developed in 1 percent of aspirin recipients, compared with 3.3 percent of placebo recipients. Although that represents roughly a 70 percent relative reduction, the absolute difference was 2.3 percentage points, equivalent to about 23 fewer dementia cases per 1,000 people.
Lead author Dr. Peter Fransquet, a research fellow at Monash’s School of Public Health and Preventive Medicine, said the finding could help move prevention toward a more personalized approach.
“Previous trials found aspirin didn’t prevent dementia when everyone was considered together,” Dr. Fransquet said. “Our findings suggest there may be more to the story. In people with this particular genetic profile, we saw substantially fewer cases of dementia among those taking aspirin. It raises the possibility that genetics could one day help us identify who may benefit from a preventive treatment, rather than taking a one-size-fits-all approach.”
Lower Dementia Risk, More Serious Bleeding
The potential protection against dementia came with a higher risk of serious bleeding. In the same genetic group, major bleeding occurred in 4.4 percent of aspirin recipients and 2.1 percent of placebo recipients, a difference equivalent to about 23 additional major bleeding events per 1,000 people.
The results draw attention to how platelets may contribute to dementia. Scientists have previously linked platelet activation and aggregation, or clumping, with dementia, but the role of overall platelet count remains less clear.
“What’s particularly interesting is that the signal wasn’t linked to the established genetic risk factors for Alzheimer’s disease and dementia,” Dr. Fransquet said. “Instead, it’s pointing us towards platelet biology and gives us a new avenue to investigate.”
What Personalized Prevention Would Require
Dementia Australia estimates that 446,500 Australians are living with dementia in 2026 and projects that the number will exceed one million by 2065.
For now, the analysis identifies a group worth investigating rather than establishing a treatment strategy. A trial specifically designed around this genetic profile would help determine whether the apparent dementia benefit is reproducible and how it compares with the bleeding risk.
“We now need to confirm the finding in other studies and ultimately test it in a trial designed specifically for people with this genetic profile. People shouldn’t start taking aspirin to prevent dementia on the basis of this study without consulting with their doctor, particularly given the increased risk of serious bleeding. If it holds up, the fact that aspirin is already cheap and widely available could make personalized dementia prevention a real possibility.”
Reference: “Platelet count polygenic scores may modify the effect of aspirin in primary prevention of dementia” by Peter D. Fransquet, Chenglong Yu, Cammie Tran, Sultana Monira Hussain, Amy Brodtmann, Andrew M. Tonkin, Mark R Nelson, Joanne Ryan, John J. McNeil and Paul Lacaze, 24 September 2026,
Alzheimer’s & Dementia
DOI: 10.1002/alz.71817

title: Scientists Build a World-First DNA Computer That Runs Without Continuous Power
content:
Researchers have developed a DNA computer that performs mathematical calculations using molecular interactions rather than silicon chips. Credit: Shutterstock
Reusable for up to 25 different calculations, a DNA computer points toward possible uses in energy-efficient computing and long-term data storage.
A DNA computer has added 10 and 3 in 30 seconds, using interacting strands in water instead of a silicon chip. Developed by researchers at Maynooth University (MU), the system can also multiply and divide without a continuous electricity supply.
The work, published in
, presents a first-of-its-kind system described as one of the most complex and fastest molecular computers yet reported.
DNA strands assemble the answer
Dr Abeer Eshra, an assistant professor and computer scientist at MU’s Hamilton Institute who conducted many of the experiments, described what is happening inside the liquid. “A small droplet of liquid contains billions, and sometimes trillions, of DNA strands. These strands interact with one another to produce a result.”
To build the computer, the team combined a small drop of water and salt with short pieces of DNA and a longer DNA scaffold in a test tube. The mixture needs only a little heat to get started and is then cooled, allowing the computation to proceed.
“The molecules interact, form a structure and that structure is the answer,” said Professor Damien Woods of MU’s Hamilton Institute. “One key innovation is that the system naturally finds that answer without needing continuous energy inputs,” he added.
Pictured are three members of the five-person Maynooth University (MU) DNA computing research team: undergraduate researcher Janet Adio, alongside Prof Damien Woods and Dr Abeer Eshra of the Department of Computer Science’s Hamilton Institute at MU. Credit: Maynooth University
Fast for DNA, slower than silicon
The researchers ran ten programs, including 100-bit computations. In one experiment, the computer added numbers in the range of about 11 million to 34 million, taking up to 14 hours to reach a result. The system also demonstrated robustness and reusability, performing up to 25 different calculations in a row.
“The reaction happens fast in the test tube, but not as fast as silicon, nor is it intended to be. But compared to other DNA computers, ours is the fastest,” said Eshra, joint first author of the
study alongside Dr Tristan Stérin. The paper’s coauthors also included Senior Research Fellow Dr Constantine Evans and undergraduate researcher Janet Adio.
Molecular computers could work inside cells
Beyond arithmetic in a test tube, the research points to possible applications in long-term data storage and energy-efficient computation. In time, molecular systems might also operate inside cells for tasks such as disease detection.
Pictured are three members of the five-person Maynooth University (MU) DNA computing research team: undergraduate researcher Janet Adio, alongside Prof Damien Woods and Dr Abeer Eshra of the Department of Computer Science’s Hamilton Institute at MU. Credit: Maynooth University
Woods explained the motivation for exploring other forms of computing. “Silicon-based computers use so much energy – 23% of Ireland’s electricity goes into computing and data storage. We’ve been blinkered by only seeing one type of computer, but there are other examples around us, including our brain.”
Maynooth’s DNA computing research is supported by a €4 million European Innovation Council grant led by Woods. The DISCO project, DNA-based infrastructure for Storage and Computation, aims to develop new ways to compute and store data using DNA technology.
“This is blue skies science. We don’t know where the future is going to take us.” Woods offered that perspective on the broader effort to explore alternative forms of computing.
Reference: “A thermodynamically favoured molecular computer” by Tristan Stérin, Abeer Eshra, Constantine Glen Evans, Janet Adio and Damien Woods, 16 September 2026,
DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-10996-5

title: Scientists Just Discovered a Major Problem With Lab-Grown Human Embryo Models
content:
Stem cell-derived embryo models offer scientists a promising way to investigate the earliest stages of human development, but their biological accuracy remains uncertain. Credit: Shutterstock
A map built from more than 14,000 embryo cells reveals what stem cell models get right about early human development and where researchers could improve them.
Under a microscope, a cluster grown from stem cells can resemble a human embryo in its first days of development. These structures, called blastoids, offer scientists a way to investigate the biology behind fertility and pregnancy success. Their appearance, however, cannot establish whether the cells inside are developing as they would in a real embryo.
University of Sydney researchers have now looked beyond that resemblance, developing a computational framework to evaluate models produced by four leading methods. Their study, published in
Cell Systems
, found that some reproduced important features of early development relatively well, but none fully matched the biology of a natural human embryo.
Studying donated human embryos involves technical and ethical constraints that have long made the earliest stages of development difficult to investigate. Growing models from stem cells gives researchers another way to explore those stages, provided they understand what the models can reliably reproduce. Blastoids are research models, not actual human embryos, and current models cannot develop into a human embryo.
“If we’re going to use these systems to answer important biological questions, we first need to know what they can reliably tell us,” said lead author Associate Professor Pengyi Yang, an ARC Future Fellow in the University of Sydney’s School of Mathematics and Statistics and Unit Head of Computational Systems Biology at the Children’s Medical Research Institute. Yang also leads the Trans-Regulatory Biology group at the Charles Perkins Center.
Associate Professor Pengyi Yang at his desk. Credit: University of Sydney
Tracing development through 14,000 embryo cells
Yang and his colleagues assembled more than 14,000 single-cell transcriptomes from human embryos at key developmental stages. Each transcriptome records the RNA molecules in an individual cell, providing clues about which genes are active. Bringing these datasets into a common framework allowed the researchers to follow molecular differences that an embryo’s outward appearance alone cannot reveal.
The resulting reference map traces how cells specialize and organize themselves during the days immediately before and after implantation, when an embryo attaches to the lining of the uterus. It gives researchers a detailed biological reference against which to examine the cells in their models.
“Our framework allows researchers to compare these models against a detailed biological reference and determine which cell types and developmental processes are faithfully reproduced, and which are not.”
Some cells have no clear embryonic match
The team compared that reference with blastoids generated using four widely used protocols developed by international research groups. They examined the cells’ molecular identities, the timing of their development, and how they were distributed among developmental branches known as lineages. A model could therefore be assessed on several aspects of its biology, beyond whether its overall shape looked convincing.
Portrait of Associate Professor Pengyi Yang. Credit: University of Sydney
Cells in some models corresponded relatively well to all three major lineages found in a natural human blastocyst, the early embryonic stage that blastoids are designed to resemble. Other models represented certain cell types poorly or contained large numbers of cells that could not be confidently matched to any known embryonic state. The differences meant that each model had its own strengths and gaps.
“But our study also shows that current models are not biologically equivalent to real human embryos, and researchers need to be careful about the conclusions they draw from them,” Yang said.
A shared standard for future blastoids
Researchers worldwide can now examine those gaps using the team’s publicly available reference datasets and benchmarking tools. Testing new models against the same reference could make their strengths and limitations easier to compare. The team hopes that this shared benchmark will also help researchers improve models more quickly and evaluate them more rigorously.
“Our work provides a roadmap for improving embryo models and ensuring scientific claims remain grounded in what the models can actually support.”
As researchers grow the next generation of blastoids, the clusters taking shape under their microscopes will have to meet a more demanding benchmark for how closely their cells reproduce early human development.
Reference: “Systematic transcriptomic evaluation of blastoid models of early human development” by Siqu Long, Hani Jieun Kim, Nazmus Salehin, Hao Huang, Xinran Zhang, Raja Jothi and Pengyi Yang, 2 October 2026,
Cell Systems
DOI: 10.1016/j.cels.2026.101738
The work was supported by a National Health and Medical Research Council Investigator Grant and a Metcalf Prize for Stem Cell Research to Pengyi Yang. Raja Jothi was supported by the Intramural Research Program of the National Institutes of Health (USA) and National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences (USA).

title: The World’s Oldest Land Animal Has a Remarkable Anti-Aging Secret Hidden in Its DNA
content:
Jonathan the tortoise. Credit: St Helena Government Communications Hub
The world’s oldest land animal carries 287 unique gene variants involved in DNA repair and other defenses against aging, offering clues researchers hope to turn into human treatments.
When Jonathan the giant tortoise hatched in 1832, Charles Darwin was still a young explorer and Queen Victoria had yet to take the throne. Nearly two centuries later, Jonathan is still alive – and scientists have discovered something remarkable about his biology. Despite his estimated age of 194, the world’s oldest living land animal has genetic controls for DNA repair and metabolism that closely resemble those of much younger tortoises.
For the past 144 years, Jonathan has lived on the remote South Atlantic island of St. Helena, a British Overseas Territory. He arrived from the Seychelles in 1882 as a gift to the governor, already fully grown, and has spent most of his life roaming the grounds of Plantation House, the governor’s residence.
Youthful patterns in Jonathan’s gene controls
To investigate the biology behind his longevity, a team led by the U.S. longevity research nonprofit Kallel examined both his DNA and the controls that regulate its activity. Their study, published October 7, 2026, in
Science Advances
, is the first to investigate a giant tortoise’s epigenome, the system of switches that helps turn genes on and off.
Jonathan has lived most of his life on the island of St Helena, a British Overseas Territory in the South Atlantic Ocean, in grounds of Plantation House – the residence of the governor of St Helena. He arrived from the Seychelles 144 years ago, already fully grown, as a gift to the governor. Credit: Joe Holland
These switches usually change over time, contributing to aging. When the researchers compared Jonathan’s epigenome with those of younger Aldabra giant tortoises, however, they found very similar patterns in the switches controlling DNA repair and metabolism.
“We found that the gene regulators involved in energy production and DNA repair have remained incredibly stable in Jonathan over almost two centuries,” said Dr. Justin Gerlach of Peterhouse at the University of Cambridge, who was involved in the study.
The team also identified 287 unique gene variants in Jonathan that they say reduce the usual effects of aging. These variants control processes involved in repairing damaged DNA, reducing inflammation, regulating insulin, and suppressing cancer. Together, the DNA and epigenome findings point to a combination of protective genetic features and stability in how key genes are regulated.
Jonathan, an Aldabra giant tortoise (Aldabrachelys gigantea), is estimated to be 194 years old. This makes him the oldest living giant tortoise, and oldest land animal, in the world today. Credit: Joe Holland
Gerlach has spent several decades studying giant tortoise ecology and conservation, but this was his first investigation of their exceptionally long lives. The giant tortoises of the Galapagos and Seychelles islands are the last survivors of animals that once dominated the ecology of many of the world’s islands.
Jonathan arrived in St. Helena as a gift to Sir William Grey-Wilson in 1882, who later became governor of the island. This image was taken around that time – Jonathan is on the left. Credit: A.L. Innes
“There are few creatures that could tell us more about aging than the giant tortoises of the Galapagos and Seychelles islands. Working with a really old giant tortoise is such a privilege: you get a sense of the tortoise being your collaborator, not your study subject,” Gerlach said.
Tortoise genetics could guide human treatments
“Nature has already solved the puzzle of aging in remarkable ways, and Jonathan’s genome provides a blueprint for cellular resilience,” said Stephen Clark, MD, PhD, founder of Kallel and senior author of the study.
Researchers say it’s good genes and lack of genetic wear and tear that have kept Jonathan living for nearly two centuries. Credit: Joe Holland
He added: “Our goal is to take these evolutionary insights and immediately translate them into practical, affordable treatments for everyday people. Aging is the greatest risk factor for nearly every chronic disease we face, and through the generosity of philanthropic partners, we can democratize access to longevity medicine.”
Reference: “Epigenetic insights into extreme longevity in the world’s oldest terrestrial animal, Jonathan” by Benjamin Vaisvil, Daniel P. Schmitt, Angela Jones, Vinayak Kapatral, James M. Ford, Madison L. Taylor, Mathia Colwell, Jonathan Hollins, Sam Pascucci, Konstantin Weissenow, Burkhard Rost, Pascal Notin, Justin Gerlach, Thomas C. Terwilliger, Li-Wei Hung, Lars Juhl Jensen, Kathlyn Reed, Todd R. Robeck, Steve Horvath, Christopher Faulk, Yanjun Ma and Stephen W. Clark, 7 October 2026,
Science Advances
DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.adw8887
The research was funded by the Voland Fund.

title: Scientists Discover a Surprising Link Between Obesity and Dementia Survival
content:
Dementia is a general term for a group of conditions that progressively impair memory, thinking, behavior, and the ability to perform everyday activities. Alzheimer’s disease is the most common cause, accounting for an estimated 60% to 70% of cases. Credit: Shutterstock
A large study found that people who are overweight or obese when diagnosed with dementia have a significantly lower risk of death than those at a normal weight.
A higher body weight at the time of a dementia diagnosis may be linked to longer survival, according to a large study of older Americans. Researchers found that people who were overweight or obese when diagnosed had a significantly lower risk of death than those in the normal weight range, even after accounting for other health conditions and lifestyle factors.
The findings, published in the
Journal of Alzheimer’s Disease
, contrast with evidence that obesity during midlife increases the likelihood of developing dementia. Although the researchers could not determine why higher weight was associated with better survival, their analysis suggests that the relationship cannot easily be explained by several common sources of statistical bias.
Higher Body Weight Linked to Lower Mortality
The survival differences varied by weight category. People who were overweight (body mass index of 25 to 29.9) had a 16% lower risk of death than those at a normal weight. Those with class 1 obesity (BMI of 30 to 34.9) had a 27% lower risk, while individuals with class 2 or 3 obesity (BMI equal to or greater than 35) had a 22% lower risk.
To investigate the relationship, researchers analyzed 4,523 participants in the Health and Retirement Study, a nationally representative study of U.S. adults ages 51 and older conducted by the University of Michigan. All participants were free of dementia when they entered the study but developed the condition later. Data collected between 1998 and 2022 allowed the team to examine weight changes before diagnosis and track survival afterward.
Could Weight Loss Before Diagnosis Explain the Results?
One complication in dementia research is that weight loss often begins long before the condition is formally identified.
Earlier research
Other potential biases could also distort the relationship. Studying only people who develop dementia can introduce misleading statistical associations between weight and mortality. Survivor bias is another concern. Obesity increases the risk of dying from conditions such as cardiovascular disease; people with obesity who survive long enough to develop dementia may be healthier than others who were initially in the same weight category.
The researchers conducted additional analyses to examine these possible distortions but found little evidence that the major biases they evaluated accounted for the observed survival differences.
“Because this finding is somewhat counterintuitive, an important question is whether it could simply be an artifact of bias. Our analyses suggest that the major sources of bias we examined do not explain the survival advantage associated with higher weight,” said Yuan Zhang, assistant professor of sociomedical sciences at Columbia University’s Mailman School of Public Health.
How Energy Reserves May Affect Dementia Survival
One possible biological explanation involves the body’s ability to withstand nutritional decline. Dementia can disrupt brain processes that regulate hunger and eating behavior, while also making it increasingly difficult for people to prepare food or feed themselves. Some individuals experience higher energy expenditure, reduced appetite, and progressive loss of muscle and body tissue.
People with greater fat stores or muscle mass may have more reserves to draw upon when eating becomes difficult. These reserves could potentially help them tolerate periods of inadequate nutrition, although the study did not establish that this mechanism explains the survival advantage.
“Nutrition can be a big problem for people with dementia,” said Chang. “They may experience wasting and an inability to eat, which can be due to changes in the brain’s central drive, leading to loss of appetite and initiative, increased energy expenditure, and difficulties feeding themselves.”
What the Findings Mean for Dementia Care
Despite the association between higher weight and longer survival, the findings do not establish that gaining weight improves outcomes for people with dementia. The observational study examined existing differences in body weight and mortality rather than testing whether deliberate weight changes could influence survival.
“This doesn’t mean that patients with dementia should attempt to become overweight or obese, as our study was not designed to test that question. But our findings do suggest that weight status may serve as a useful prognostic signal for survival at the time of dementia diagnosis. They also support the notion that nutrition is a key factor in the health and survival of people with dementia,” said Chang, associate professor of social and behavioral sciences at NYU School of Global Public Health and the study’s lead author.
Determining whether fat stores, muscle mass, nutritional status, or other physiological differences account for the association will require further research. Body weight may nevertheless provide useful information about survival prospects when dementia is first diagnosed.
“While our analysis examined several forms of bias, and there are very plausible physiological reasons for the potential benefits of a little extra weight in this context, we still don’t know exactly why people who were overweight or obese had a lower risk of death. Regardless of the underlying mechanism, however, weight status at the time of a dementia diagnosis can still serve as a meaningful prognostic signal,” noted Chang.
Reference: “Body mass index and mortality in incident dementia” by Virginia W. Chang, Eleanor Hayes-Larson, Hui Zheng and Yuan S. Zhang, 25 March 2026,
Journal of Alzheimer’s Disease
DOI: 10.1177/13872877261491694
This work was supported by the National Institutes of Health (grant numbers R00AG070274, R00AG075317).
