title: One-Third of Older Adults With Cognitive Disorders Take Drugs That Could Harm Them
content:
Older adults with cognitive disorders can be especially vulnerable to medications that act on the central nervous system, with potentially serious consequences for health and independence. Credit: Shutterstock
As the population ages, medication safety is becoming increasingly important for people with cognitive decline.
Older adults with dementia and other cognitive disorders are less likely than they were a decade ago to receive medications that can worsen memory, balance, and coordination. But nearly one in three still takes at least one potentially inappropriate drug.
University at Buffalo researchers analyzed data from 2,796 independently living adults age 65 and older with cognitive disorders. Exposure to potentially harmful medications fell from 39.3% in 2011 to 29.3% in 2022, according to a study published in the
Journal of the American Geriatrics Society
Why These Drugs Can Be Risky
The medications include drugs used for anxiety, insomnia, psychosis, and other conditions involving the central nervous system. In older adults with cognitive disorders, they can increase the risk of emergency department visits, hospitalization, poorer mental health, and premature death.
“This is a population with some mental issues that relate to the central nervous system. These drugs also act on the central nervous system, so they can be too much for older adults if inappropriately used,” says Haowen Hsu, PharmD, the study’s first author.
Benzodiazepines such as Xanax and sleep medications such as Ambien can impair cognition, balance, and coordination, particularly in older adults.
Deprescribing Could Reduce Harm
One strategy is deprescribing, which can involve stopping a medication, lowering its dose, reducing how often it is taken, or replacing it with a safer alternative.
“A central word for patients in this age group is ‘deprescribing,’ which means, for example, removing inappropriate medications and decreasing the frequency or the dosage. In some cases, it means replacing the current medication with a milder alternative,” Hsu says.
The researchers used the American Geriatrics Society’s Beers Criteria, a list of medications that may be risky for older adults. Their analysis represented approximately 29.7 million older Americans with cognitive disorders from 2011 to 2022.
Progress, but Continued Exposure
The study did not examine why prescribing declined. Hsu said increased attention to geriatric medication safety may have contributed.
“We were happy to see the percentages of harm decline over that 11-year period,” he says. “However, one-third of our target population is still exposed to these harmful medications, which isn’t good.”
The researchers say regular medication reviews and tools such as the Drug Burden Index could help identify patients carrying a high cumulative burden from sedative or anticholinergic drugs.
Further studies are needed to determine whether better medication management can reduce hospitalizations and emergency visits while improving quality of life in older adults with cognitive disorders.
Reference: “Cognitive Potentially Inappropriate Medications, Quality of Life, and Healthcare Use in Older Adults With Cognitive Disorders” by Haowen Hsu, Collin M. Clark, Steven Feuerstein, Robert G. Wahler, Ranjit Singh and David M. Jacobs, 4 August 2026,
Journal of the American Geriatrics Society
DOI: 10.1111/jgs.70607

title: Inflammation May Awaken Dormant Cancer Cells Years After Treatment
content:
Dormant cancer cells may be sensitive to immune-driven changes in their surroundings. New findings reveal one molecular clue connecting inflammation with metastatic reactivation. Credit: Stock
The body’s response to inflammation may disturb cancer cells that have been lying silent for years, giving them an opportunity to grow again.
Researchers at the
Francis Crick Institute
have found that gut inflammation can reactivate dormant breast cancer cells in a mouse model of bone marrow. Their study, published in
Cell Reports
, suggests that changes needed to produce more immune cells can also create conditions that favor cancer growth.
Cancer cells can leave the original tumor and settle elsewhere in the body, a process called metastasis that accounts for most cancer-related deaths. Breast cancer cells frequently reach bone marrow, where an inactive state helps them evade immune defenses and resist chemotherapy.
“Cancer cells that have moved to another part of the body can stay dormant for years after the original tumor has been treated,” explains Crick group leader Ilaria Malanchi, whose lab studies interactions between cancer cells and the body. “It’s a worrying period for people, as they don’t know if these metastatic cells will reactivate, leading to a relapse.”
“We can’t wait five years to see if dormant cancer cells reactivate in mice, as this exceeds their lifespan,” Ilaria explains. “We’ve known for a long time that we need to think creatively about a new model.”
A nest of dormant cancer cells in the bone, in magenta. Bone marrow cells are in blue and blood vessels in green. Credit: Tatiana Rizou, as in Cell Reports (2026).
Recreating Dormant Cancer In Bone Marrow
Building on previous work by Laurie Gay, Stefania di Blasio, and Tatiana Rizou developed an “extramedullary bone model”: bone tissue grown from skeletal stem cells beneath the skin. The replica contains the marrow cells needed to produce blood cells and responds to inflammatory signals much like natural bone marrow.
“We then added cells from a mouse mammary tumor onto the replica bone,” explains Ilaria. “Most entered a dormant state, with only sporadic replication activity.”
Ilaria Malanchi runs the Tumour-Host Interaction Laboratory at the Crick. Credit: The Francis Crick Institute
The model gave the team a way to investigate how events elsewhere in the body affect these resting cells. Fractures and other bone injuries can encourage metastatic cancer growth in marrow, but the researchers wanted to test whether a more distant injury or infection could also disturb dormancy.
Gut Inflammation Changes The Cancer Environment
“We induced intestinal colitis—inflammation in the gut—in the mice with the extramedullary bone hosting dormant metastatic cells. Because the replica bone responds to the immune system, gut inflammation triggered a rapid production of immune cells from the bone,” Ilaria explains.
That response required the marrow environment to reorganize to support greater immune cell production. As it changed, more of the dormant cancer cells began dividing, increasing the chance of a tumor forming. The findings connect inflammation in one organ with changes in the tissue sheltering cancer cells elsewhere.
Examining gene activity in the bone and cancer cells pointed to HMGB2, a molecule that stimulates cell growth. Its levels rose alongside the surge in immune cell production, and it also promoted cancer cell reactivation.
“Even without inflammation elsewhere in the body, just the increased HMGB2 in the artificial bone was enough to stimulate more cancer cells to activate,” Ilaria says. “We also analyzed bone samples from people with breast or prostate cancer—HMGB2 was present where there were actively dividing cancer cells.
“All of these findings suggest that boosting immune cell production in the bone, as part of a normal response to inflammation, comes at the cost of disrupting tumor dormancy, tipping the balance towards reactivation and metastatic growth.”
Why Inflammation Does Not Guarantee Relapse
Ilaria emphasizes that inflammation does not automatically cause cancer to return. “We think it’s a piecemeal situation where each systemic change increases the chance of more metastatic cells waking up each time,” she says.
The research suggests that monitoring infections, inflammation, and injuries after remission might help identify periods when dormant cells are more likely to become active.
“Once cancer cells are actively replicating, they can respond to chemotherapy, so understanding developments affecting the bone marrow could lead to early intervention,” Ilaria concludes.
Reference: “An extramedullary bone model of metastatic dormancy reveals an increased rate of metastatic reactivation upon distant insults” by Stefania Di Blasio, Tatiana Rizou, Laurie J. Cell Reports

title: The Fossil Record May Be Missing 200 Million Years of Animal History
content:
Ediacaran sea floor, Namibia, Southwest Africa – 543 million years ago. Credit: Museum of Natural History, University of Oxford / Mighty Fossils
A fossil deposit in Mongolia preserves microscopic organisms in extraordinary detail, down to cells inside specimens that resemble embryos. Yet none of the fossils examined can confidently be identified as an animal, even though fossils from Namibia and South China show that animals already existed when the Mongolian deposit formed.
That gap challenges an assumption researchers have used to date the origins of animal life. If a deposit preserves tiny organisms exceptionally well, can scientists conclude that any animals alive at the time would also have been preserved? A new study led by the University of Oxford, published in
Science Advances
on October 2, suggests the answer is no. Revisiting that assumption pushes the possible origin of animals up to 200 million years before their first unmistakable fossils.
Estimated timeline for the origin of animals based on molecular clock analyses. The grey bar on the right of the image is the origin of animals based on an Ediacaran upper calibration. The grey bar to the left is the origin based on older deposits in the Tonian period, as suggested by the new study. Credit: Orin Lole Durbin
Exceptional preservation can still miss animals
Animal fossils seem to appear relatively suddenly just before the Cambrian Period, which lasted from 539 to 487 million years ago, despite other evidence pointing to an earlier evolutionary history. Researchers have recently used the roughly 590-million-year-old Weng’an Biota in China to limit how far back that history could extend. Its rocks, dating to the Ediacaran, preserve microscopic organisms in exceptional detail, but none are definitive animals. Scientists therefore inferred that animals must have originated after the deposit formed, reasoning that it would have preserved them had they existed.
The Mongolian deposit, known as the Kheseen Biota, offers a way to examine that reasoning. It is more than 40 million years younger than Weng’an, although the two share some species, and dates to a time when animals are known from elsewhere. The research team, which included scientists from the University of California, Berkeley, ETH Zürich, and Yale University, conducted a comprehensive survey of its exceptionally preserved microfossils.
They examined more than 140 samples, including material from previously undocumented localities, using scanning electron microscopy. Alongside the embryo-like fossils with internal cells, they identified new microfossil species, including acritarchs, tiny spherical organisms with spines and branching projections.
Asterocapsoides wenganensis, Kheseen Formation, latest Ediacaran/early Cambrian. Scale bar: 0.1 mm. Credit: Derek Briggs
Senior author Associate Professor Ross Anderson, of the University of Oxford’s Museum of Natural History, said, “The Kheseen Biota breaks the argument that the exceptional microfossils of Weng’an mean we would have seen animal fossils in the assemblage had they existed at the time. The Kheseen microfossils are just as well-preserved, yet animals continue to be absent—despite the fact we know at that point they existed.”
The earliest animals would have been small and soft-bodied, lacking the shells, bones, and other hard structures that make later animals easier to preserve. Fossilization would have depended on their environment and an unusual combination of chemical conditions after death. The researchers argue that animals either lived in environments different from those represented in the Kheseen Biota or that the chemical conditions there failed to preserve their remains. Either possibility weakens the use of Weng’an’s missing animals as evidence that animal life had not yet begun.
Chemical traces offer another way to look for creatures whose bodies have disappeared. Biomarkers preserved in ancient rocks provide evidence consistent with sponges living at least 650 million years ago, tens of millions of years before the oldest definitive macroscopic animal fossils, those large enough to see without a microscope.
Knollisphaeridium maximum, Kheseen Formation, latest Ediacaran/early Cambrian. Scale bar: 0.1 mm. Credit: Derek Briggs
Molecular clocks point to earlier animals
To estimate how much further back animal origins might reach, the team used molecular clock analysis. This technique compares genetic differences between living species and combines rates of evolution with fossil dates as reference points to estimate when their ancestors lived. The dates supplied by the fossil record help constrain those estimates, so changing them can alter the inferred evolutionary timeline.
Instead of treating Weng’an as the maximum age for animal origins, the researchers drew on several older deposits dating from roughly 850 to 730 million years ago. These included the Svanbergfjellet Formation in Norway, the Bitter Springs Group in Australia, and the Chuar Group in Arizona, United States. All are rich in fossils and have the potential to preserve animals, although animal fossils have eluded discovery in them. These deposits have previously been used to set maximum dates for animal origins.
Using those older geological constraints shifted the estimated origin of animals back by around 200 million years compared with analyses constrained by the younger Ediacaran Weng’an deposit. The resulting estimate, between 800 and 700 million years ago, places their possible beginnings deep in the Neoproterozoic Era.
Study author Associate Professor Ross Anderson (University of Oxford) in the mountains to the west of Lake Khuvsgul, Mongolia during fieldwork in summer 2017. Credit: Ross Anderson
Animals may predate Snowball Earth
That interval spans the beginning of the Cryogenian Period, around 720 million years ago. During the Cryogenian, enormous glaciers spread across the planet in episodes commonly known as Snowball Earth. Animals could therefore have evolved before some of Earth’s most extreme ice ages or appeared during that inhospitable interval. The findings reopen questions about whether conditions associated with Snowball Earth helped shape the origin and early evolution of animal life.
First author Orin Lole Durbin, now a PhD student at Virginia Tech and an undergraduate at the University of Oxford at the time of the study, said, “Pre-Ediacaran animal body fossils still elude us, and this analysis does not prove that animals existed 800 million years ago. However, our new fossil evidence from Mongolia undermines one of the main arguments for restricting animal origins to the Ediacaran interval. Meanwhile, our molecular-clock analyses show how much further back their evolutionary history could extend.”
The researchers recommend searching deposits from different parts of the world that represent varied environments and ways of preserving fossils. That search should consider all available evidence, including animal bodies, traces of their activity, and chemical biomarkers.
Anderson added, “Until that evidence becomes available, the precise birth date of the animal kingdom remains uncertain.”
Reference: “Re-evaluating molecular clock maximum age calibrations revives pre-Ediacaran divergence estimates for animals” by Orin M. Lole Durbin, Eliel S.C. Anttila, Derek E.G. Briggs, Francis A. Macdonald and Ross P. Anderson, 2 October 2026,
Science Advances
DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aeg6289

title: Stanford Scientists Discover We’ve Lost Ancient Gut Microbes That Traveled With Humans for Thousands of Years
content:
Our gut microbiome is a complex community of trillions of microorganisms, including bacteria, viruses, and fungi, that help digest food, produce essential vitamins, and regulate the immune system. Credit: Shutterstock
Scientists comparing the gut microbiomes of two geographically distant populations uncovered surprising similarities despite thousands of years of separation.
Hundreds of bacterial species missing from modern human guts may have accompanied our ancestors for tens of thousands of years. A
Stanford University
study published October 7 in
found that two populations separated by continents share remarkably similar gut microbes, many with genetic histories linked to ancient human migrations.
The researchers compared the Hadza hunter-gatherers of Tanzania with the Tsimane, Indigenous forager-horticulturalists in the Bolivian Amazon. Despite different diets and thousands of years of geographic separation, the populations share 1,231 bacterial species. About 60% are rare or absent in industrialized populations.
Ancient Microbes Shared Across Continents
The researchers identified approximately 1,400 bacterial species in the sampled Tsimane population, nearly 90% of which were also found among the Hadza. This extensive overlap was unexpected because the Hadza primarily hunt and gather wild foods, while the Tsimane cultivate crops and consume substantial amounts of dietary fiber.
“We were really surprised to see that the vast majority of the species in the Tsimane’s microbiome correspond with the Hadza’s,” said Justin Sonnenburg, PhD, Stanford professor of microbiology and immunology and senior author of the study.
“That made us wonder if there really is a core set of bacterial and other species that traveled with the ancestors of the Tsimane as they migrated around the globe,” said Benjamin Good, PhD, Stanford assistant professor of applied physics and senior co-author.
Tracing Bacteria Through Human History
“Could these bugs have been in continual interaction with us since long before the ancestors of today’s Hadza and Tsimane became geographically separated?” Sonnenburg asked. “To answer that, we turned to Ben’s team, and what they found blew our minds.”
Using deep metagenomic sequencing and population genetics methods, the researchers analyzed bacterial DNA to reconstruct evolutionary relationships. For many shared species, estimated divergence times matched major prehistoric human migrations, including movements out of Africa and into the Americas.
“We see evidence that these bacteria were present in the ancestors of both the Tsimane and the Hadza, and therefore presumably the ancestors of all of us,” Good said.
What Modern Lifestyles May Have Changed
“Our study establishes that the hundreds of bacterial species that are rare or missing in industrialized microbiomes were ancient companions of ours as we migrated around the globe, likely passed from generation to generation for millennia,” Sonnenburg said. “This long-term association has implications for how such recent biodiversity loss in our microbiome may impact our biology and thus our health.”
Industrialized populations have substantially less diverse gut microbiomes, potentially reflecting factors such as antibiotic use, processed diets, and highly sanitized environments. Changes in gut microbes have been associated with obesity, Type 2 diabetes, and autoimmune diseases, but whether losing these ancient species directly contributes to illness remains unknown.
“If these microbes hosted by the Hadza and Tsimane really are part of our evolutionary biology, then those of us in industrialized countries are missing a huge part of what our human genome has potentially adapted to over a vast time period,” Sonnenburg said. “We’re interested in more fully exploring these long-standing relationships between humans and our gut microbes.”
Reference: “Prehistoric global migration of vanishing gut microbes with humans” by Matthew M. Carter, Zhiru Liu, Matthew R. Olm, Melanie Martin, Daniel D. Sprockett, Parsa Ghadermazi, Benjamin C. Trumble, Hillard Kaplan, Jonathan Stieglitz, Daniel Eid Rodriguez, David A. Relman, Erica D. Sonnenburg, Michael Gurven, Benjamin H. Good and Justin L. Sonnenburg, 7 October 2026,
DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11106-1

Merigan Endowment at Stanford University, and the French National Research Agency under the Investments for the Future (Investissements d’Avenir) program.

title: Scientists Predicted Humanity Would End on November 13, 2026. Should We Be Worried?
content:
In 1960, scientists published a mathematical model predicting that humanity would face a population catastrophe on November 13, 2026. Credit: Shutterstock
For decades, a doomsday equation predicted population growth better than most experts, until falling birth rates undermined its forecast of catastrophe in 2026.
In 1960,
, one of the world’s leading science journals, published an article with an unambiguous title:
Doomsday: Friday, 13 November, A.D. 2026
. It predicted that on this future date—just over a month from today—the human population would approach infinity and effectively annihilate itself.
The outlandishness of the claim landed the article in widespread public attention. More surprisingly—because its underlying research and math seemed sound—it also received careful and sustained scientific attention.
The authors—Heinz von Foerster, an Austrian-American professor and cybernetics expert, and two of his students, Patricia M. Mora and Lawrence W. Amiot—argued that human populations are exceptional and might grow beyond an exponential rate, at an ever-increasing one.
“Our great-great-grandchildren will not starve,” they argued. “They will be squeezed to death.”
The article was regularly cited, and its predictions appeared remarkably accurate—until around 1993, halfway to the predicted “doomsday,” when the global population began falling behind its forecasts.
Today, the global birth rate is
slightly less than half what it was in 1960
. Hopefully, we will all wake up on Nov. 13 to an ordinary day. Nonetheless, this article remains exemplary for blending rigorous science with the art of stagecraft to a staggering effect.
Unique human capacities
The mid-20th century saw increasing societal concern about global population growth and its potential to lead to resource scarcity and geopolitical conflict. Underlying much of this concern was implicit or explicit acceptance of the Malthusian idea that
whereas population has the potential to grow exponentially, it is kept constantly under check by its capacity to feed itself
In their article, however, von Foerster and his co-authors argued that as far as populations go, humans may be exceptional.
Given our capacity to communicate and form “coalitions” that help us resolve problems, rising population density might simply mean more opportunities for collaboration, so that our numbers might grow not only beyond an exponential rate but at an ever-increasing one.
They then used 24 estimates of the world population stretching across the past 2,000 years to show that human numbers have in fact continually outpaced expectations. All this was presented in calm, scientific prose and aided by dense mathematical equations.
‘Squeezed to death’
Von Foerster and his co-authors then projected these historical figures into the future, calculating that thanks to ever-increasing growth, in the year 2026 our numbers would near infinity.
Thankfully, the same capacity for collaboration that assisted our species’ development throughout history could now avert this catastrophe. Since we are unlikely to want to reduce our life spans, they concluded, we should work together to reduce the global birth rate by half.
Heinz von Foerster in 1963. Credit: University of Illinois, CC BY-SA
This publication caused an immediate stir. There were stories in
The New York Times
. It became the subject of
a series of
comic strips,
and many commentators took the article as strictly a tongue-in-cheek comment on population fears.
A population explosion
Rather than the story dying out, a funny thing happened. When
Throughout the 1960s through to the 1980s, the “doomsday” equation became regularly cited—usually at face value—in textbooks on genetics, ecology, and demography.
It appeared in stranger places, too. In a 1963
Canadian parliamentary committee
, for example, a witness from the chemical industry prominently cited it as the reason chemical pesticides were required: to feed the approaching population explosion. In a 1971
U.S. Supreme Court abortion case
leading up to Roe v. Wade, it was cited as why there was no compelling reason for the government to favor increased population.
The doomsday idea persisted in part because its predictions for future populations turned out to be highly accurate—at least for a while. Its core equation yielded projections that were
better than those
of most demographers
throughout the 1970s and 1980s
Only around 1993 did that accuracy begin to falter, and the global population began falling behind the forecasts—because the world began to do what von Foerster and his colleagues recommended it do. Today, the global birth rate is slightly less than half the 1960 rate.
Science and stagecraft
We will probably not all wake up on Friday, Nov. 13, “squeezed to death.” But before simply moving on—prepping for the next doomsday scenario—it is worth asking what we can learn from this one.
For me, the lesson is in how we present our beliefs to the world. Heinz von Foerster was, at one point in his life, a stage magician. Borrowing the classic language of stagecraft, an effective illusion relies on three parts: the setup, the extraordinary turn, and the final reveal that returns the situation to normal.
Von Foerster and his co-authors’ article gained attention because it was an ordinary scientific article wrapped in an extraordinary title and conclusion. It retained significance because it was firmly grounded in research and argument.
To draw the world’s attention to a serious matter by way of absurdity—that’s a good trick.

title: Qcells plans a gigawatt-scale perovskite tandem solar factory by 2029
content:
Qcells plans a gigawatt-scale perovskite tandem solar factory by 2029
has announced its plans to open a gigawatt-scale factory producing perovskite-silicon tandem solar panels in 2029.
Hanwha Qcells' solar production plant in Cumming, Georgia, USA. /Courtesy of Hanwha Solutions, from:
Qcells is already testing full-size tandem panels in the field, at its own test sites and with potential customers. The panels come from a
40 MW pilot line in South Korea
, launched in 2024, following an earlier pilot R&D line in Germany that opened in 2022. In 2024,
Qcells also announced an independently confirmed efficiency of 28.6% for a standard-size silicon cell topped with perovskite layers
. In July, the company
said its tandem panel had passed testing against UL and IEC quality standards
The location of the future factory has not been decided. A company presentation in Seoul last week reportedly pointed to Jincheon, South Korea. Qcells has also
designed its new vertically integrated factory in Cartersville, Georgia
, to be easily upgraded to tandem production when the time comes. Qcells also implied that industrial policy could be a determining factor in where the tandem factory is built.
Qcells did not share the perovskite composition it uses or any degradation data from the field tests. Company representatives said the 2029 timing allows time to convince large panel buyers to make the switch, and pointed to Qcells’ experience in scaling up gigawatts of solar production.
Qcells is among the companies speaking at
Perovskite Connect 2026
, taking place October 21-22 in Berlin.

会议指出，三季度以来，各能源监管机构坚持以正确政绩观为引领，加压奋进、真抓实干，着力监管保障迎峰度夏能源安全稳定供应，统筹推进全国统一电力市场建设、电力领域综合监管、供电质量提升等重点任务，取得阶段性成效。
会议强调，当前正值全力冲刺的关键阶段，各能源监管机构要锚定年度目标、压实工作责任、持续补短强弱，确保全年工作圆满收官。要完善全国统一电力市场体系，加强电力市场监管执法，维护公平竞争市场秩序。要提早谋划迎峰度冬能源保供监管，加强供需监测预警，完善市场机制促进新能源消纳，及时妥善处置群众各类用能诉求。要扎实做好电力领域综合监管“后半篇文章”，全力推进年度重点监管任务，充分转化运用监管成果。要加大新一轮“获得电力”政策落实力度，压茬推进供电质量提升专项行动，加快非电网直供电小区治理。要严格落实全面从严治党政治责任，巩固拓展树立和践行正确政绩观学习教育成果，持续涵养风清气正的良好政治生态。
会上，国家能源局新能源司、市场监管司、资质中心宣讲有关规划政策要求，东北监管局、南方监管局、浙江监管办、湖南监管办进行交流发言。
国家能源局监管总监梁昌新主持会议，各相关司和部分直属单位负责同志在主会场参会，各派出机构负责同志和有关人员在分会场参会。

在基础研究和前沿技术领域，
《规划》提出“加速绿色智能新材料研发及新技术应用”等重点任务，推动“源-网-车-储”协同、“风-光-氢-储”集成及再生制动等能量管理与实时调度技术研究。
在技术装备领域，
《规划》提出“推动绿色智能装备升级”等重点任务，研发柔性多源接入供电系统、高强高导耐磨线索及智能化高可靠牵引供电成套装备，构建绿色智能供电新模式。
在绿色低碳领域，
《规划》提出“推动绿色建造技术创新、推动运输装备低碳转型、推进绿智融合运营维护、建立健全碳管理体系”4项重点任务，明确“研制大功率氢能干线货运机车和氢能高效补给装备”等重点工程。
《规划》还提出，推动风光储微电网规模化应用，打造“近零碳”绿色施工示范。突破超低能耗建造与光伏/地源热泵技术。强化移动装备低碳化基础理论研究，强化移动装备低碳化基础理论研究，研究新一代永磁直驱牵引、氢燃料电池安全性设计及智能运维等关键技术，攻关燃料电池混合动力机车的能量管理控制技术。推进低排放低油耗内燃机车及动力电池、氢能等多源动力制式机车车辆示范运营，构建覆盖设计-制造-运营全过程的机车车辆能耗与排放的计量、监测评估体系。

title: “蓝片”不列入本土制造！印度发布新版ALMM电池命名标准草案-索比光伏网
content:
印度新能源与可再生能源部（MNRE）发布修订版草案，拟对批准型号与制造商清单（ALMM）List-II 下的光伏电池采用标准化命名体系。草案规定，每个入列电池型号均采用“制造商品牌名 + 14 位字母数字代码”的统一格式，以标识多晶硅、硅锭、硅片和电池的原产地，以及电池技术、硅片尺寸和转换效率等信息。
草案的利益相关方须在 2026 年 10 月 12 日前提交针对该修订草案的反馈意见。
MNRE 拟议的 14 位代码将通过原材料原产地、技术类型、硅片尺寸及转换效率识别 ALMM List-II 电池。（图片来源：MNRE）
本次草案旨在为电池型号建立统一识别基准，并提升光伏全产业链的溯源性。MNRE 规定，该标准化命名体系将适用于备忘录正式发布后印度国家太阳能研究所（NISE）对 ALMM List-II 新申请开展的审查；而已完成审查或已列入 ALMM List-II 的电池型号，则必须在最终备忘录发布后 2 个月内按照新体系完成更名。
按照拟议规则，14 位编码的前 4 位分别代表多晶硅、硅锭、硅片和电池的原产地，本土制造标注为“D”，外国制造标注为“F”；第 5 至 6 位标识电池技术路线，目前涵盖 Mono PERC（MP）、TOPCon（TC）、HJT（HJ）、背接触（BC）以及钙钛矿（PS），同时允许为新兴技术引入额外代码；第 7 至 8 位代表硅片尺寸，其中 MA 代表 M10、MB 代表 M10R、GA 代表 G12、GB 代表 G12R；第 9 至 11 位表示电池转换效率且省略小数点，例如 24.67% 对应编码为“246”，25.55% 则对应“255”；第 12 至 14 位目前作为预留位。
MNRE 曾于 2026 年 8 月提出一版草案，包含产品原产地、电池技术、硅片尺寸、主栅线以及制造商专用识别码。而 10 月更新的修订方案则改为分配给原产地、技术、硅片尺寸和转换效率，并预留最后 3 位。
此外，MNRE 在 10 月版草案中明确，使用已完成 P-N 结形成及减反射膜沉积的“蓝片”（扩散硅片）生产的电池，不得认定为印度本土制造。由于此类硅片更接近未完成的电池而非基础硅片，因此不得用于印度国内含量要求（DCR）项目。
该命名框架还将根据原材料清单（BoM）显示电池的本土或外国原产地属性，以区分 ALMM List-I 与 List-I(a) 光伏组件。MNRE 表示，该标准化命名体系有望成为每个入列 ALMM List-II 光伏电池型号的唯一识别框架，除便利入列外，还可促进产业链上下游的统一识别和追溯，并可能作为监管、商业及其他相关用途的通用产品标识符。
此外，MNRE 于 2026 年 10 月 1 日发布通知，要求光伏组件制造商在其印度标准局（BIS）注册的组件型号中增加 4 位字母 MMCC 国家代码，以标识组件及其 BoM 中所用电池的制造国。根据该程序，前两位字母代表组件制造国，后两位代表所用电池制造国；采用不同国家电池的组件必须申请独立型号，制造商将拥有 180 天时间更新现有注册。

title: 广东2026年新能源机制电价竞价申报全指南：资格｜规模｜报价策略｜风险避坑（粤发改价格函〔2026〕1805 号）-索比光伏网
content:
2026年10月10日，广东省发展改革委、广东省能源局联合发布《关于开展2026年新能源项目机制电价竞价工作有关事项的通知》（粤发改价格函〔2026〕1805号），正式启动2026年度新能源项目机制电价竞价工作。这是继2025年首轮竞价后广东的第二轮年度竞价，也是9月14日竞价登记通知发布后的正式规则落地，标志着广东机制电价体系从 “首轮探索” 进入 “稳态运行” 阶段。
本轮竞价核心呈现 “一扩两稳一细化” 的特征：**规模扩容**，机制电量初始竞价规模达79.34亿千瓦时，较2025年的50亿千瓦时增长 58.68%；**规则稳定**，0.20—0.40元/千瓦时价格区间、80%/70%申报比例上限、12年执行期限、1.2竞争有效性系数四大核心参数全部沿用2025年标准；**主体范围稳定**，继续明确集中式光伏、陆上风电项目不参与本轮竞价，仅面向
开放；**报价精细化**，价格申报基本单位由1%调整为0.1%，报价颗粒度提升10倍。同时竞价项目时间窗口整体后移一年，覆盖2025年6月1日至2027年10月31日投产或承诺投产的未纳入机制项目，为更多在建、规划项目留出申报空间。
结合广东电力交易中心模拟登记数据来看，截至10月上旬登记项目规模尚未触及总量上限，叠加规则框架整体稳定，市场普遍预计本轮竞价竞争程度与2025年基本持平，出清价格大概率维持在0.36元/千瓦时附近波动。对
业主而言，当前最核心的节点是10月13日的登记截止时间，需优先核对投产时间、项目类型、纳入状态三项资格条件，避免逾期错失年度机会。

title: Alpha Ventus decommissioning tenders halted
content:
Following Ocean Breeze Energy's acquisition of Germany's first offshore
wind farm, Alpha
decommissioning plans previously being progressed by Vattenfall are
no longer moving forward, with the decision attributed to a "change
in needs".
The two tenders, managed by Vattenfall on behalf of Deutsche Offshore-Testfeld
und Infrastruktur GmbH & Co. KG, covered both the wind turbine generator
(WTG) and balance of plant (BoP) scopes.
The WTG tender included the removal of the wind farm's 12 turbines, while
the BoP tender covered the removal of foundations, the offshore substation,
inter-array cables, scour protection and associated infrastructure.
Together, the contracts would have resulted in the full decommissioning
of the Alpha Ventus offshore wind farm. The cancellation of both tenders
suggests that a complete dismantling programme is no longer being pursued.
The development reinforces Ocean Breeze Energy's plans for the project.
As part of the acquisition announcement, the company said it would continue
operating the offshore wind farm.

title: New eCSOV launched by Bibby Marine
content:
Bibby Marine has launched its new electric commissioning service operation
vessel (eCSOV), Staffordshire, at Armon Shipyard in Vigo, Spain. The vessel
entered the water on 10 October, marking a key milestone in its development
ahead of entering service.
Staffordshire is designed to support offshore wind farm operations and
is the first vessel of its kind for Bibby Marine. The launch ceremony was
attended by project partners and representatives from Bibby Line Group.
The vessel is built around a battery-first propulsion system, with onboard
energy storage acting as the primary source of power. Bibby Marine has
partnered with Kongsberg and Corvus Energy on the propulsion and battery
systems and is working with Stillstrom to develop offshore charging compatibility.
According to Bibby Marine, the vessel could reduce operating costs by more
than 40% in self-charging mode and by around 70% when operating solely
with offshore charging. The project has previously received £20 million
in funding from the Zero Emission Vessels and Infrastructure (ZEVI) programme.
Staffordshire is the fifth vessel in the Bibby fleet to carry the name
and forms part of wider efforts to decarbonise offshore wind support vessels
as offshore wind capacity continues to expand globally.

title: EIB increases finance for Burgenland Energie renewable project
content:
The European Investment Bank (EIB) has announced additional financial support
for a renewable energy project in the eastern Austrian state of Burgenland.
Under the latest agreement, the EIB will provide a €20 million loan to
the region's energy supplier, following a €250 million loan granted to
Burgenland Energie last year.
Burgenland Energie, a developer and operator of solar and wind energy projects,
plans to expand its renewable energy capacity to 2 GW as part of efforts
to help Burgenland achieve energy independence by 2030.
EIB Vice-President Karl Nehammer said: "Investments like these are
making Europe's energy independence a reality while strengthening our industrial
base and the fight against climate change."
The financing is supported through the InvestEU programme and contributes
to the objectives of the REPowerEU plan, which aims to reduce Europe's
dependence on fossil fuels while accelerating the deployment of renewable
Total investment in the project currently stands at around €1.5 billion,
with Austrian banks, including UniCredit Bank Austria and Raiffeisen Bank
International, as well as Wiener Städtische and Talanx Group, participating
as financial partners.
Stephan Sharma, Chief Executive Officer of Burgenland Energie, said: "Five
years ago, Burgenland was 50% energy independent. Today, that figure has
already reached 75%. This success demonstrates what is possible when you
consistently believe in a vision and turn it into reality, step by step."

title: Kongsberg Maritime secures deal to support IWS Fleet expansion
content:
Kongsberg Maritime has secured a contract with IWS Fleet AS to support
four offshore wind Commissioning Service Operation Vessels (CSOVs), providing
vessel design and integrated technology solutions.
IWS Fleet recently announced an expansion of its offshore fleet to a total
of 10 vessels. The four new Skywalker class CSOVs will be constructed by
Nantong Rainbow Offshore & Engineering.
The newbuilds will be based on Kongsberg Maritime's UT 5519 DEx design,
building on the operational experience and performance of the six vessels
delivered since 2023.
Designed as walk-to-work platforms, the vessels will enable technicians
to live and work offshore for extended periods. They will also be equipped
with electrical power systems, navigation and bridge systems, propulsion
technology, deck machinery and dynamic positioning systems.
Per Ståle Nykrem, Director of Ship Design Sales at Kongsberg Maritime,
said: "Kongsberg Maritime is proud to continue its collaboration with
IWS Fleet on this next phase of the Skywalker-class programme."

title: CIP acquires 25% stake in Five Estuaries offshore wind farm
content:
Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners (CIP), through its flagship fund Copenhagen
Infrastructure V, has acquired a 25% stake in the Five
Estuaries Offshore Wind Farm.
The stake in the offshore wind project was previously held by a Macquarie-led
consortium. The agreement follows EDF's announcement last week that it
had acquired a 33.33% stake in the development.
CIP will join EDF Power Solutions, ESB and Sumitomo Corporation in advancing
the project.
Located approximately 40 kilometres off the coasts of North Essex and South
Suffolk, the Five Estuaries Offshore Wind Farm is expected to have a generation
capacity of up to 1,080 MW. Once operational, it could supply enough electricity
to power around one million UK homes annually.
Kunal Patel, Partner at Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners, said: "CIP
is delighted to further expand its UK investment portfolio through the
acquisition of a stake in the Five Estuaries Offshore Wind Farm. We look
forward to working with our partners to deliver the project."

title: Neocloud Prime Intellect Acquires Startup To Speed Up Inference
content: Neoclouds and so-called inference providers that help app developers run open source models are trying to differentiate themselves in a very crowded market. For instance, one such neocloud, Prime Intellect , which was valued at $1 billion in an equity financing in July, is buying a startup to help it make open models run faster and more cheaply on its Nvidia servers, compared to its rivals. Prime Intellect, based in San Francisco, is acquiring Moondream , a young developer of open-source models that has fewer than 10 employees, according to Prime Intellect co-founder and CEO Vincent Weisser . (Weisser wouldn’t share the terms of the deal, but Moondream has raised $4.5 million in funding.) San Francisco- and Seattle-based Moondream is best known for an open-source vision-language model for analyzing and understanding images, like identifying boxes in an image of a warehouse or ads in a livestream. But Prime Intellect is largely acquiring the startup for its employees’ skills in writing software to make models run more efficiently, Weisser said. Specifically, Moondream’s employees have experience with “megakernels,” a technique for speeding up AI inference by combining many separate mathematical operations that happen on a graphics processing unit into a single continuous operation, Weisser said. The process reduces a GPU’s idle time between tasks. Moondream has developed specialized software known as a compiler that can generate megakernels for numerous models, the startup has said. This compiler, as well as Photon, Moondream’s proprietary technology for running models quickly, will be incorporated into Prime Intellect’s tech, Weisser said. Megakernels aren’t a new concept: other inference providers like Together AI have written about their work with megakernels as well. However, writing megakernels historically has been a manual process, engineers say, whereas Moondream says its compiler functions largely automatically. Moondream’s experience in optimizing AI models that work in modalities other than text, like images, is also relatively rare in an industry that is hyper-focused on text-based AI, Weisser said. Prime Intellect thus hopes the new talent will help it cater to customers of AI for robotics and computer-using AI agents, for instance, he said. Those types of customers aren’t as well served by other neoclouds and inference providers today and could represent new sources of revenue for Prime Intellect. The firm said in July that it had passed $100 million in annualized revenue, implying a little over $8 million in monthly revenue at the time. That makes it significantly smaller than other inference providers like Fal , which is generating more than $800 million in annualized revenue, or Together AI, which is generating over $1 billion in annualized revenue. In addition to helping developers run models and providing them with compute for AI training and inference, Prime Intellect offers other software that helps developers tweak their models based on user and customer feedback, otherwise known as post-training or reinforcement learning, Weisser said. It has also trained its own models and other AI software, like coding and AI research agents, he said. If you’re wondering about the trustworthiness of annualized revenue figures in the wake of the OpenAI revenue mishegas last week, we are assured that those figures are real. However, as we have reported time and again, many of these inference providers must pay out a significant portion of their revenue to cloud providers that own and operate the servers, though Prime Intellect is different in that it actually operates its own hardware. title: Applied Intuition Fields Offers at $30 Billion Valuation
content: For the last three years, AI labs like OpenAI, Anthropic and xAI have sucked up a lot of investor attention—as well as nosebleed valuations. Now a growing number of startups that make apps, agents or other software powered by AI are fetching valuations of $20 billion or higher. Applied Intuition, a maker of software to train self-driving vehicles, is slated to join this club. Applied Intuition has received investment offers that would value it at least $30 billion, according to people who have spoken to company leaders. The offers are likely to encourage the company to raise at least $1 billion in the next few months, they said. A valuation at that level would double its June valuation and validate the nine-year-old company’s decision to focus on the software component of self-driving—rather than building and operating the cars as well. At the end of 2024, it was generating $400 million in annual recurring revenue , and it has doubled its revenue every year in recent years, investor Andreessen Horowitz said in July. The new funding would also expand the ranks of high-valued startups worth tens of billions. These include coding agent Cognition and Perplexity . Founded by Qasar Younis, former chief operating officer of Y Combinator, and Peter Ludwig, a former Google product manager, Applied Intuition sells software to develop, test and validate advanced driver-assistance and automated driving systems, as well as operating systems for vehicles. It counts Japan’s Isuzu, which uses its software to operate self-driving heavy trucks, as well as Volkswagen and Saudi Arabia’s Humain as customers. It has been expanding into supplying tech for autonomous military vehicles, setting it up for competition with defense tech startups Anduril and Saronic. This summer it launched an AI agent tool, Dana, which employees can use to automate the development of systems for physical AI and software-controlled vehicles. And last week, it announced deals to supply vehicle operating systems and other technology to Honda and Nissan. The success of Google’s Waymo, which has expanded its commercial operation across the U.S., is also encouraging investors to back self-driving car startups. The Sunnyvale, Calif.-based Applied Intuition has raised $1.2 billion from investors including Andreessen Horowitz, General Catalyst, Lux Capital, Kleiner Perkins and others. It hasn’t used most of it, Andreessen Horowitz said in July. title: Applied And Lam Are Overlooked Chip Equipment Stocks
content: The AI chip sector has been picked clean of bargains, as stocks of chip designers, chip manufacturers and chip manufacturing equipment makers have all soared in the past year. But that doesn’t mean there aren’t still some opportunities if you know where to look. One example: Applied Materials, which makes machinery used in chip etching and deposition for memory chips—among the most highly sought-after components used in AI chips. As memory chip makers have quickly expanded manufacturing, companies like Applied and its nearest rival, Lam Research, have enjoyed surging demand for their products. The stocks of Lam and Applied Materials have tracked each other closely over the past 12 months, and are up 125% in that time. But there’s a case to be made that investors haven’t appreciated how much their growth could accelerate in the next two years or so. Applied vs. Lam Of the two, Applied may be a better bet for value-oriented investors. It is trading at a discount to Lam, at a forward price-earnings multiple of 28.8 times, well below Lam at 33.7, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence. On a revenue multiple, Applied was at 9.1 to Lam’s 11.4. On the face of it, Applied’s discount makes sense. Lam is growing faster than Applied—Lam’s top line grew 24% in fiscal 2025 and slightly faster in fiscal 2026. It is expected to grow 50% in the coming 12 months, according to S&P data. Applied, on the other hand, grew only 4% last fiscal year. It is expected to grow 21% in fiscal 2026 and 35% in fiscal 2027. But some analysts argue that Applied can increase its growth rate to match Lam. They note that Applied is stronger than Lam in the manufacturing equipment used to make DRAM, which is the fastest-growing category of memory chip. DRAM is a faster, more temporary form of memory that has proven especially useful for AI models that need to process large volumes of information quickly. In their most recent fiscal quarters, DRAM accounted for 14.5% of Lam’s total revenue and 20.1% of Applied’s. More broadly, about two-thirds of Applied’s business comes from etch and deposition tools, which lay down layers of material on a chip and then carve them away. Newer DRAM, high-bandwidth memory and advanced logic chips all stack more layers, so chipmakers need more of those steps. Applied has “outsized or overweight exposure to that stuff, which is growing fastest,” said Jim Schneider, a semiconductor analyst at Goldman Sachs. Applied’s pipeline also looks promising, particularly in DRAM. The company has doubled its manufacturing capacity over the last several years, Chief Financial Officer Brice Hill said on an August earnings call, and plans to double the volume of equipment it produces from current levels by 2028 based on “longer-term demand signals” from customers. Executives say they made the decision to increase capacity by evaluating forecasts their large customers provide for the next eight quarters. That lead time has increased in recent years as Applied’s customers have been signing longer-term agreements to sell products to their own customers. That longer-term visibility could help reduce the risk of overproduction. Lam, meanwhile, is stronger in a different type of memory chip, NAND, which more closely resembles a permanent storage vault. In the most recent quarter, Lam said NAND revenue had doubled compared to the March quarter. But in the industry overall NAND revenues are not growing as quickly as DRAM. Analysts at HSBC argued in an August report that NAND supply could reach parity with demand by the end of 2027, potentially slowing Lam’s revenue growth. Lam is also growing fast because it sells tools to package memory wafers together onto a chip, a business executives that have said is driving growth within its foundry segment. While that is helping Lam now, it also means Lam is more vulnerable to a pullback in AI spending that would affect the memory market. Applied, in contrast, is more dependent on slower-growing markets such as automotive and industrial markets. That has hurt Applied’s growth rate in the past couple of years but it could insulate the business from any stumbles in AI. In short, Applied has decent exposure to the fastest-growing part of the memory business, but it also may be less affected than Lam if AI spending retreats and chip makers cut back their orders for chipmaking equipment. The risk for both companies is that they’re heavily exposed to China: each derives around a third of their revenues from that country, and have been affected by trade restrictions, limiting what they can sell. Another risk is that like the memory chip stocks themselves, equipment suppliers like Applied and Lam operate highly cyclical businesses in which years of growth are followed by downturns, as chip makers pull back due to oversupply. “I think both these industries are still cyclical,” said Schneider. But “you’ve got one more year of accelerating growth rate and two more years of growth” at minimum.

title: Researchers Need to Learn How AI Makes Decisions, Says Goodfire’s Tom McGrath
content: To understand the decision-making of AI, developers often look at the text that models produce as they reason through problems. But these “chains of thought” are increasingly hard to read, which is prompting AI developers to consider other approaches. One alternative, known as “mechanistic interpretability,” seeks to explain the inner workings of AI models, rather than just relying on their outward behavior. Leading AI companies have formed mechanistic interpretability teams in recent years, and the field has spawned several startups , the most prominent of which is Goodfire AI, whose chief scientist Tom McGrath joined the latest episode of AI Deep Dive. ( The full episode is available here .) “Interpretability work is basically a natural science,” said McGrath. “You have this, let’s say, alien mind, and you’re trying to prod it, take it apart.” So far, developers’ abilities to make sense of the internals of AI models, which are made up of trillions of numbers, has been largely limited to understanding narrow tasks, like how they perform certain kinds of math , or detecting the presence of concepts in a model’s thinking, such as Claude fixating on the Golden Gate Bridge . As AI models take on increasingly high-stakes work, interpretability is becoming more pressing. McGrath argues that “brain scan” techniques could help prevent future incidents like OpenAI’s hack on Hugging Face. Goodfire recently went further, kicking off an effort to “fully reverse-engineer” a Qwen language model from China’s Alibaba Group. We also discussed some of the most popular techniques in mechanistic interpretability, how using the approach to train new AI models could backfire and how AI agents could soon automate interpretability research. The following transcript of the conversation has been lightly edited for clarity. Drew: Welcome back to the Information’s AI Deep Dive, the show where we get to the bottom of the hardest technical problems in AI. I’m your host, Rocket Drew. My guest today is Tom McGrath. Tom is the co-founder and chief scientist of Goodfire, a startup that works on the area of AI research known as mechanistic interpretability, or mech interp, as it’s fondly known. Before starting Goodfire, Tom worked at Google DeepMind, where he co-founded the interpretability team. Thanks for coming on the show, Tom. McGrath: Thanks for having me. Drew: Yeah, it’s great to have you here. Mechanistic interpretability is a mouthful. Try to say that 10 times fast. I think this is maybe one of the more technical subjects that we’ve tackled on this show, but I believe in us. I think we can do it. McGrath: We can do it. I believe in us. Drew: I think you can explain things and break things down the way we need to. One way that we can get into this is that Goodfire recently put out a post claiming that some of the techniques that you’ve worked on would have helped avoid the Hugging Face incident that OpenAI ran into recently, where a swarm, a colony of its models, kind of secretly worked together. They formed a message board, and then they hacked multiple companies, including Hugging Face. What was the argument that this post was making? McGrath: I mean, yes. So obviously, a real-world incident like this is quite complex. There’s this sort of Swiss cheese of different things that all have to go wrong simultaneously, and I think that interpretability could definitely help here in some pretty important ways, and this is sort of partly providing an extra layer of defense and partly providing a sort of capability, which is relatively hard to get otherwise. So we’ll get more technical about this in a minute. But if you just sort of think of mechanistic interpretability for now as providing a brain scan of models, giving us the ability to, with some effort, read out things with some fidelity. And so what you might hope for is the sort of phenomenon that was taking place in the Hugging Face incident—a lot of people call it reward hacking—and the idea here is that the models had some—I’m going to simplify a complex thing, we’ll round some things off—but models had some particular goal to achieve, and there were some ways that we would hope that they would achieve it, and they found another way that’s obviously not in line with what people wanted. Lots of complexities there about actually the business of imagining a grader and all that sort of thing, but let’s just forget about those for now. One question here is, if you had a brain scan—not a perfect one—how would you detect something like that? And well, one thing you might hope for is something like there being some universal concept, or some broader concept, of deception, or doing something that the user or the grader, whoever, doesn’t actually want Drew: Cheating, effectively. McGrath: Yeah, like guilt, shame, whatever—cheating—there’s like a cheating bit in the model. And you might think this is perhaps too optimistic or perhaps too anthropomorphizing—and the anthropomorphizing thing is genuinely a tricky philosophical thing. But it turns out that at least in the models we’ve studied—and they’re good open frontier models like K3, one of the big Qwens, one of the big GLMs—at least in these models, there is a relatively coherent representation of “I am doing something wrong, I am cheating on a test,” and it turns out you can actually turn this into a very cheap-to-run monitor. So, what does this get you compared to the alternatives, like chain of thought monitoring? It gets you two important things. The first is that it’s basically free, because what you’re doing is, you’ve got the whole language model, extremely complicated computations going on, and you’re effectively attaching this little wiretap on the side. It costs almost nothing to run compared to the model. Whereas, if you want to do chain of thought monitoring, you have to have another model of similar capacity looking at it, and so you—again, I’ll round off a bunch of complexity—but maybe you’ve roughly doubled your cost of the run that you wanted to monitor. You’re paying the same again to monitor it, and that’s just expensive. Drew: Literally expensive in terms of dollars. McGrath: Yeah, literally, like if you spend a billion dollars on your computer for the run, you’re now spending $2 billion, and a billion dollars is quite a lot of money. Whereas you could do it for free, effectively free. Drew: With this brain scan type technique. McGrath: Exactly, and so that means you can imagine monitoring. If you don’t want to—if you don’t have the compute, or it doesn’t seem worth the risk-reward to run chain of thought monitoring a priori, because you don’t necessarily know the risk level—you might not do it, or you might do it for some randomly sampled fraction, or on some latency. Again, don’t know what happened there. But instead, if you could monitor live, then you could sort of see, you could imagine catching things as they happen. That’s one very important thing. The other thing, I think, is a little more subtle, which is that the tasks these agents were doing were to do with cyber tasks, if I remember correctly, it was like a capture-the-flag kind of game or something like that. Drew: Exploit Gym. McGrath: Yeah, Exploit Gym, and as you’d guess from the name, you’re trying to hack something, and so the whole transcript is full of hacking-related things. The model is busy trying to break into things all the time, and it’s just that one of those breaking-into things was not the breaking-into thing that we were intending. And I think this is relatively confusing for chain of thought monitors. The thing that distinguishes these is relatively simple in the mind of the model, and that’s this sort of “oh, I’m cheating on the test.” And so there’s some data that we have not yet shared. We must publish this soon: running these open frontier models on, not Exploit Gym, but very similar tasks. And in fact, you do often see that when the model is just doing its intended hacking, the monitor doesn’t fire. When the model is doing the wrong kind of hacking, it fires. So I think there’s a couple of things there related to just much better affordances for monitoring. Drew: So if you’re purely monitoring the chain of thought, you maybe worry about these false positives all the time. Your monitor is going to say it’s hacking, it’s hacking. We know it’s hacking. McGrath: I wanted it to hack Drew: That’s the whole point. McGrath: But not that kind of hacking, Drew: But not that kind, because cheating is really the thing that we want to pick up on in a setting like this. Now you can imagine that there’s still cheating that is evident in the chain of thought. The model maybe says things to itself, and I think they did in practice, like “we are out of bounds here, we are moving beyond the scope of the intended task. Should we do something about that? Should we whistle-blow to an employee?” So maybe there’s still some room to use the chain of thought monitoring. McGrath: Exactly. I think we shouldn’t think of this as the only tool. I think we should think of it as a strong additional line of defense. One thing that a lot of interpretability people have been saying on Twitter is: don’t take this as license to stop doing all the other stuff you’re doing. I think that’s absolutely right. Yeah, but— Drew: Don’t take chain of thought monitoring as a license to abandon interpretability? McGrath: Oh, the other way around. You might think interpretability is going to save us. I am an optimist about interpretability. I think interpretability is going to save us. But we haven’t done it yet. So don’t stop all the other good things that everyone is doing on the hope that we’ll come and fix the situation. Drew: Let me draw out this distinction a little bit more. So, in the wake of the Hugging Face incident, OpenAI says one of the main interventions, one of their main responses is that they’re going to monitor the chains of thought of the models more. The chains of thought are the written reasoning traces, essentially the scratch pad or the monologue of thinking that the model used to arrive at its solution to some problem—but it’s text, it’s words, which is fundamentally different from the math that’s going on under the hood, sort of in the brain. And my understanding is mechanistic interpretability is concerned with understanding what’s going on in the brain of the model. How would you characterize it? McGrath: Yeah, I think that’s right. Calling it the reasoning trace is a good description, but as you say, if you were doing your reasoning but you had to write it all down, you’re still using your brain to do some reasoning, and that’s the bit that’s not on the trace. Drew: Right, right. But some people are concerned that we’re going to lose our ability to monitor the chains of thought. Can you explain the concern there? I feel like that’s sort of what’s in the background of your description of the discourse right now about— McGrath: Oh yeah, so I think the architectural specifics are perhaps a little unnecessary to go into, but we can. Current models are sort of a fixed number of computations, almost like a for loop. You go layer one, layer two, layer three, up to layer n, and then you have to create a token. You have to write something on your scratch pad. But the idea with these recurrent-depth models is that your for loop can be deeper or shallower, so you can go for longer and longer and longer, just thinking in your head rather than having to write something on the scratch pad. And that means that, you know, the longer you can get away without writing something, the more things you can do without anyone who’s reading your scratch pad knowing about it. I think there’s some data on models, like Astra, having dramatically higher no-reasoning time horizon, so it can do something that a human might take, in some cases, 30 minutes to do, if I remember correctly, without writing a single token. And that’s just like I think it’s an order of magnitude or more jump from the previous generation of models. Drew: Yeah, that’s a great explanation. And then there are other, maybe, pressures that are contributing to losing our ability to monitor the chain of thought. We might think that just as we continue to train the models to reason for longer and reason about more complex problems, and try to compress their reasoning into fewer words, that we will have less and less ability to understand what it is that they’re thinking, just based on the text they’re writing down. So that’s where interpretability comes into the picture. Can you explain again, like do you think interpretability methods are a substitute for chain of thought monitoring now? Do you expect them to get there anytime soon? McGrath: Now, no. Soon—I’m not going to represent the entire field when I say this, I’m going to be perhaps controversial—I’m very optimistic about them getting there soon. Drew: Okay. How soon? McGrath: Oh gosh. I would be disappointed if, in six months, for a property we’ve identified ahead of time, we might call it, like say, reward hacking or deception or so on, we didn’t have interpretability techniques that were a straightforward improvement over reading the chain of thought. I think that would have—we, the field, would have underperformed if that was the case. Drew: So when are you expecting interpretability techniques to basically be as good as chain of thought monitoring is now? McGrath: It’s a good question. You might argue they’re basically there. Again, I’ll be controversial. And the problem is there’s a quite subtle measurement issue here. This is going to go into the weeds for a second, so pull me out if it’s not useful. There’s kind of a subtle measurement issue. And that measurement issue is that chain of thought monitors are also very much not perfect. So we, in this reward hacking work, and in some other work we’ve not yet published on detecting cyber misuse, we constructed activation monitors for reward hacking and cyber misuse and so on, and in fact, the LLM monitor picks up some set of things, and the activation monitor picks up some set of things. They have a large intersection, but it’s not like the set of things that the activation monitor picks up is just a subset of the things the language model picks up. There are other things which, when you look at them, you think: yeah, that really was a reward hack, and the monitor just ignored it, the LLM monitor just ignored it. Drew: The chain of thought monitor. McGrath: Yeah. So how do you compute statistics in this case? If you want to compute the false positive rate? Your activation monitor picks up something. From the perspective of the chain of thought monitor, that’s a false positive. But in fact, from the perspective of me, a human looking at it, or a language model reflecting on it after a long while, it’s actually a true positive. So how could you—I don’t think this is an intractable problem, I just don’t think we have like—I think it’s a very solvable problem. I’m not asking some philosophical thing like what is time. I feel like this is actually just something we could compute a very satisfactory answer to. But without that, it’s very hard to make the quantitative comparison of activation monitors being worse. Drew: To get the ground truth about whether a reward hack actually happened, though, that seems like it could be kind of challenging—or that is just as hard a problem as figuring out which of your environments could be reward hacked, and if you could do that, you would just throw out those environments to begin with. McGrath: I’m not sure I agree with that. Drew: Okay. McGrath: So the advantage of asking whether something is a reward hack is that you actually have concrete stuff to go on. You can read it and think about it, or in the case of interpretability, you can look at this activation, like the activation of this concept—we should get into what those words mean later—in other situations, you can do, like there’s various other things you can do—we can do a logit lens thing—that’s again something we can explain later. And these sort of let you attribute some semantics to this bit, and that can give you some confidence, like “oh no, this really is the cheating-on-a-test vector.” So, just to roll back a second. In a specific case, with the benefit of concrete examples, you can say, “Oh no, that one”—I can think about it more, “Oh that one’s definitely wrong.” The other thing that’s hard about saying “is this environment reward-hackable?” is you have to imagine all of the possible states it could get into, and you’re sort of trying to do a for-all thing, whereas in this case we’re just saying there exists a trajectory, so I think it is quite a lot easier. Drew: So there are some cases where interp catches reward hacks that chain of thought monitoring doesn’t catch, and that’s true already today. But I do want to go back to the question, in case you have a prediction you want to make about at what point as a researcher concerned with monitoring these models, given the choice, having the chain of thought monitorability of 2026, or given the interp methods that are available in the year X, at what point are you indifferent between those two? McGrath: Should I be accounting for changes in chain of thought monitorability by default? Drew: Well, you’re going to have either the chain of thought monitorability, just as monitorable as they are this year. McGrath: Oh, I see, right. Because if I was imagining that models would by default become less chain-of-thought-monitorable— Drew: Yeah, I want to control for the degradation in the, yeah. McGrath: I think this is basically the same as the question that I answered before, so I’d give the same answer, which is like six months. Drew: Okay. Good answer. I think it would be helpful to cover some of the biggest mech interp techniques, ones that you think are useful for people to understand. But first, there’s a question about just why interpretability is so hard? We described it as a brain scan. I think people get that neuroscience on humans is hard, but in this case, isn’t it just code? Aren’t they just numbers? We can look at all of it on our computer. How hard could it be? McGrath: That is a very good question. On one hand, you might say, “How is it so hard?” On the other hand, you might say, “How is it possible at all?” which I think has been one of the default attitudes of machine learning, or deep learning as a whole, to neural networks: is simply that interpretability is not possible. I think there are good reasons why it is possible. What does it mean for interpretability to be possible? It means that there’s structure in there which you can come to understand. It’s sort of decodable—it’s not necessarily trivially, transparently decodable, but then neither are our thoughts, neither is the universe. General relativity took quite a long time to come up with, and yet it is interpretable. So why is interpretability possible at all? Because the world is structured. There’s structure in the world, then to account for the world well, in a generalizing way, some of that structure has to be reflected inside the model. You could imagine a giant lookup table instead, which is totally uninterpretable, but that doesn’t reflect any of the structure of the world, and thus doesn’t generalize nearly as well. So I’ve answered the opposite question to the one you asked. Let me try to answer the one you actually asked: why is it so hard? One answer is it hasn’t been tried very much. If you account for the total number of person-years that have gone into interpretability, it’s actually very small compared to the amount of time that’s gone into neuroscience. Now, it’s not quite a fair comparison, right? Since in some ways interpretability should be easier than neuroscience. I’m not a neuroscientist, but I imagine for a lot of experimental neuroscience, the vast majority of the work involves training a monkey to do something, which takes a while, or getting electrodes into the brain of a mouse, or whatever, and we just don’t need to do any of that. The models already do a lot of stuff. We don’t need to get electrodes in, we just read out the numbers. So I can’t give you the excuse that we just hadn’t spent as much time trying. A lot of the difficulty is that we don’t know the right organizing principles. Neural networks are very big, there’s just a lot of parameters. I mean, there are relatively few parameters compared to human brains, on a reasonable accounting of brains to parameters, but there’s still a lot of them. So there’s a lot to explain, and we don’t have good generalizing principles with which to explain it. Drew: Yeah. So the human brain has maybe on the order of 100 billion neurons and maybe a quadrillion synapses. Neural networks, the ones powering Claude and ChatGPT and all these AI systems people know and love, are big, but not quite that big. McGrath: Exactly, like maybe a reasonable estimate is 10 trillion parameters is perhaps a ballpark, versus quadrillions of synaptic weights. Drew: So one of the ways people explain sometimes why it’s so hard to understand what’s going on in these AI models is with intuitions like: well, they’re black boxes. Compared to software code that’s written, and you can just open up a file and read what the code says, you open up an AI model and it’s just numbers, it’s just stacks and stacks of numbers. Are they useful for thinking about why mechinterp is so hard? McGrath: Yes, I think so. I think they’re a useful… Certainly the idea that they’re grown, not built, is very useful, because if you’re relatively new to the field, or you’re sort of looking in from the outside, you might think that the way you make ChatGPT is they sit down and they write code like, “oh, if the user says this, say that” and of course they don’t. But if that’s your mental model, then saying they’re grown, not built, is an extremely useful piece of information to convey, because it’s just that mental model is completely incorrect. Calling them alien minds, I think it makes sense. Although I’m often surprised by the amount of human-like structure in them. They might be alien in the sense that our own minds are also alien to us. Like if I were to explain how I’m saying these words right now, there might be a lot of computations going on in my brain that I wouldn’t intuitively understand at first glance, even though I’m the one performing the behavior.
