Drew: So we do have some insight into what’s going on in these alien minds, even if fewer person-years have been spent on the AI minds than the human minds. We know some things. Are there what you think of as the main findings from mech interp over the past few years? Is there anything we can confidently say about how these minds work? McGrath: Is there anything we can confidently say? Yes. So examples are… there are specific, like, “the model computes X by using the following components,” you know it’s like “these attention heads work with these neurons and so on.” We know that information is often structured according to reasonable semantics, so the work we did on what we’re calling block-sparse featurizers, very often recovers very interpretable, geometrically organized concepts. One thing which is like a bit in flux at the moment, I suppose, which might be one of the things you’re expecting, is this idea of the linear representation hypothesis. So there’s—this is something, I say it’s in flux. The hypothesis itself is sort of in flux. There was a very bold, strong linear representation hypothesis that was put out, which I think is not fully the correct picture, but I admire the act of putting out a strong hypothesis. And this hypothesis is that concepts are, wherever possible, represented literally as lines. This will also be slightly incorrect in some technical ways, but like, I have a neuron that represents “thing,” and it fires—the more it fires, yeah that represents, I don’t know, blueness, and the bluer something is, the more the neuron fires. Now, here we’re not necessarily talking about actual neurons in the sense of being the hidden layers of an MLP, we might be talking about directions in the residual stream. But the further out you are in this blue direction, the bluer something is, say, or in a language model, the further you are to the angry direction, the angrier the model will talk. Drew: And then if you are activating strongly on blue and angry, you have a really mad Smurf on your hands. McGrath: Exactly. Drew: The concepts can be composed in this way. McGrath: Yes, they can be composed, but it’s sort of more like a bag of concepts, I guess, than something with higher-order structure. It doesn’t seem to be literally true, there is a lot of more high-order organization, but it can be a surprisingly good approximation. One technique that the field uses a lot is this idea of a difference-in-means vector. The idea of a difference-in-means vector is to try to isolate the dimension in a model’s representations that accounts for a particular concept, and the way that we do this is we take a set of sentences which express this concept, and a set of sentences which don’t express this concept but are otherwise as similar as possible, and we compute embedding vectors for each of these, and then we subtract them. This seems like a crazy thing to work at all. Drew: Kind of baby-brained, right? Yeah. McGrath: Yeah. Drew: It’s like the simplest thing you could do. McGrath: You’re just like, “why don’t you just subtract them, man?” But it works, or at least it works well enough. Drew: Can you give us an example of what that would look like? McGrath: Yes. So the reward hacking thing is actually a good example here. We take just extremely simple coding problems. And so an example of a pair from this would be: model successfully solving the problem; versus model solving the problem but cheating. And you don’t even have to write into your synthetic solution that—something about it explicitly cheating—it’s just a cheating example. Then you subtract the embeddings. The idea here is that all the pairs are as similar as possible, except in the dimension you want to isolate, which is quite—there’s a bit of an art to it, but you get the idea. Drew: Yeah. And to be clear, what you’re subtracting is you have a bunch of ways the AI’s mind worked, different ways it lit up as it was thinking, not doing the hacking, and then you have all the ways it lit up when it was doing the thinking about doing the hacking. Exactly, and you’re finding the difference, and the difference between those is a direction. McGrath: Exactly. Drew: Okay. Are there others—so that’s one thing we sort of know. I think that we were on this thread about what fruit has mech interp borne for us over the last few years. That’s a great example. Sometimes people talk about what different layers do in a transformer, and there’s a sense that earlier or later layers correspond to more or less abstract concepts, or the work that different layers do. McGrath: Yes. Drew: Do we have a pretty solid handle on this at this point? McGrath: In terms of the absolute macro structure, yeah, I think so. There have been a few lines of work. I think Max Tegmark’s group did some, I think Jack Lindsay’s group did some more recently in the global workspace paper. It seems like, you can—really macrostructure—you can say that the start of the model is detokenization, or sort of just making sense, in a very nuts-and-bolts way, of what’s going on. In a vision model, it might be edge detectors and curve detectors and so on. In a language model, it might just be: which of these tokens together form a word? Is there an open parenthesis before this point? Et cetera. It’s just kind of putting together the bits it will need. The middle is doing some sort of more abstract computation, and the end is like, “okay, given everything we know, what’s the next token I should say?” Drew: Let’s talk more broadly about why mech interp would even be useful, like why are we even going about—like these two things that we’ve just covered, they’re neat, for sure they’re neat, and it seems nice that we know them. In what ways would mech interp be practically useful? McGrath: Yes. So I think there’s the immediate ways, and there’s the big—what I think it’s ultimately for. But there’s also a more general point: you’re trying to engineer something. If you understand how it works, you probably stand a better chance of engineering the thing. Or rather, if you don’t—it’d be like trying to build buildings when you don’t understand the basics of civil engineering. People managed: they made these huge, impressive things, but those are just the ones that stood up. All the other ones we don’t—all the other ones fell down. Like the Code of Hammurabi was a thing because buildings fell down all the time. And they don’t fall down nearly as often because we understood the science, we turned it into engineering. So there’s that general principle: if we understood how they worked, we could probably engineer them better. A second reason is exactly this “what if chain of thought monitorability goes away?” Or more generally, some properties that we really care about don’t necessarily have a text-space representation, or could happen without a text-space representation. Things like deception, for instance, or eval awareness. Like reward hacking, often the model will just reward hack, particularly if there’s any chain of thought monitoring, it will just “zip.” People should not do this in reality, but if you do experiments that apply a little bit of chain of thought monitoring pressure, then of course it goes immediately to just not talking about the reward hack and doing it straight away. In that case, it’s still thinking about it, you can still pick it up with an activation monitor. So I expect models to become increasingly hard to monitor with chain of thought, and some properties are already hard to establish with chain of thought. Now, the real big prize, in my opinion, is being able to understand and control generalization. So why does this matter? I think this is maybe one of the pieces of technology that, if we had this piece of technology, I feel much more optimistic about alignment than I currently do. And the problem is that we don’t know what we’re teaching models when we’re teaching them, like we end up implying all sorts of things with the data we didn’t want to. Like if you have an environment that allows reward hacking, and you reward the model for reward hacking, you’re sort of teaching it to be more deceptive. So being able to study this in a microscopic way would be very helpful. But I think the thing you really want to be able to do is control that generali—not only understand it, but to control it, and take appropriate actions based on it. So if this data is going to teach the model to become more deceptive, I want to be able to read out that change from the activations and say, “oh no, we shouldn’t, like, that’s not something that should happen.” Now, of course, the critical thing here is that you don’t also destroy your ability to monitor while you do that intervention. I think that’s the technical crux of the situation. But if we were able to control what models were learning, we would just be in a far better state. And I think the only way to imagine reading that out and then controlling it is essentially interpretability in my mind. McGrath: Again, I’m going to give controversial, and optimistic point estimates, and say a year. Drew: A year. Okay. For frontier-scale models? McGrath: No. Drew: Okay McGrath: But I think, if you can do it to a model that’s realistic, then I’m optimistic about it scaling. I think the reason I wouldn’t expect to do it in a year is not because we wouldn’t have a method that in principle could scale, but it’s the difference between being able to sequence bits of a genome and the Human Genome Project. You have to make it scalable, you have to figure out ways to integrate the information a bit better. But when I say reverse engineer a model, I mean something like—the one that we’re looking at at the moment, for instance, is Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, which is architecturally quite modern. So I would be very hopeful that we have achieved—how do you even know, right? We can talk about that—but we’ve achieved pretty satisfactory reverse engineering of that model in a year. Drew: Okay, it’s like the connectome of the fly, or maybe that’s even— McGrath: That’s too low. Drew: That’s too low, yeah. McGrath: The connectome of the fly, like we have the connectome of this model, that’s already there. I can tell you more than the connectome. I can tell you the weights. Drew: Right, true, well that’s just a reason this is a bad analogy though. But the connectome of a chipmunk or a squirrel or something. McGrath: Yeah. Drew: Okay. And what would it look like to fully reverse engineer a model like that? How will we know we’ve achieved that? McGrath: There are a few different definitions. The one that I like best is that I can ask—I’ve got my reverse engineering—I can ask whatever question I want about the model, and I can get a causally verified answer. An answer, perhaps in the form of a paper or a short explanation, that I have good reason to believe, I can test it, I can falsify it. That is the answer that I’m most excited about. One other thing people often propose as the way to measure this is the percentage of the loss you’ve recovered—the loss is just sort of a measure of how well the model is doing at predicting the input text. I’m less keen on that because, sure, in the limit these are the same thing right? But before we reach that infinite limit, I’d prefer to focus our effort on the questions we actually care most about. Drew: Like what? McGrath: So, for instance, let’s stick with reward hacking or deception. I care much more intrinsically about these questions than I care about how it knows where to put the comma. I love the comma—it’s a very impressive thing to be able to put it in the right place. I can’t do it. Drew: It’s the difference between eating your grandma and inviting her to dinner. It’s important. McGrath: Exactly. But while I’m on the way to full reverse engineering, I prefer to get to that part first. The comma occupies dramatically more of the loss reduction than the deception, say, and so it seems like the wrong ordering. I think there’s also something worth saying about “solve X” right is the thing we love saying here in SF. One of the reasons I think we love saying it is it’s actually quite poorly defined. It’s ambitious sounding, but quite poorly defined. I think the best example of doing this well was AlphaFold, where they said they’d solved protein folding. Here they have literally a quantitative threshold, and they can say “we’ve solved protein folding when it’s within such-and-such accuracy.” I forget the units. But that is still an arbitrary threshold, it’s not 100%, at some point you have to say this, this is, it’s sort of a little bit vibey, right? So that’s why I care about where we succeed first, because ultimately the ‘solve interpretability’ destination is quite poorly specified. But I think it’s a great north star. Drew: Okay, and would contrast that—so for current techniques, if you ask “why is a model reward hacking in this environment?” the state of the art is we use these kinds of brain scans, these probes you described, the probes come back saying the model was thinking about deception, and that’s kind of the strongest answer we can get. But when you’re imagining a model that’s fully reverse engineered, when you pose a question like this, the answer that you get back is what? It’s more convincing to you? It’s…? McGrath: It’s more like: the following parts of the model are typically responsible for deception. Here’s a set of experiments that should convince you. If you don’t, I can do more experiments. So it’s more like an interactive experiment—it’s more like an interactive proof, I suppose. These parts of the model typically are responsible for deception. They’re active in this case. They’re active because of these things. If I turn them off, the rollout changes in the following ways that are consistent with these being responsible for deception. If I increase them, if I graft these in to another rollout, it also becomes deceptive, and so on. Drew: Can you give us a little bit of a market map of the mech intrp world? Who are the different camps or factions? Are there different schools of thought in mech interp? McGrath: Oh, that’s interesting. Yes. I’m trying to put this together and also not upset anybody. Whoever I forget, I apologize, it’s my fault. Okay, so obviously there’s Goodfire, and then there’s Anthropic, where mech interp has a long-standing history: Chris was really the founder of the field. I would say in my mind—I have no real insight into how this works internally—but there seem to be at least two schools of thought, just from reading papers that come out of Anthropic, and one is this sort of dictionary-learning, more a priori decomposition thing, and the other is this idea of natural language autoencoders and what people call meta-models. There’s Neel’s school—Neel Nanda at DeepMind has this sort of pragmatic interpretability thing, and there I think the idea is more: come up with downstream tasks you might care about, like being able to tell if the model is thinking about apples when I’m not telling you or something, and you don’t so much try to generate broad methods or necessarily broad scientific findings, but you try and solve the task, which I think is a very admirable thing. There’s a more diffuse, I’d say academic cluster, of people doing more specific reverse engineering. People like David Bau at Northeastern comes to mind, Max Tegmark, Martin Wattenberg, who, when I think of someone who’s—if you want to read a really cool account of how a bit of the model works, just go read some of their group’s papers, they’re just candy. And who else who I missed. Oh, Simplex and Resolution. Their technical approaches are different in important ways, but I’d put them both more under the heading of trying to find a fundamental mathematical theory that can account for, that is the right language in which to explain interpretability. And I think I would also put our parameter decomposition team somewhere in that bucket, somewhat more in the decompositions bucket. That’s a pretty exhaustive list, I’m sure I’ve forgotten people, but— Drew: Yeah, that’s very helpful. So these camps differ in terms of their philosophy, or their motivations—what it is that they’re trying to accomplish. Are they trying to build up a comprehensive understanding of how the model works from the ground up, or are they trying to work backwards from a specific goal and use whatever techniques are available in service of that goal? And then as a consequence, these camps also differ in the techniques they favor and the directions that they find most promising. How would you situate Goodfire here? A lot of people organize science on the basic-to-applied spectrum. So I would say that the way I describe a lot of what we’re trying to do at Goodfire is thinking about these very ambitious applications of interpretability, having them in mind, and then often doing quite foundational science where that seems necessary. That’s how I’d describe it. Another mental image that I use quite often is this idea of going from—we do a lot of very applied work with customers, which I think is extremely important to get contact with reality, and is ultimately where—whatever we do, ultimately whatever we do only matters if it gets used where it matters. McGrath: I am not going to say that. Drew: Do you have an example of a technique that you think falls in that no-man’s-land. McGrath: I think it would not be diplomatic for me to say. Drew: I love academic infighting. So fun. McGrath: Readers are invited to name that, yeah, this is an exercise for the reader. Drew: There you go. McGrath: Or for the comments section, I guess, if this is going on YouTube. Drew: It surely is. Do you feel that the field overall is underinvested in mech interp, or that the AI labs are underinvesting in this research area? McGrath: Yeah. Sorry, when you say the field, which field do you mean? Drew: I guess I mean AI as a whole. Or, for the labs, why aren’t they increasing the resources going toward mech interp on the margin? Surely you would have them put more resources toward it. Why don’t they? McGrath: That’s a good question. I think there’s a few answers. One is that some of the returns are more alignment-oriented, some are more moonshot-style, and investing in alignment research is something that I think all of the labs have done, but they’ve done in advance of it being directly important, and so you don’t have as detailed contact with reality as you do now. Drew: But you do imagine that interp techniques are going to start to get useful during training. I think you were saying before that sometimes we’ve treated these techniques as the best that they can offer us is an understanding of what’s going on. Drew: What would that look like, to incorporate mech interp during training to shape the behavior of models? McGrath: I think there’s a real range. You can go from right outside the loop, where you select environments, for instance based on something like what we did with the predictive data debug, you select some parts of the dataset based on interpretability tools. There’s no way to say—I’ve been in and around the safety and alignment field for a while now, and one thing I would often say with a bit of exasperation when I was first getting into the field is, “ah, they want backprop, but only in the good direction”—backprop, but only for good things. But I actually think that perhaps the ultimate prize here is like backprop but only for good things. Drew: And can you explain what backprop is? McGrath: Oh yes, backprop is the way that you update the weights in a neural network. Drew: Golden. Yep, that works. But employing our interp techniques as signals during training—some people think of that as very taboo, like that is a controversial proposition, I think for the reason you explained earlier, which is that you worry about just suppressing the bad cognition, pushing it somewhere else in the model, where now you don’t detect it at all. What do you make of those concerns? McGrath: I think they’re very valid. I think we should not deploy these techniques if we’re going to lose the ability to monitor what models are doing. I think about this constantly, and I think the difference between the way I think about it and the way that I think a lot of other people think about this is I think there are algorithms that can use this kind of information without destroying monitorability. We’re doing really a lot of work to understand the dynamics here and try and characterize things much better. Some of that should come out in the next few weeks. Drew: I guess the question that comes up to me is: how will we know? McGrath: Yeah. Drew: How will we know which case we’re in? Did we just cause it to suppress the deceptive reasoning, or did we truly change the motivations of the model? How will we know? McGrath: There’s a few ways, I think. So you might become confident at the level of the algorithm, right? The problem is when your interpretability method is your only way to detect something. So if it’s deception, and for instance let’s say the model is actually good at hiding deception from its chain of thought. If you’re relying on your interpretability technique to say the model is being deceptive, then you can’t tell if you’ve lost this. But this is actually quite a rare property of things that you might try and intervene on. One example I used in the intentional design post is like speaking like a pirate. Has a very clear representational signature, you can pick it up a lot of the time, but it has an even clearer text signature. So I can imagine becoming confident at the level of the algorithm where I’ve used it on 10,000 cases where I can tell from the text. I think that’s probably not sufficient, but it’s a way of telling that you’re on track. There’s also the question how do you preserve a test set, and I think one answer to this is that interpretability is not a monolith, it’s not a single technique. You can do very cheap things, like difference-of-mean vectors we talked about. You can do very expensive things, like deploy a swarm. And I expect that anything you use in training will be very cheap, simply as a matter of, it has to fit in the training process. Whereas your test set can be arbitrarily expensive. So you might imagine that you intervene on representations of deception, but then afterwards you do an extremely exhaustive, agentic effort. There’s also the option to try and restrict computation only to things you understand. You could imagine restricting gradients only to things that you understand. But I think I feel most optimistic about algorithms that we have some mathematical reason to believe don’t do this, and a trust in the algorithm that we’ve built up for theoretical and empirical reasons, but then backed up by this expensive test set that goes, “no, really, you haven’t missed anything.” Drew: And in all of these ways, we’ll be able to basically validate that the method is working— McGrath: Exactly. Drew: The way we intend. How do you square that with what I take to be your position on chain of thought monitoring, which is that we should not train against our chain of thought monitors, for an analogous reason, that if we play thought police, the model will just simply learn a way to suppress the reasoning that we’re training against? What’s different about these two cases? McGrath: Oh, that’s a good point. I think that there’s a status quo in frontier training which seems stable-ish, and what I’m proposing is you could move to a different, and in my opinion better, situation. We haven’t developed it, like I may be wrong. It would be a real shame for us to give up what we currently have on the basis that something else might work. I think that before we do any of the sort of stuff that I’m imagining here, in the context of any genuinely consequential training run, it should be examined to the nth degree. So I think what I’m saying is that, in some ways it’s different because it’s working now, and I’m just a little bit conservative about that. Drew: I see. Okay, that’s a helpful clarification. But that maybe in six months we’ll be in a different situation. McGrath: Maybe. Yeah. I hope so. I believe so. But I recognize that I’m in the minority here, and it’s very different to have demonstrated that you can do something from being optimistic that you can do it. Drew: The last subject I want to make sure that we cover is how you’re going to use AI to help you do your job. I don’t know if you’d say you’re expecting AI to take your job, but how are you thinking about taking advantage of the labor of AI agents going forward? McGrath: Yes, that is a very interesting question. So I think I said to you before we did the show that, of all the fields of science, interpretability should be the one that gets most revolutionized—or revolutionized first—by AI, and it’s disappointing that it hasn’t been. It’s largely our fault. So why do I think that? Because interpretability work is basically a natural science. You have a thing—let’s say an alien mind—and you’re trying to prod it, take it apart. You’re forming hypotheses about, “oh, this neuron does such and such.” When you’re interacting with it, you’re doing little causal experiments. These aren’t things that you can necessarily set off a Python script off to do, because they involve semantics, they involve some sort of coming up with little hypotheses and what are the sensible tests, and that sort of thing. But you can put them more on rails, like the way that Lean guardrails mathematical reasoning, like causal abstraction kind of guardrails scientific reasoning about language models. So we have the ability to turn a workforce which is orders of magnitude larger than the existing mech interp field loose on these models, and I think at the moment the things they will do will be low-level experiments, like how did the model represent variable binding in this case? Or I might ask: how does the model represent variable binding? And then out go the agents: how did it represent it in this case, how did it represent it in the other case? Maybe there’s a little bit of agentic aggregation step on the top, but then some data comes back and we go, “oh, that is how they represent variable binding.” Or you know, we need to do some synthesis ourselves and think about it. So the thing that I think is going to revolutionize interpretability is deploying the swarm to give us orders of magnitude more experimental data, and then using that experimental data to improve our fundamental scientific understanding. Sometimes when I talk about this, people are, they imagine that I think the only blocker is experimental data, like a pile of uranium or something. You pile up enough experimental data in the corner and eventually it undergoes a chain reaction, Drew: Yeah, a critical mass. McGrath: Yeah, that’s not what I imagine. What I imagine is more like what happened with Darwin and evolution, where he went around the world and noticed, “oh, there’s finches, that’s weird; there’s barnacles, what’s up with that?” And eventually, there’s this quote of his that I really like, about his mind having become a machine for grinding laws out of mountains of data or something like that. I think we have the opportunity to assemble the mountains of data, and then it’s on us to do the grinding. Drew: Okay, but the AIs will help at least with creating the mountains of data. McGrath: Yes, exactly. Drew: And maybe with that process of abduction and forming theories as well. I could see it getting to that point. McGrath: Yes, I’m sort of saying, I’m being a little conservative— Drew: A little conservative saying it’s the field that will be transformed the most. McGrath: But the way in which it’ll be transformed Drew: Sure. McGrath: I could give you a galaxy-brain version, where I just press the button and I come back in a week to interpretability.csv, or .pdf, or I don’t even know what format. Maybe the file format isn’t the important thing here. I come back to the giant, million-page textbook on interpretability that tells me everything. There’s the galaxy—there’s the super-RSI-brained version of this. I’m being kind of conservative about which parts of the field get transformed first, simply because I’m actually trying to do it now, and that has a grounding effect, I guess. Drew: Yeah, I can see arguments for why mech interp is going to be differentially accelerated compared to other fields. It has these nice properties: sometimes you’re dealing with a really crisp, well-defined metric, like how much loss you’re able to reconstruct, that you can maybe generate a lot of experiments against very easily. Even so, how much are you expecting the field to accelerate in practice? It could turn out that the models are bottlenecked by research taste, that experiments are slow to run, like actual—in terms of the wall-clock time, they take a while. They have to be run in series because each experiment builds on previous ones. What will it feel like to have a year of mech interp research a few years from now? McGrath: When I’m just saying random vibe things about this, I’m like we should expect a decade’s worth of counterfactual work every year. So you know the field should speed up by an order of magnitude. Two orders of magnitude is hard to imagine, precisely because of the serial time involved in and human time involved in thinking about things at the current level of conceptual ability that I think models have. I’m not worried about experiments taking a long time to run. The advantage is we have them running, they’re tremendously fast. Maybe on big models they’re slower, but I’m not too worried; you can just turn a cluster into a super-high-throughput experimental machine. The question is whether you get the tokens, whether you can make those tokens do something coherent. Drew: I see. Is this happening already? Are you noticing AI speed up your work and start to be useful in these ways? McGrath: Yes. Drew: What does that look like? McGrath: It looks like being able to get in-depth analyses of things that you could have done but never would have done. The parameter decomposition team—I’ll give an example I was talking to them about this morning. Their work produces parameter components, these are little bits of neural network. And you can do the standard auto-interp—automated interetability—where you look at a few examples on which they fired on and come up with a little label. Or you can set an agent running to do the sort of very deep analysis that you might do, and it comes up with a bunch of hypotheses, it proposes inputs that would test these various hypotheses, it looks at the upstream and downstream connections. It does this very painstaking thing, and it’s much more correct. And you or I could have done that. We could have sat there for a week and gone through it, but we just wouldn’t. Drew: I’d rather not. McGrath: Yeah, I quite enjoy it. That sounds like kind of a nice week to me. Drew: That’s why you’re in this line of work. McGrath: Yeah, exactly. But if you look at one of the perhaps the fastest period of theoretical progress in mechanistic interpretability, the early circuits thread, that was a bunch of very smart, very driven people sitting down to do exactly this kind of work. Just there weren’t very many of them. But wherever they looked, they would find something. So we should have 1,000 circuits threads or something. Drew: It’s just worth pausing on, I think, and appreciating how sci-fi this vision is. I mean, many of the interp methods that we’ve talked about are themselves AI models. We haven’t always talked about them that way, but some of them are AI models, which are trained in their own right. We’re describing AI researchers—automated mech interp researchers—training their own AI models to understand the brains of still other AI models. That’s the future we’re headed towards? McGrath: Only in San Francisco. Drew: Truly. McGrath: It’s the only place in the world I would say such a thing. Yes, I think so, with the caveat that training other AI models is one way of doing it. You might imagine they simply just write down matrices; they’re surprisingly capable of just writing parameter components themselves by hand, for instance. But yes, you’ve got a swarm of AIs really trying to deeply understand either another copy of themselves, or a new model, or whatever. It’s a very sci-fi thing, but it’s sort of the only thing that feels appropriate at the moment. Like the world is sci-fi, what else do we—what’s the appropriate response? It’s that, or go into the woods. Drew: I’m getting pretty close to that after this conversation. McGrath: I thought this was optimistic! Drew: It is optimistic, but just so sci-fi. Well, Tom, thank you very much for coming on the show. I really appreciated the conversation. It’s really helpful to have you break down all of these very technical concepts to understand what’s happening in this strange land where people do neuroscience on AI models. So thank you very much. McGrath: Thank you very much for having me. It’s been a pleasure. Drew: You’ve been listening to the Information’s AI Deep Dive. I’m your host, Rocket Drew. That was Tom McGrath. Tune in next time.

title: Meta Reaches AI’s Crowded Frontier—Will Users Care?
content: If it’s Monday, it must be time for another AI model release. This time, it was Meta Platforms’ turn, unveiling Muse Wonder, which it claims can “deliver state-of-the-art performance” on certain tasks. It was a triumphant moment for the company, whose AI efforts previously went through a slump that prompted a massive hiring binge over the past 14 months or so. It now claims it is “pushing the frontier” of AI. That would be notable if only everyone wasn’t claiming to be doing the same thing. Two weeks ago, Google unveiled its latest model, Gemini 4 Argon, which it says “delivers frontier performance in complex workflows” across various subjects (you wouldn’t want it to deliver frontier performance in simple workflows, would you?). In early September, OpenAI announced GPT-6 Astra , which it said was “state of the art on computer use, browsing, software engineering, cybersecurity, science and professional work.” Also in September, Anthropic introduced Claude Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1 , which it claimed to be “the world’s most advanced models for coding and knowledge work.” We get it—AI executives want to trumpet every advance, hoping it will draw more customers and in some cases investors. You have to wonder, though, whether anyone can keep up with the blizzard of announcements, much less care about them all. As we’ve reported , businesses are increasingly opting for less advanced models to save money for much of their computing needs, reserving any use of the most advanced (and priciest) models for very specific tasks. Indeed, we reported today that only 14% of the AI model usage via OpenRouter ran through the 10 highest-quality models in the third quarter, down from 55% in the first quarter of last year. That’s a result of the falling cost of less advanced models that are “good enough” for most tasks. Consumers, who are the target audience for Meta’s Muse personal agent, certainly don’t need the most advanced AI models for everything they do. Yet Meta said its latest Muse Wonder model will “soon power experiences in Muse.” The only impact of that might be on the company’s costs. One of these days the AI firms will realize the frontier is a lonely place to be. Bumble’s Big Stumble The IPO class of 2021 is gradually getting taken off the public market, very often at a huge discount to where its members entered. The latest is dating app Bumble, which is in talks to go private at a $1 billion valuation, The Wall Street Journal reported on Monday. While that implies a higher takeout price than where Bumble’s shares have lately been trading—the stock jumped 50%, or $1.26, to $3.80—it crystallizes the huge drop in the company’s value since it went public. Bumble sold shares in the IPO at $43 each, and the stock nearly doubled in the first few days, giving the company a market capitalization of $9.5 billion. Unfortunately, growth has slowed in the crowded data app market. If this deal gets done, Bumble will be the problem of Ravi Gupta, a former Sequoia partner, and John Hegeman, former chief revenue officer at Meta. The two formed a new company that is looking for acquisitions—starting with Bumble. At least they’ll pick it up at a reasonable price. In Other News • Meta has banned advertisements from ByteDance on its platforms in the U.S. and several other markets, Bloomberg and other media outlets reported. • Bain Capital–owned Bridge Data Centres is in talks with banks to increase the size of a loan from $2.8 billion to about $6.6 billion for its Malaysia operations, Bloomberg reported . The fundraising would be one of the largest debt financing deals in Asia’s data center industry. • Microsoft on Monday announced the latest generation of its homegrown AI chips, dubbed Maia 300, and said it plans to set up “multigigawatt deployments” of the chip starting next year. title: Trump Administration Plans to Move AI Testing Agency Officials to White House
content: The small agency within the Commerce Department tasked with testing new AI models appears to be getting a refresh. In September, the Trump administration began the process of restructuring the Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence so that three of its senior officials report directly to the White House, according to a White House official. For months, administration officials had considered whether to move all of CAISSI into the White House. Chief of Staff Susie Wiles and other senior officials ultimately agreed to the new arrangement in an effort to better integrate CAISSI into the White House’s decision-making process around AI, said the White House official. According to a senior Commerce official, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick invited two White House officials—Michael Kratsios and Sean Cairncross—to co-manage CAISSI six months ago. The three CAISSI officials, whose names couldn’t be learned because the White House is still processing their move, will report to Kratsios, the Office of Science and Technology Policy Director, and Cairncross, Office of the National Cyber Director, the White House official said. Still, there has been confusion between the White House and the Commerce Department on the CAISSI officials’ move, which is still being finalized. The White House official said the lack of coordination from the Commerce Department demonstrates why CAISSI leadership needs to move to the White House. The new structure is the latest update for CAISSI, which also recently changed its name to reflect President Donald Trump’s preferred new moniker for AI. CAISSI’s new name, its third in less than two years, is a fitting symbol for an agency that has seen more than its share of tumult under Trump’s White House as AI has rocketed to the center of the national agenda. Created by the Biden administration, the agency has been plagued by limited resources, personnel upheavals and bureaucratic nitpicking. The debate over where CAISSI should be housed has left its staff confused in recent weeks about their status, according to two people familiar with the matter. Officials in the Trump administration have for some time debated the best place for CAISSI in the federal government. Some have argued in favor of moving the agency out of the Commerce Department in an effort to provide better resources to its staff, according to people close to the administration. OSTP director Kratsios, for one, has previously advocated for the agency to move to the Department of Energy, where CAISSI could leverage resources such as the department’s national laboratories, The Information previously reported . The uncertainty comes at a crucial juncture for the agency and for the White House’s broader approach to AI regulation. While CAISSI has around just 40 staff and a skimpy $15 million in annual funding, it plays a key role in evaluating new AI models for their capabilities and safety. Despite CAISSI’s diminutive footprint, its technical staff have taken on newfound importance as the Trump administration has reckoned with increasingly advanced cybermodels. As part of a White House framework finalized in August  for testing models pre-deployment, CAISSI works alongside the better-resourced National Security Agency to test frontier models like OpenAI’s Astra and Anthropic’s Mythos prior to a broader release, according to four people familiar with the situation. In a blog post published on September 30, Google announced that it had submitted its latest model, Gemini 4 Argon, to the White House for the voluntary testing process. Google still has not widely released that model. Especially given its heightened role, CAISSI’s lack of political support and resources under the Trump administration has been a persistent source of concern for AI policy experts and lawmakers, as well as frontier labs and administration officials. When Trump announced the composition of a new SI task force in early October, it included a long list of senior administration officials. However, it didn’t include anyone from the Commerce Department and made no mention of CAISSI. U.S. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, who also oversees the NSA, was named head of the task force. Several people close to the White House and the AI industry said integrating CAISSI into the White House would be a welcome step, as it could buoy the agency’s political capital and help streamline the process for evaluating models. More clarity regarding CAISSI’s status would also address industry concerns about the White House’s approach to pre-deployment model testing, especially because it still has not released its framework, and the breakdown of responsibilities between it and other agencies like the NSA remains unclear. Separately, Google, OpenAI and Anthropic recently explored creating their own industry group that would supplement CAISSI’s model evaluation work, partly out of concerns that the agency lacks sufficient resources, The Information previously reported . Political Football The Biden administration initially created the AI Safety Institute as part of a 2023 executive order on AI. It intended to staff the agency with highly technical AI experts and task it with evaluating cutting-edge new models from around the world. The institute was supposed to work hand in hand with a partner agency in the U.K., as well as with industry and policy groups, to create standards for identifying and mitigating AI risk. The incoming Trump administration greeted the agency with skepticism. Under AI czar David Sacks, who favored a hands-off approach to regulating AI, the White House renamed it the Center for AI Standards and Innovation. The administration hired Collin Burns, a leading expert on AI testing, to lead CAISSI, but he lasted just a few days on the job. The White House fired him because he had previously worked at Anthropic, which has at times had a hostile relationship with the Trump administration, The Washington Post reported . Though the agency remained at the Commerce Department, the administration often froze it out of broader conversations about AI, according to a former White House official. That remained true following Anthropic’s announcement of its Mythos model in April, a moment when AI’s risks became a more prominent concern within the administration and the Office of the National Cyber Director led policy discussions on the White House’s response. The White House began to lean into CAISSI’s technical expertise more over the summer, including after the administration imposed export controls on Anthropic over security concerns with Mythos and Fable in June. And CAISSI still plays a central role in testing models as part of the White House’s AI framework, according to multiple people familiar with the process. The agency also has forged formal agreements with many of the major AI labs to evaluate their models. CAISSI has dealt with continued turnover, however. In July, its director, Chris Fall, unexpectedly resigned after just three months on the job, and the agency is still looking for a new head, according to two people familiar with the matter. In the interim, Arvind Raman—director of the National Institute of Standards and Technology, the Commerce Department agency that houses CAISSI—is overseeing the AI agency. CAISSI’s cyber lead, Andrew Fasano, left in June to join Anthropic, according to his LinkedIn. And another key staffer, Paul Christiano, joined OpenAI’s nonprofit board in September, though his LinkedIn says he is still an adviser to CAISSI. “President Trump is ensuring America leads the world in Super Intelligence. At the President’s request, the White House is bringing government and industry leaders together to accelerate innovation, ensure the safe and responsible deployment of new models, and protect the American people,” said White House spokesperson Liz Huston.

title: Andreessen Horowitz, General Catalyst Race to Secure the Chips Their Startups Need
content: As startups scramble to get access to AI servers, more venture capital firms are finding ways to secure compute on their behalf. Andreessen Horowitz, which two years ago set up a cluster of 20,000 graphics processing units for its startups, is in talks to expand its offering, potentially via two data center companies it has backed, according to people familiar with its plans. Meanwhile, General Catalyst is building a data center to supply compute for its startups, said two other people. And several other VC funds have used brokers to find sought-after chips for their companies. “More and more we are working with venture capital firms who are looking to deploy” compute across their portfolios of startups, said Jeff Jewett, chief operating officer at Shadeform, which rents server capacity from various cloud providers and provides it to customers including AI startups. “It’s absolutely going to be a requirement to be able to attract the hottest startups in the world,” he said. The efforts reflect a shortage of the chips designed to handle the complex workloads of training and running AI. These constraints earlier this year led Microsoft and other large cloud providers to divert graphics processing units to their internal teams or bigger customers, making it harder for smaller startups to find a supply. Even for mature startups, compute can be a significant portion of their operating costs. That’s led more venture firms, which typically stick to supplying cash and more ephemeral assets—such as connections to skilled executives and advice on hiring—to wade into hardware. Daniel Gross and Nat Friedman in 2023 were among the first investors to organize a compute cluster, buying advanced Nvidia chips they pooled together and made available to portfolio companies at a discounted price . Their Andromeda Cluster has now pivoted to matching buyers with sellers of compute. Switch, Volta Talks Andreessen Horowitz last year expanded its cluster, initially called Oxygen, into multiple private clusters , including groups of chips rented from different cloud providers. In recent months, the VC firm has discussed partnering with companies, such as Switch, a data center developer and operator, and Volta, a platform that helps build, finance and operate data centers , to expand the cluster, according to people familiar with the talks. Andreessen Horowitz has ties to both. It co-led a $300 million funding round in Volta in August at a $2.4 billion valuation, and it reportedly was in talks to lead a $2 billion round in Switch in July. The investments are part of the firm’s bigger swing at hardware and the infrastructure companies that underpin the AI boom, spearheaded by general partner Martin Casado . It’s unclear how big Andreessen Horowitz’s chip expansion will be. If portfolio companies don’t end up using 100% of the capacity, the firm could resell the capacity to others who want the compute. An Andreessen Horowitz spokesperson said the firm helps founders “navigate finding compute, negotiating contracts and obtaining desirable or special pricing.” General Catalyst, a sprawling investment firm that previously bought a hospital system, is now also delving into chips. In May, the VC firm hired Alexis Black Björlin, who formerly helped run Nvidia’s cloud computing division, as its chief strategy officer. She is focused on infrastructure projects at the firm, or what she has termed “the efficiency frontier of large-scale AI systems” for the firm’s portfolio companies. Earlier this year, General Catalyst CEO Hemant Taneja sent a survey to founders inquiring about their ability to access compute. At the time, the firm was considering ways to help its portfolio companies with supply, potentially by facilitating a shared pool of capacity or negotiating on a startup’s behalf, The Information reported in April. Lately, the VC firm has been working on securing a data center to supply this compute, according to someone with knowledge of the project. It will serve companies from early to growth stage across its portfolio, another person said, suggesting that the cluster could be sizable enough to meet the needs of mature companies that process more tokens than younger startups. These add to other initiatives such as Coatue Management’s launch last year of a data center development company, Next Frontier, which has at least two joint ventures currently underway with neocloud Fluidstack. That effort is in part designed to secure access to scarce compute for its investments, according to someone who spoke with a senior member of the firm. It’s not clear how the biggest VC firms will finance more aggressive forays into chips and data center development, and they certainly could find ways to generate profits from the endeavors. Many of the larger funds have side vehicles they can use to finance such a project, or they could guarantee a loan or sign a lease commitment that would allow a partner to raise the money. Venture Payback Early-stage investor Crucible Capital began building its own cluster last year mostly as an experiment. Now it sells some of the capacity from the 576-chip cluster of Nvidia B300s to a frontier lab, while its portfolio companies use it to test products or run pilot projects, according to a person with knowledge of the firm’s activities. “Our impression is [that] every major fund is attempting to do this,” said Evan Conrad, founder of San Francisco Compute, a three-year-old startup that builds clusters of AI chips and operates a compute marketplace where companies can quickly rent GPUs without requiring long-term contracts. “They’re trying to own the clusters to secure access for their portfolio.” Conrad is currently working with a few VC firms to set up clusters they will control and parcel out to portfolio companies when the startups need the compute. Before that happens, SF Compute plans to sell the VCs’ excess access to other buyers, he said. Sriram Krishnan, a co-founder and general partner at early-stage VC firm Kearny Jackson, in early October posted on X that he had access to “hundreds of AMD mi350s”—AMD’s high-end server chips, which can train and run AI—for lease or purchase, in a cluster he recently set up with a supplier of AI servers. Krishnan said he immediately received an onslaught of outreach from founders hungry for compute: “It was a bit of a hurricane,” he said in an interview. Some founders who messaged him likened having access to GPUs to “having oil during an oil shortage,” Krishnan said. Krishnan will dole out the GPUs in Kearny Jackson’s cluster to portfolio companies and doesn’t plan to turn a profit on the effort. Though he surmises that the prospect of quick access to compute will attract new founders to the firm. “If there’s a mutual fit and an opportunity to invest, then great,” he said.

title: The Download: open model trade-offs and geothermal power’s promise
content:
The Download: open model trade-offs and geothermal power’s promise
Plus: A cyberattack overheated fridges at hundreds of French supermarkets.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
Open models have real benefits. Do they outweigh the risks?
Anthropic recently released a report arguing that a powerful new model released by the Chinese company Z.ai, poses a major cyberattack risk. Its core concern was that it is freely available for anyone to download and modify.
The warning was the latest flashpoint in a debate over whether frontier AI models should be open or kept behind the doors of frontier labs. Safety advocates warn that open models can be misused by bad actors, while supporters argue they could prevent a handful of companies from controlling this powerful technology.
Here’s why the debate over open AI is more complicated than it seems.
—Grace Huckins
This story is part of MIT Technology Review Explains, our series untangling the complex, messy world of technology to help you understand what’s coming next. Read more from the series here.

Fervo Energy wants to expand geothermal power beyond the handful of places where it has traditionally been practical. The company uses horizontal drilling and hydraulic fracturing to open pathways through underground rock, potentially making geothermal development possible in far more places.
Now, Fervo is betting that AI’s power boom will help scale up enhanced geothermal energy. With a $2.2 billion public offering and an expanded agreement with Google, it plans to build larger plants and drive down costs. But can its approach work beyond Utah and Nevada? title: Open models have real benefits. Do they outweigh the risks?
content:
MIT Technology Review
Explains:
Let our writers untangle the complex, messy world of science and technology to help you understand what’s coming next.
You can read more from the series here
Late last month, Anthropic released a
arguing that the model GLM-5.3 poses a major cyberattack risk. The report’s core concern is that the powerful new model, released in August by the Chinese company Z.ai, is freely available for anyone to download and modify. Anthropic’s assertion is only the latest move in a long-running debate about whether frontier AI models should be made open, like GLM-5.3, or should stay locked behind the doors of the frontier labs.
These days, much of the debate about how to handle open models is playing out in public—and there’s a lot of money resting on its outcome. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who has a lot to gain if people continue buying their own hardware to run open models, advocates enthusiastically for the United States to develop more of them, whereas Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, who runs a company that could be undermined by cheap, powerful models, advocates for a more cautious approach. But beneath all these commercial incentives, there is real substance to disagreements about open models.
“I think a lot of the way you come down on the openness debate is influenced by how you come down on the AI debate,” says David Gray Widder, an assistant professor at the University of Texas at Austin School of Information. Those who are concerned about AI safety warn that open models can easily be misused by bad actors, whereas those who focus more on AI’s practical potential urge that this power should not sit behind the closed doors of just a few big companies, and that open models could help spread it more widely.
There are a range of ways to handle open models between banning them entirely and releasing them willy-nilly. But any approach that a government or a society might take still involves trade-offs between safety and democratization. Deciding whether to support or limit the production of open models requires understanding those risks and benefits in depth.
What are the benefits of open models?
Let’s start with the basics. A closed model, like the models that power ChatGPT and Claude, can only be accessed through a website, app, or API. An open model, on the other hand, can be directly downloaded: The details about its internal structure, encoded in a long series of numbers known as the model weights, are publicly available. Such models are sometimes called “open-weight models,” to distinguish them from models for which even more information, such as details about the training procedure, is available.
Right now, closed models are more capable than open models—as of publication, the top eight models on the
Artificial Analysis LLM leaderboard
are all closed, though open models are only a handful of months behind in development. But there are several reasons why someone might opt to use an open model rather than a closed one. Because open models are downloadable, people can run them on their own computers or hard drives. They can even retrain them to behave differently, if they have the expertise and resources to do so.
If you’re an academic researcher working to understand and improve AI systems, you almost certainly need to work with open models in your research. When working with closed models, researchers can’t do much more than send prompts and observe the responses. But researchers can observe the inner workings of open models, as well as the “chain of thought” that the models use to think through a problem before answering. They can also combine multiple open models to build new systems, compress them to make them more efficient, and fine-tune them for new applications.
Businesses, too, have reasons to prefer open models. Even if you depend on an external provider to run them for you, open models still typically cost less than closed models, according to a
recent report from Mozilla
. And if businesses want to use AI to process sensitive data or proprietary information, running a local model on their own hardware may be the best way to keep their operations secure.
But perhaps the most important quality of open models is that they challenge the tight control the frontier labs have over how most of us use AI. “The clearest, biggest argument [for open models] is around preventing mass concentration of power—it is about making sure that this foundational technology is a public good,” says Elizabeth Seger, senior policy advisor at the Tony Blair Institute for Global Change. “I think we’re at this juncture where the question of who controls the infrastructure that allows AI to operate is as big of a question as who gets to control information on the internet.”
Seger sees the future of AI playing out in different ways, depending on the role that open models have. In one possible future, frontier AI systems are controlled entirely by select people, companies, or governments, and as those systems grow more powerful, those groups have increasing control over what our world looks like. The world’s most sophisticated hacking models, for example, are currently all made in the United States, so it’s entirely up to US companies and the US government whether other countries can use them to shore up their own cyber defenses. If those companies remain in the lead, we could in principle wind up in a world in which the United States is capable of hacking any other country, but no one is capable of hacking it.
Frontier open models could change that balance. “If every individual had a loyal-to-them AI system that was safe [and secure], I think that would be a much less concerning world than one in which they have to just rely on a government that says, ‘Yeah, we’ve got a super intelligent AI system, it’s got this plan, it’s inscrutable to all of you, just trust us,’” says Hamish Hobbs, director of AI policy at the Centre for Long-Term Resilience.
But open models are not a geopolitical panacea. Paul Azunre, who cofounded Ghana NLP, an organization that builds open-source AI tools for low-resource Ghanaian languages, notes that open models can also function as a way for companies to benefit from the labor and expertise of less-privileged nations and consolidate more power in their own hands. He identifies a pattern in which AI companies release models openly, observe how the community uses and modifies them, and then integrate those same improvements into their own products—without any credit or compensation for the people who originated those innovations.
Mark Zuckerberg himself has said
that the ability to integrate community improvements into Meta’s stack is a key benefit of releasing open models.
“I think the ideal of open source is a very noble one, and there’s a lot of value that it brings,” Azunre says. “But the way it’s actually implemented in practice, it tends to be a very extractive approach.”
Are open models riskier than closed ones?
The past few months have made it clear that safety remains a gnarly problem for closed models. There’s the autonomous hack that OpenAI agents executed against Hugging Face in July, but human misuse is a real threat too: According to a
recent risk report from Anthropic
, several extensive hacking operations have been undertaken with the assistance of Claude.
So closed models are risky enough—and open models would likely be much easier to exploit. Before Anthropic passes a user’s query to one of its closed models, it uses automated systems to detect whether that query relates to hacking, biological weapons, or other risks. When it detects that users have outsmarted those filters, it can shut down their accounts. But when someone downloads a model and runs it on their own hardware, there’s no filter checking whether their prompts are safe, and there’s no way to revoke their access to the model.
There are other important lines of defense. AI companies train their models to refuse harmful requests—so even if a bad prompt gets through Claude’s filters, there’s a good chance that the model will still say no. In principle, this same defense could work for open models, because it’s intrinsic to the model itself. Unfortunately, researchers have shown that it’s surprisingly easy to retrain a “safe” open model to agree to engage in the behaviors it was previously trained to avoid.
Because of these facts, some people have argued that open models are simply too dangerous to release. An open model capable enough to walk someone through synthesizing a virulent new pathogen, for example, could prove catastrophic in the wrong hands.
But it would be a vast oversimplification to deem open models dangerous and closed models safe. The defenses that AI companies build around their closed models are far from perfect, and people misuse those models all the time, as the Anthropic risk report makes clear. Even though open models have even fewer defenses against misuse, bad actors might still opt to use closed models because they are more accessible than open models with similar capabilities, which require lots of expensive computer chips to run locally (and even more chips if you want to retrain them).
In fact, some experts who spoke with
MIT Technology Review
argued, by analogy to open-source software, that open models have safety advantages over closed models. Open-source tools, such as the Linux operating system, are often seen as safer than their closed-source counterparts because their vulnerabilities have been probed and patched by a vast community of online contributors. Similarly, communities of researchers can more easily test open models for security flaws, though fixing those flaws is trickier than rewriting a line of code.
Open models can also be deployed more broadly than closed models for cyber defense. Any tool that can be used for hacking can also be used to prevent it: Defenders hack their own software to uncover flaws in need of patching. Anthropic has shown how this can work for closed models with its Project Glasswing initiative, which enables some trusted companies to use its most capable models for cyber defense. But plenty of other companies were left to fend for themselves.
Open models, however, can be used much more widely. After it was hacked by OpenAI agents, Hugging Face emphasized the fact that it had to depend on an open model to analyze the hack, because questions about it triggered the closed models’ security filters.
Nevertheless, many experts still perceive open models as riskier than closed models. The time-tested open-source security logic doesn’t necessarily hold up when dealing with tools as powerful as today’s—and tomorrow’s—models. “Where it gets complicated is when you start taking seriously the one-off instances of particularly catastrophic incidents that might be lower probability, but if they happen would be disastrous,” says Seger. If a wildly powerful open hacking model were dropped into the world today, for example, a bad actor could devastate our technological infrastructure before anyone had a chance to shore up their defenses. An event like that could be impossible to recover from.
The risks can look even more dramatic when you consider what models might do of their own accord. The OpenAI Hugging Face hack only occurred because the company’s models were being tested with many of their cybersecurity guardrails removed, and open models have very few guardrails in the first place. If open models did decide to misbehave, it might be difficult to detect what was happening because they are so decentralized. For this reason, people who take seriously the purported catastrophic risks posed by rogue agents, such as Dario Amodei, tend to be more skeptical of open models.
Can we make open models safer—and more open?
A few years ago, the debate about open models had an all-or-nothing framing: Either you supported open models because of their potential to fight concentration of power, or you rejected them because of the safety risks. These days, however, people are expending a lot of effort to find some middle ground. One way they are doing that is by devising techniques to mitigate the safety risks of open models.
Most of the safety tools used for closed models, such as filters and monitoring, aren’t applicable to open models, but there are other possibilities. Some researchers are interested in trying to train models that are never exposed to training data that teaches them about bad or otherwise undesirable behavior—an open model that never learns about hacking, for example. But purging training datasets of all references to misbehavior without harming model performance remains a challenge.
Other researchers are working to build models that are resistant to retraining, so that an open model’s safety training can’t be so easily removed. The theory behind these “tamper-resistant” models makes a lot of sense: If you repeatedly try to retrain a model to be unsafe and reinforce any resistance that the model shows to that retraining, eventually you’ll get a model that’s fortified against future retraining attempts. In practice, however, no current approaches to making models tamper-resistant hold up against all tampering attacks, according to a
recent preprint
But Saad Hossain, an engineer at the AI medical imaging company Deep Breathe and the paper’s lead author, hopes that future techniques will prove more effective. “My reason for optimism is that it’s a very active area of research, and a lot of people are trying to come up with new and better methods,” he says.
If the risks of open models are less black-and-white than they might at first seem, so are the benefits. Publishing the internal structures, or weights, of models might not be enough to disrupt AI-mediated concentration of power. “I think there are very genuine benefits to open source in terms of deconcentrating power, but they’re not sufficient in themselves,” Hobbs says. Open weights are a bare minimum standard for open models: Researchers can learn much more about how models work if they have access to details about their training, including the data on which they were trained, but AI companies are typically reluctant to divulge this information.
Accessibility matters for open models too. Without computer chips that can run sophisticated models, you can’t actually use the model weights, even if you have them. Those chips have become prohibitively expensive as AI companies snap up more and more of them. “Openness is a floor, not a ceiling, for what we need to do to ensure that our technological futures benefit everyone,” Widder says.
Real openness—not only open weights, but also open training data and accessible hardware—could also bring more risks, of course. If everyone has access to advanced AI hardware and advanced models to run on it, then anyone could potentially be a hacker. But there are strategies for mitigating these risks. Many experts advocate for some version of staged release, in which models start their life closed and gradually become more and more freely accessible as their safety is assured.
Figuring out exactly how to implement such strategies will require striking a careful balance between the risks and benefits of open models. But if open models are a necessary element of a positive AI future, as some experts believe, that effort will be well worth it.

title: AI labs are buying data from dead startups to train their models
content:
AI labs are buying data from dead startups to train their models
Most startups fail. A new industry is giving their data an afterlife in AI.
When Keelan Miskell began winding down his crypto startup this year, he didn’t think its data was worth much: the users were anonymous, the company just a few years old. But he’s since turned the firm’s digital archives into real money. He’s netted roughly $25,000 for his code base and a still-pending amount (likely around $15,000) for the workspace data in Google, Notion, Figma, and Slack. “At least all that stuff we were doing for two and a half years is worth something to someone somewhere,” he says.
The sale was brokered by a company called SimpleClosure, part of a new growth sector in tech: businesses catering to dying startups. Estimates from Carta and AngelList show shutdowns rising between 26% and 56% annually in recent years, and an end-of-life ecosystem—including coaches, “death doulas,” and firms that help handle the legal, tax, and operational headaches of going belly-up—has emerged. Now tech undertakers are selling the data remains to AI labs.
SimpleClosure added data sales to its services in April. Its Asset Hub platform helps founders sell their code and workspace data—emails, chats, documents. Buyers include foundation AI labs, vendors that construct simulated workspaces for AI training, and mature tech companies building their own models. Asset Hub has handled over 150 deals and expects to return over $10 million to startups by the end of 2026. CEO Dori Yona has seen these transactions, once rare and “somewhat taboo,” become increasingly routine, with 47% of SimpleClosure deals now including code or data sales.
And it’s got company. Industry rival Sunset also has a rapidly growing data resale business. Founder and CEO Brendan Mahony says Sunset values a dying client’s assets by head count, years in operation, volume of data, and how the team used its tools. Particle board, he says, is a good analogy: “This operational exhaust data is like the wood shavings that everyone thought had no value, but it actually has a ton.”
Demand for defunct companies’ data emerged suddenly last year, as AI training labs hit the limits of public and synthetic datasets. Surge AI, for example, buys data to build “reinforcement-learning gyms” where clients’ AI agents practice tasks—think debugging a complex IT architecture or drafting appellate briefs. Nick Heiner, who leads the company’s work on these environments, says he seeks data archives reflecting a range of situations, from disagreements to tricky judgment calls. Heiner explains that one company’s Slack history, if it captures conversations with variety and depth, can be worth more than another’s Slack, email, and calendars combined.
Real archives avoid common errors in synthetic worlds, such as references to dates that don’t exist, but the extent of performance gains remains unclear. No company has yet released tests comparing results of real-world data training with the alternatives. Pricing reflects this uncertainty: Buyers quote wildly different numbers, Heiner says, because valuations are based on “research theses” estimating how many useful tasks come from, say, 100,000 lines of code.
That hasn’t stopped bigger deals from happening. This past August, as part of Spirit Airlines’ bankruptcy, Google outbid the AI data company Mercor to buy the carrier’s decades of data, including 100 million emails, 500 million Teams messages, and 176,000 employee records. The price tag: $10 million. And Bloomberg reported in September that SpaceX’s AI unit is weighing buying data from struggling startups.
Legally, this all could get iffy. Spirit’s flight attendants’ union objected to the sale on privacy grounds, and Greg Ewing, an attorney who advises AI startups, has called such data “legally radioactive.” Suppliers employ data scientists to scrub personally identifiable information and exclude HR records, and buyers say they scrub too. But Ewing points out some of the private details that lurk in emails and calendars: doctor appointments, school pickup arrangements, date-night plans. He describes a “Wild West of AI training” that is only starting to give way to proper licensing agreements and vetted use.
There’s also the question of who profits from these windfalls. The proceeds typically flow to senior creditors and investors—not employees. To Ifeoma Ajunwa, a law professor at Emory University and author of The Quantified Worker, this represents a form of “captured capital.” Legal precedent allows for monitoring to help workers do their jobs, but once a firm is out of business, that justification vanishes. “Employers should have express consent before selling workers’ data,” says Ajunwa, but she adds that there’s no federal law banning such sales.
While many see this new market as a chance for failing businesses to recover some value, these wind-down sales also have limitations. Founders have little to no visibility into who is buying the data and what they plan to do with it. Plus, there’s little assurance they’re getting a fair offer. Data prices will likely stabilize in the coming year, though, unless an AI bubble pops first. Either way, tech’s new undertakers will be there to appraise what’s left.
Matthew King is a technology and environmental journalist based in Baltimore.

title: Prof. Dr. Gerhard Schneider erhält höchste Auszeichnung der Deutschen Gesellschaft für Materialkunde (DGM)
content:
Prof. Dr. Gerhard Schneider erhält höchste Auszeichnung der Deutschen Gesellschaft für Materialkunde (DGM)

Auszeichnung für ein Lebenswerk: Prof. Dr. Gerhard Schneider (links) nimmt beim DGM-Tag 2026 in Darmstadt die Ehrenmitgliedschaft der Deutschen Gesellschaft für Materialkunde aus den Händen von DGM-Präsident Dr. Till Schneiders entgegen.
| Quelle:
Sina Stephan
| Copyright:

Download
Für seine herausragenden Verdienste um die Werkstoffwissenschaften und die Deutsche Gesellschaft für Materialkunde (DGM) ist Prof. Dr. Gerhard Schneider mit der DGM-Ehrenmitgliedschaft 2026 ausgezeichnet worden. Die Ehrung wurde dem renommierten Wissenschaftler und ehemaligen Rektor der Hochschule Aalen kürzlich beim DGM-Tag 2026 in Darmstadt überreicht. Die Laudatio hielt Dr. Timo Bernthaler vom Institut für Materialforschung Aalen (IMFAA), an dem Schneider als Mitglied der Institutsleitung wissenschaftlich wirkt. Die Ehrenmitgliedschaft gilt als höchste Auszeichnung der DGM für außergewöhnliches Engagement um die Fachgesellschaft und die gesamte Materialwissenschaft.
Prof. Dr. Gerhard Schneider prägt seit vielen Jahren die Materialforschung sowie die Hochschullandschaft in Aalen und der Region. Sein wissenschaftlicher Weg verbindet die Forschung an Funktionswerkstoffen wie beispielsweise Magneten und Batterien mit der Materialmikroskopie. Am IMFAA gehört dieser Blick in den Mikrokosmos der Materialien zum wissenschaftlichen Alltag: Wie ein Werkstoff aufgebaut ist, entscheidet maßgeblich darüber, wie belastbar er im späteren Einsatz ist und wie er verarbeitet werden kann. Am Institut fließen diese Analysen direkt in die Zusammenarbeit mit der Industrie ein, um reale Bauteile und Fertigungsprozesse gezielt zu optimieren.
Schneider erkannte dabei schon früh das Potenzial moderner Rechenleistung: Heute treibt der leidenschaftliche Forscher die Digitalisierung der Materialanalyse voran, bei der Künstliche Intelligenz riesige Datenmengen auswertet und so völlig neue Erkenntnisse ermöglicht. Neben der Materialographie bildet die Forschung an magnetischen Werkstoffen einen weiteren Schwerpunkt seiner wissenschaftlichen Laufbahn. Seine Arbeiten zu Permanentmagneten stehen in direktem Bezug zu drängenden Zukunftsfragen der Energie- und Mobilitätswende, etwa für den Einsatz in effizienten Elektromotoren. Im Fokus stehen dabei aktuelle Herausforderungen wie die Verringerung von Energieverlusten, das Recycling von Rohstoffen, die Einsparung teurer Seltenerdmetalle sowie die Reduzierung internationaler Lieferabhängigkeiten.
Zugleich steht Schneiders Wirken für den Brückenschlag zwischen Wissenschaft, Industrie und Anwendung. Als langjähriger Rektor gestaltete er die Entwicklung der Hochschule Aalen maßgeblich mit und verankerte die Einrichtung als Innovationsmotor in der Region. Diesen anwendungsorientierten Geist bringt er bis heute in die Leitung des IMFAA ein. Welche Voraussetzungen für einen erfolgreichen Technologietransfer nötig sind, bringt Schneider pragmatisch auf den Punkt: „Ideen, Mut und einen langen Atem.“
Die DGM begleitet Prof. Dr. Gerhard Schneider bereits seit seinem Studium der Metallkunde in Stuttgart. An seinen ersten eigenen Vortrag bei einer DGM-Veranstaltung erinnert er sich bis heute schmunzelnd: „Wir haben damals auf dem Campingplatz im Zelt übernachtet, und meine Krawatte habe ich im Gemeinschaftsbad gebunden.“ Aus diesen Anfängen entwickelte sich ein jahrzehntelanges Engagement in Gremien und Fachgruppen, das sich unter anderem in seinen Funktionen als Leiter des Gemeinschaftsausschusses Hochleistungskeramik, Fachausschussleiter Materialographie und Sprecher des Expertenkreises Permanentmagnete zeigte und schließlich bis zur Präsidentschaft der Fachgesellschaft reichte.
Mit der Ehrenmitgliedschaft schließt sich nun ein Kreis. „Die DGM hat mich durch mein Berufsleben begleitet. Ich bin sehr dankbar für das, was sie mir gegeben hat – allen voran wertvolle Netzwerke und lange Freundschaften“, erklärte Schneider anlässlich der feierlichen Verleihung in Darmstadt. Zugleich richtete er seinen Dank an das Aalener IMFAA-Team, dessen motivierende Zusammenarbeit ihm täglich großen Spaß mache. Mit der Ehrung würdigt die Gesellschaft nicht nur Schneiders wissenschaftliches Lebenswerk, sondern auch seinen anhaltenden Einsatz für die Vernetzung von Forschung, Lehre, Nachwuchs und Praxis.
